topics.name: Thales of Miletus
topics.scope: Everything is ultimately water (the first arche); the move of explaining nature WITHOUT gods; falling in the well while watching the stars; reportedly predicting a solar eclipse; cornering the olive presses to prove a philosopher COULD get rich if he cared to.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thales; IEP: Thales; Core Knowledge Sequence (Greek origins of philosophy)
topics.framing_note: WONDER-LED birth-of-reasoning topic, vivid T1 base. The real payoff is the MOVE: he asked 'what is everything MADE of?' and answered with nature, not a god-story. Lead with the named scene (the well, the eclipse, the olive presses). Answer = the vivid act or the single arche (water), never 'what year' or rote labels.

topics.name: Anaximander & Anaximenes
topics.scope: Anaximander: the first stuff is 'the boundless' (apeiron) — not water but a limitless something; an early guess that life crawled out of the sea and humans grew from fish-like creatures. Anaximenes: the arche is air, thickening into wind, cloud, water, stone, thinning into fire.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Anaximander; IEP: Anaximenes; Milesian school surveys
topics.framing_note: The other two Milesians continuing Thales' move: still hunting the one basic stuff, but smarter. 'The boundless' in plain words in the stem, never 'apeiron'. Memorable payoffs: the boundless can't run out (unlike water); Anaximenes makes everything ONE stuff at different densities (air squeezed = stone). Answer = the vivid idea, not the Greek term.

topics.name: Heraclitus & the Doctrine of Flux
topics.scope: 'You cannot step in the same river twice' — everything is in constant change; the world is an ever-living fire kindling and going out; the hidden logos (order/reason) running through it; strife and opposites as what holds the world together ('the road up and the road down are one'); the weeping philosopher.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Heraclitus; IEP: Heraclitus
topics.framing_note: Half of the marquee CONTESTED pair (is change real?) — present his side at full strength, no verdict; the Parmenides answer is the rival. The river line is a clean MOVE: follow why a river is never the same water. Lead with the vivid image (the river, the ever-living fire). Gloss 'logos' as hidden order in plain words.

topics.name: Parmenides & the One
topics.scope: Change and motion are an ILLUSION; what-is simply IS, eternal and unchanging; you cannot even think or speak of 'what is not'; so nothing can come from nothing or pass into nothing; the senses lie, only reason reaches truth; the poem framed as a goddess revealing the Way of Truth vs the Way of Opinion.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Parmenides; IEP: Parmenides
topics.framing_note: The other half of the change-is-real fork and the harder side — keep tier high. It sounds insane (nothing ever changes?) which is the hook; the distractors are Heraclitus' flux and the Milesian stuffs. CONTESTED: no verdict, choices are real rival positions. Answer = the reasoning move ('you can't have what-is-not'), not the term 'monism'.

topics.name: Zeno's Paradoxes of Motion
topics.scope: Arguments DEFENDING Parmenides that motion is impossible: Achilles can never catch the tortoise because he must first reach where it WAS, by which time it has moved on, forever; the flying arrow is motionless at every instant, so how does it move?; crossing a room means crossing infinitely many half-distances first.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zeno's Paradoxes; IEP: Zeno of Elea
topics.framing_note: Pure MOVE/scenario topics — the SCENE is the question, follow the logic. Achilles-and-the-tortoise is the marquee accessible rung (vivid, kid-graspable). Set it up as a genuine puzzle: choices are real attempted resolutions, not the label. T5 can probe the infinite-halves version. Answer = where the reasoning bites or breaks, never 'Zeno' or 'paradox'.

topics.name: Pythagoras & the Pythagoreans
topics.scope: 'All is number' — reality is built from mathematics; the secret brotherhood with its strange rules (don't eat beans, don't poke a fire with a knife); discovering that musical harmony is whole-number ratios on a string; the harmony of the spheres; belief in the soul's rebirth; the legend he forbade eating beans even to flee.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pythagoras; IEP: Pythagoras
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA goldmine and a vivid T1 anchor — the cult, the bean horror, music-as-numbers. Lead with the bizarre specific (the bean taboo, plucking a string to hear a ratio). The real MOVE is 'reality is hidden NUMBER' — the harmony discovery proves it. Keep the famous theorem secondary to the wonder. Answer = the vivid fact/rule, not a date.

topics.name: Democritus, Leucippus & the Atom
topics.scope: Everything is tiny uncuttable bits — atoms — moving in empty void; nothing exists but atoms and the void; the variety of the world is just atoms of different shapes hooking together; an astonishingly modern guess made by pure reasoning; Democritus the cheerful 'laughing philosopher' who laughed at human folly.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Leucippus; IEP: Democritus (Atomism)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. The hook is that they GUESSED the atom ~2,400 years early with no microscope, by argument alone (you can't cut matter forever). 'Atom' literally means 'uncuttable' — teach that. The laughing philosopher is the vivid handle. Answer = the idea (uncuttable bits in empty void) or the vivid trait, never the word 'atomism' as a label.

topics.name: Empedocles & the Four Roots
topics.scope: Everything is made of four 'roots' — earth, water, air, fire — mixed and separated by two cosmic forces, Love (which joins) and Strife (which splits); an early sketch of evolution by surviving combinations; the wonder-working healer who, by legend, leapt into the crater of Mount Etna to prove he was a god.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Empedocles; IEP: Empedocles
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE; the Etna leap is pure wonder (lead with it, label the legend AS legend — tradition says he jumped, one sandal supposedly thrown back up). The substance is the four elements + Love-and-Strife as mixing forces (the classical four elements start here). Answer = the four roots or the vivid leap, not a recitation. Drama-in-stem must still pay off in a real move/fact.

topics.name: Anaxagoras & Mind (Nous)
topics.scope: Everything contains a portion of everything; what sets the whirling cosmos in order is Nous — Mind; and the scandalous claim that the sun is not a god but a white-hot stone bigger than the Peloponnese, and the moon shines by reflected light — for which he was charged with impiety and forced to flee Athens.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Anaxagoras; IEP: Anaxagoras
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. The marquee scene: calling the sun a hot STONE, not a god — the daring move of demoting a god to physics, and getting prosecuted for it. Lead with that. 'Mind' (Nous) as the ordering force is the other rung — gloss it plainly. Answer = the vivid claim (sun = glowing rock) or 'Mind orders the cosmos', never the date of his trial.

topics.name: Socrates the Gadfly of Athens
topics.scope: Who Socrates was: the snub-nosed stonemason's son who wrote NOTHING; called himself a gadfly stinging the lazy horse of Athens; went barefoot, ignored money; everything we know comes from Plato and Xenophon
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead, the named subject carries the stem. Payoff = the vivid self-image (the gadfly stinging the sluggish city) and the strange fact he wrote nothing, so others recorded him. T1 base: he went barefoot and ignored wealth. Avoid 'name his teacher' trivia; the answer is the memorable gadfly move, not a date.

topics.name: The Socratic Method (Elenchus)
topics.scope: Questioning a confident expert step by step until his own answers contradict each other; he claims to teach nothing, only to deliver ideas like a midwife; the conversation ends in honest puzzlement (aporia)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates (the elenchus); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; AP/IB Philosophy
topics.framing_note: THE reasoning-move template for the whole bank. MOVE topic: the SCENE is someone sure he knows, cornered by his own answers. Payoff = the method itself (keep asking until the contradiction surfaces), not the word 'elenchus' (that goes to context). The midwife image is the vivid handle. Choices = real conversational moves, plainly worded.

topics.name: The Oracle at Delphi
topics.scope: His friend asks the Delphic oracle if anyone is wiser than Socrates; the answer is no; Socrates, baffled, sets out to disprove it by interviewing 'wise' men, and finds they only THINK they know, so his wisdom is knowing he does not know
topics.source: Plato, Apology; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates
topics.framing_note: STORY then MOVE. Lead with the riddle: the oracle calls Socrates wisest and he refuses to believe it. Payoff = the resolution he reaches (he is wiser only because he KNOWS he is ignorant while the others fake it). Vivid T1 hook: a man who hears he is the wisest and immediately tries to prove it wrong.

topics.name: The Trial of Socrates
topics.scope: Athens charges him with corrupting the youth and impiety (not believing in the city's gods); at 70 he refuses to grovel, half-jokes he deserves FREE MEALS as a reward, and is condemned by a jury of 500 citizens
topics.source: Plato, Apology; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Core Knowledge; AP/IB Philosophy
topics.framing_note: Emotional core, STORY/DRAMA. Lead with the named charges (corrupting the youth, impiety) and the courtroom. Payoff = the defiant move: instead of begging, he proposes he be REWARDED with free meals. Answer is the vivid act of defiance, never 'how many jurors'. The injustice is shown straight; no modern editorializing.

topics.name: The Death of Socrates
topics.scope: Friends arrange his escape from prison; he refuses (the Crito argument: he owes the laws obedience even now); he drinks the hemlock calmly, walks until his legs go numb, and his last words ask a friend to repay a debt of one rooster to Asclepius
topics.source: Plato, Crito and Phaedo; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: The bank's emotional peak, STORY/DRAMA. Marquee payoffs: he could have FLED but drank the hemlock; the eerie last words 'we owe a rooster to Asclepius.' The Crito refusal is a real MOVE (does a citizen owe the laws obedience even when wronged?) — a genuine fork, no verdict. Answer = the vivid choice or the famous line.

topics.name: The Examined Life
topics.scope: 'The unexamined life is not worth living' — said at his trial when offered exile if he would just stop questioning; he answers that a life without self-examination is not worth living, and chooses death over silence
topics.source: Plato, Apology; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. Set the scene: offered his life if he will just shut up, he refuses. Payoff = the reasoning behind the famous line (a life never questioned is not worth living to him), tied to the choice it cost him. Treat the maxim as a position to weigh, not a slogan to recite; choices are real life-stances in plain words.

topics.name: Socratic Irony
topics.scope: His trademark feigned ignorance: he plays the humble student begging to be taught, then his innocent questions expose that the 'expert' never understood his own claim — humility as a weapon
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates
topics.framing_note: MOVE gem, subtler so it skews high. The SCENE: a know-it-all flattered by a meek questioner who 'just wants to learn,' then trapped by his own answers. Payoff = recognizing the false modesty is the tactic, not real confusion. Keep it concrete (a boastful general, a smug merchant); the answer is the move, 'irony' lives in context.

topics.name: The Sophists
topics.scope: Traveling teachers who, for high fees, trained ambitious young Athenians to WIN arguments and sway crowds; their boast was 'making the weaker argument the stronger' — persuasion as a sellable skill, detached from truth
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Sophists; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras; AP/IB Philosophy
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, present as a REAL stance to reason against, not a villain gallery. Payoff = the recognizable practice (paid to make the weaker case sound stronger; winning over being right). Sets up the manipulation/rhetoric the fallacy ladder later names. Contrast with Socrates (who took no fee and chased truth). No sneering; show why the sell-a-winning-argument move is tempting.

topics.name: Protagoras: Man the Measure
topics.scope: 'Man is the measure of all things' — the wind that feels cold to me and warm to you really IS both; truth is relative to the perceiver, so there is no view from nowhere; the most famous relativist claim of the ancient world
topics.source: Plato, Theaetetus; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Sophists
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED MOVE — relativism as a serious position, no verdict. Put the claim in Protagoras's mouth (each person is the measure; one wind truly cold to me, warm to you). Choices = competing positions on whether truth is perceiver-relative; the key matches HIS reasoning. The self-refutation worry (is relativism itself only 'true for you'?) is the natural T5 fork.

topics.name: Gorgias the Rhetorician
topics.scope: The dazzling speech-master who claimed words have the power of a drug over the soul; his provocative three-step argument that nothing exists, and if it did we couldn't know it, and if we knew it we couldn't tell anyone
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Sophists; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gorgias; Plato, Gorgias
topics.framing_note: MOVE gem with wonder. Lead with the vivid image (speech as a drug that moves the soul). Payoff = his escalating argument (nothing exists; if it did we couldn't know it; if we knew we couldn't tell anyone) — a stunt showing what pure persuasion can 'prove.' Answer = the argument's chain; the contested 'nihilist' label lives in context.

topics.name: The Euthyphro Dilemma
topics.scope: Socrates corners a man rushing to prosecute his own father for piety's sake: is something holy BECAUSE the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is ALREADY holy? Either way, divine approval can't be what makes the good good
topics.source: Plato, Euthyphro; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Ethics; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates
topics.framing_note: Foundational MOVE that RECURS across religion + ethics; a live fork, no verdict. Vivid frame: a man so sure of piety he is suing his own father, undone by one question. Choices = the two horns, plainly worded (goodness defined by command vs. independent goodness the gods merely recognize). User is not Christian; symmetric voice. The dilemma stays OPEN.

topics.name: Plato and the Academy
topics.scope: The broad-shouldered wrestler ('Plato' was a nickname meaning broad) who survived Socrates' execution and founded the Academy in a grove outside Athens, the first lasting school; over its door, the legend that none ignorant of geometry should enter
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: STORY lead, the named subject carries the stem. T1 base: 'Plato' was a wrestler's nickname for his broad build. Payoff = he founded the first real school, the Academy, with geometry demanded at the door. Avoid 'what year' or 'which city' rote; the answer is the vivid founding image, not a date.

topics.name: The Allegory of the Cave
topics.scope: Prisoners chained since birth facing a wall, taking flickering shadows for reality; one is freed, dragged up a painful path into blinding sunlight, sees the real world, then returns to the dark and is mocked for saying the shadows are not real
topics.source: Plato, Republic VII (514a-520a); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato: The Republic; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology
topics.framing_note: Marquee thought-experiment; make the SCENE the question. T1 hook: people who have only ever seen shadows think the shadows are real. Payoff = the move (the freed prisoner learns appearance is not reality, and the truth-seer is mocked when he returns). The cave carries the tier, not the word 'allegory.' Choices are plain positions, not jargon.

topics.name: The Theory of Forms
topics.scope: Every real chair is a flawed copy of one perfect Chair you never see but somehow recognize; the changeless, perfect originals (the Forms) are more real than the changing things we touch; above them all sits the Form of the Good, like the sun that lets everything be seen
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; AP/IB Philosophy
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, appearance-vs-reality. Concrete handle: a perfect Chair no carpenter ever built, that every real chair imitates. Payoff = recognizing the move (the unchanging original is treated as more real than the copy). Gloss 'Form' plainly as the perfect original. The Form of the Good as the sun of the mind is the vivid T4-T5 rung; no verdict on whether Forms truly exist.

topics.name: The Ring of Gyges
topics.scope: A shepherd finds a ring that turns him invisible, and uses it to seize the kingdom; Glaucon's challenge: give the same ring to a good man and a bad man, and would anyone stay honest with NO chance of getting caught? Is justice only a fear of punishment?
topics.source: Plato, Republic II (359a-360d); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Ethics and Politics in the Republic; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato: The Republic
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED ethics fork, no verdict. Vivid T2 hook: a ring that makes you invisible, so no one could ever catch you. Put the challenge in Glaucon's mouth (everyone would turn unjust if they could get away with it) against Socrates' reply (the just soul is better off even unseen). Choices = real competing positions in plain words; the key matches the speaker's reasoning, never a label.

topics.name: Justice in the Republic
topics.scope: To see justice in one soul, Plato builds it large in a whole city: each part doing its own proper work and not meddling in another's; the just city mirrors the just person, and injustice is the parts at war with each other
topics.source: Plato, Republic IV; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Ethics and Politics in the Republic; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato: The Republic
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic. The handle: Plato studies justice in a whole city because it is 'written larger' there than in one person. Payoff = his answer (justice is each part doing its own job, not interfering with the others) and the city-soul mirror. Present as Plato's position to weigh, not the final word on justice; choices are real rival accounts of what makes a community just.

topics.name: The Philosopher-King
topics.scope: Plato's notorious claim that cities will never escape their troubles until philosophers become kings or kings turn philosopher; rulers trained for decades in truth, owning no property and no private family so nothing can corrupt their judgment
topics.source: Plato, Republic V-VII (473d); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Ethics and Politics in the Republic; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato: The Republic
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic with a genuine fork. Lead with the bold claim (no city is well-off until philosophers rule or rulers philosophize). Payoff = the reasoning (only one who knows the Good should hold power) AND its obvious danger (who guards the guardian? rule by the wise can become rule by the unaccountable). Present both sides straight, no verdict; choices are real positions on who should hold power.

topics.name: The Tripartite Soul and the Chariot
topics.scope: Plato splits the soul into three: reason, spirited honor-loving drive, and raw appetite; in the Phaedrus a charioteer (reason) struggles to steer two winged horses, one noble and obedient, one wild and unruly, toward the heavens
topics.source: Plato, Republic IV and Phaedrus (246a-254e); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
topics.framing_note: MOVE with a vivid image. Handle: a charioteer fighting to control one well-behaved horse and one wild one. Payoff = the inner conflict picture (reason should rule appetite and use spirit as its ally) and what each horse stands for. Keep the Greek part-names in context; the SCENE of the struggling chariot carries the tier. Justice in the soul = the three parts in their right order.

topics.name: The Ladder of Love (Symposium)
topics.scope: At a drinking party, the priestess Diotima teaches Socrates that love is a ladder: it starts at one beautiful body, then climbs to all beautiful bodies, to beautiful souls, to beautiful laws and ideas, and finally to Beauty itself, unchanging and pure
topics.source: Plato, Symposium (201d-212c); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE, higher tier. Vivid frame: a wise woman teaches that love is a STAIRCASE that should keep climbing. Payoff = the ascent (from one beautiful person upward to Beauty itself) as the move, not the dinner-party setting. Distractors are coherent rival ideas of what love is for. Keep it about the climb of desire toward something higher; the contested metaphysics stays unresolved.

topics.name: Recollection and the Slave Boy (Meno)
topics.scope: To prove learning is really remembering, Socrates takes an untaught slave boy and, asking only questions, leads him to a geometry truth he was never told; Plato's claim: the soul knew it before birth, and we recover knowledge we already had
topics.source: Plato, Meno (80d-86c); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic. Vivid frame: a boy who was never taught geometry works out a proof from questions alone. Payoff = Plato's startling conclusion (he must be REMEMBERING, not learning fresh, so the soul knew it before birth). Present recollection as Plato's position, with the rival reading (good questioning, not memory) as a real distractor; no verdict. 'Anamnesis' lives in context.

topics.name: Plato's Banishment of the Poets
topics.scope: In the ideal city Plato would expel most poets and storytellers; his charge: art is a copy of a copy (a painted bed imitates a real bed, which imitates the perfect Form), so it sits three steps from truth and stirs the passions reason should govern
topics.source: Plato, Republic X (595a-608b); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato's Aesthetics; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
topics.framing_note: MOVE gem, subtler so it skews high. The hook: Plato would BANISH the poets from his city. Payoff = his reasoning (art imitates the physical world, which already imitates the Forms, so it is a copy of a copy and inflames feeling over reason). Present as a real position to weigh against art's defenders; no verdict. The 'copy of a copy' image is the handle.

topics.name: The Myth of Er
topics.scope: The Republic ends with a soldier, Er, who dies, sees the afterlife, and returns to tell it: souls being judged, choosing their next lives from a heap of lots, then drinking from the river of Forgetfulness before rebirth; a myth Plato invented to teach that our choices echo beyond one life
topics.source: Plato, Republic X (614a-621d); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA gem, pure wonder, higher tier. Lead with the vivid scene: a slain soldier wakes on the funeral pyre and reports the afterlife. Payoff = the memorable image (souls CHOOSE their next life, then drink from the river of forgetting). Frame honestly as a myth Plato crafted to make a point about responsibility, not as doctrine; the user is not Christian, symmetric voice on afterlife stories.

topics.name: Atlantis as Plato's Invention
topics.scope: The sunken island-empire of Atlantis appears NOWHERE before Plato; he invented it in two late dialogues as a cautionary tale of a proud naval power that overreached and was swallowed by the sea in a day and a night, a foil for his ideal city
topics.source: Plato, Timaeus and Critias; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Plato; Encyclopaedia Britannica: Atlantis
topics.framing_note: STORY gem with a corrective payoff, accessible tier. The hook everyone has heard: the lost city of Atlantis. Payoff = the surprise (Plato MADE IT UP as a teaching fable; there is no older source) and its purpose (a warning about an arrogant power that overreached). Answer = that it is Plato's invented parable, not a real lost continent; avoid feeding the 'real Atlantis' myth.

topics.name: Aristotle & the Lyceum
topics.scope: The peripatetics who walked the colonnades while teaching; Plato's star pupil who broke with the Forms to study the actual world; the vast school that catalogued everything from constitutions to octopuses.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle; IEP: Aristotle (general)
topics.framing_note: STORY lead, vivid scene-setting base of the strand. The memorable payoff: he taught while WALKING (peripatetic = 'walking about') and studied real things — dissecting animals, collecting 158 city constitutions — instead of Plato's abstract Forms. Answer = the walking school or 'study the world, not just ideas,' never 'what year was it founded' rote. Tutoring Alexander allowed ONLY as 'it shaped how he thought,' not trivia.

topics.name: The Golden Mean
topics.scope: Virtue as the balance point between two vices — courage sits between cowardice (too little) and recklessness (too much); generosity between stinginess and wastefulness; the mean is relative to the person and situation.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics; Core Knowledge; Nicomachean Ethics Bk II
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE MOVE with everyday handles — every kid can grasp courage between cowardice and recklessness. Lead with the concrete scene (the knight who flees vs the knight who charges a dragon alone), choices are real positions. T4 twist: the mean is NOT a fixed midpoint — it's relative to the agent, and some acts (murder, spite) have no virtuous mean at all. Answer = the balance reasoning, never the term 'golden mean' as a label.

topics.name: Virtue Ethics & Eudaimonia
topics.scope: The good life is FLOURISHING (eudaimonia) — activity of the soul in line with virtue over a whole life, not fleeting pleasure or piled-up wealth; 'one swallow does not make a summer.' Ethics asks what KIND of person to be, not just which acts are right.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics; IEP: Aristotle: Ethics; Nicomachean Ethics Bk I
topics.framing_note: SPINE keystone — the third great ethics MOVE (virtue) alongside duty and consequences. Eudaimonia-vs-hedonism is a REAL fork: present pleasure-seeking as a serious rival position, no verdict imposed. The payoff move: flourishing is an ACTIVITY across a lifetime, not a feeling you can buy — 'one swallow does not make a summer.' Gloss eudaimonia as 'flourishing / the good life'; the scene carries the tier, not the Greek.

topics.name: Virtue as Habit
topics.scope: We become brave by doing brave acts, just as a builder learns by building; 'we are what we repeatedly do, so excellence is not an act but a habit.' Character is trained like a craft, through repetition, not born or merely understood.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics; Nicomachean Ethics Bk II
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic with a sticky everyday handle. The memorable payoff: virtue is a SKILL you build by practice — you become honest by doing honest things, the way a harpist learns by playing, not by knowing the theory. Lead with the apprentice/craft scene; the answer is 'character is trained by repeated action,' never the bare word 'habit.' Connects to the bank's character-formation spine; no verdict needed.

topics.name: The Four Causes
topics.scope: Four answers to 'why does this exist?' for a bronze statue: the bronze it's made of (material), the shape/design (formal), the sculptor who made it (efficient), and the purpose it serves (final). Full explanation needs all four.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Metaphysics; IEP: Aristotle: Metaphysics; Physics Bk II
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — a transferable thinking tool, not vocabulary. Anchor on ONE vivid object (the bronze statue, or a wooden table) and walk all four 'why' answers so the kid can apply it anywhere. The payoff at each rung is matching a 'why' to the right cause (the WOOD vs the CARPENTER vs what it's FOR). Gloss each cause in plain words; answer = the right kind of explanation, never the Latin labels.

topics.name: Telos & the Final Cause
topics.scope: Everything in nature aims at an END — the acorn 'aims' at the oak, the eye AT seeing; nature does nothing in vain. Aristotle's purpose-driven view of the world, later challenged when science dropped built-in purposes.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Biology; IEP: Aristotle: Metaphysics; Physics Bk II
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, CONTESTED in the long run. Lead with the vivid acorn-to-oak or 'what is an eye FOR' scene. Present teleology as a real, powerful position — then note (in context) that modern science questions whether nature has built-in purposes, so present the purpose-view and the no-purpose-view as a genuine fork, no verdict. The answer is the end/purpose reasoning ('the acorn aims at the oak'), never the word 'telos' as a label.

topics.name: The Syllogism & Valid Form
topics.scope: The first formal logic — 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal.' If the form is valid and the premises true, the conclusion MUST follow. Validity is about the SHAPE of the argument, not the topic.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Logic; IEP: Aristotle: Logic; Prior Analytics
topics.framing_note: FOUNDATION of the whole fallacy ladder — teach valid form so the later invalid look-alikes land. The marquee move: a conclusion 'follows' because of the SHAPE, not the subject (swap in dragons or merchants, the same form holds). T5 contrast: a true conclusion can come from a BAD argument, and a valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false. Answer = whether the inference actually follows, never the term 'syllogism.'

topics.name: The Function Argument
topics.scope: A good knife is one that cuts well; a good flute-player plays well — so what is a HUMAN for? Aristotle's answer: our distinctive function is reason, so the good human life is reasoning well. The 'ergon' argument grounding virtue ethics.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics; Nicomachean Ethics Bk I
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic with a clean concrete ladder. Lead with the everyday objects (a good knife cuts, a good eye sees) then turn the question on the kid: what is a PERSON good at that nothing else is? The payoff is the reasoning step — 'a good X does its special job well, and our special job is to reason.' CONTESTED edge: does a human even HAVE a fixed function? Present that doubt as a real position. Answer = the function reasoning, not a label.

topics.name: Practical Wisdom (Phronesis)
topics.scope: Knowing the right thing to do in THIS situation — the seasoned judgment book-rules can't capture. The wise person reads what a moment calls for; you can know the textbook and still lack it. Distinct from cleverness, which serves any end.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics; IEP: Phronesis; Nicomachean Ethics Bk VI
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, skews higher. The payoff: morality isn't a rulebook you apply mechanically — it takes JUDGMENT to see what a particular situation demands (the general who knows when to retreat vs press). T5 distinction: practical wisdom aims at GOOD ends, while mere cleverness can serve any end, even a wicked one. Lead with a real judgment-call scene; answer = the situated-judgment reasoning, gloss phronesis as 'practical wisdom.'

topics.name: The Three Kinds of Friendship
topics.scope: Friendships of utility (useful to each other), of pleasure (fun together), and of virtue (loving the other for who they are) — only the last is true and lasting; 'a friend is another self.' The first two dissolve when the use or fun runs out.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Ethics; IEP: Philia; Nicomachean Ethics Bks VIII-IX
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, accessible LOW-tier handle every kid recognizes. The payoff: there are three reasons people are friends — usefulness, fun, or genuinely valuing the person — and only the third survives when circumstances change. Lead with concrete cases (the friend who vanishes when you can't help them vs the lifelong one); 'a friend is another self' is the gem line. Answer = which KIND of friendship a scene shows, never a jargon label.

topics.name: Man the Political Animal
topics.scope: Humans are 'political animals' who can only fully flourish in a community (polis); one who needs no community is 'either a beast or a god.' We are made for shared life — language itself exists so we can argue about justice, not just signal like animals.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Political Theory; IEP: Aristotle: Politics; Politics Bk I
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic touching the political-philosophy spine. The memorable payoff: we are 'political animals' — we don't just live NEAR each other, we're built for shared life, and someone who needs no community at all is 'either a beast or a god.' The vivid hook: animals make NOISE, but humans have LANGUAGE precisely to debate right and wrong. Answer = the made-for-community reasoning, not the bare phrase. No modern-politics verdict; this is about human nature.

topics.name: The Unmoved Mover
topics.scope: Every motion is caused by something prior, but the chain can't go back forever — so there must be a first cause that moves everything else without itself moving, drawing the cosmos toward it like a beloved draws a lover. 'Thought thinking itself.'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Metaphysics; IEP: Aristotle: Metaphysics; Metaphysics Bk XII
topics.framing_note: STANDALONE prestige gem, skews high. The striking move: the first mover causes motion NOT by pushing but by being desired — it moves the heavens 'as the beloved moves the lover.' Feeds Aquinas' First Way later (note the lineage in context). Present as Aristotle's reasoning about why the causal chain needs a starting point; keep it about the ARGUMENT, no verdict on God's existence. 2-3 rungs only; answer = the 'first unmoved cause' reasoning, not a label.

topics.name: Catharsis & the Poetics
topics.scope: Why we ENJOY watching tragedy: it purges pity and fear (catharsis). Aristotle's anatomy of a great tragedy — the hero's reversal (peripeteia), the moment of recognition, and the fatal flaw (hamartia) that brings a good person down.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Aesthetics; IEP: Aristotle: Poetics; Poetics
topics.framing_note: STANDALONE wonder gem — the surprising puzzle: WHY do we pay to watch a hero destroyed and feel BETTER for it? Aristotle's answer: tragedy purges (catharsis) our pity and fear by letting us feel them safely. The vivid hooks: the reversal where fortune flips, the recognition scene, the noble hero's single fatal flaw (hamartia). Connects to the aesthetics strand's paradox-of-tragedy. Answer = the purging/flaw reasoning, gloss the Greek terms plainly.

topics.name: Zeno of Citium & the Founding of Stoicism
topics.scope: The merchant shipwrecked off Athens who lost his cargo, read about Socrates in a bookshop, and founded a school; teaching free to all on the painted porch (the Stoa Poikile) that gave Stoicism its name.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism; Diogenes Laertius, Lives VII; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
topics.framing_note: STORY-LED, vivid T1 base. The shipwreck is the hook: ruined merchant turns the worst day of his life into a philosophy. Answer = the named place (the painted porch / Stoa) or the vivid turn (losing everything led him to ask what's truly his to lose). The oracle told him to 'take on the color of dead men' — read old books. No -ism jargon at low tiers.

topics.name: The Dichotomy of Control
topics.scope: Some things are up to us (our judgments, choices, effort), some are not (the body, reputation, the past, other people); peace comes from working hard on the first and releasing the second. At T5, the subtle cases (is my reputation up to me? my health?).
topics.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus
topics.framing_note: THE marquee Stoic MOVE and the strand's keystone. A concrete scene (a knight frets the crowd will boo, or rain ruins the harvest) — choices are real responses, the answer is the move: pour effort into what's yours, accept the rest. Deepen across tiers into hard cases. This is a livable practice, not dusty doctrine. Plain language, no 'dichotomy' in the stem.

topics.name: Epictetus: From Slave to Sage
topics.scope: Born a slave, crippled when his master twisted his leg (he calmly warned it would break, then said 'I told you so'); freed, he taught that 'it is not things that disturb us, but our judgments about them'; the Enchiridion (handbook) written by his student Arrian.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Epictetus, Discourses (Arrian)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. The leg-breaking scene is the unforgettable hook — the slave is freer in his mind than his master is. Answer = the vivid act or his core move ('it's not the thing, it's your judgment of it'). His being a slave who out-freed emperors is the strand's emotional spine. No 'who wrote the Enchiridion' attribution-trivia; the human detail carries it.

topics.name: Marcus Aurelius & the Meditations
topics.scope: The most powerful man on Earth writing a private notebook to himself, in his tent on the war frontier, never meant for anyone to read; reminders to do his duty, accept death, and not be corrupted by the purple robe; 'the Meditations' is that notebook.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
topics.framing_note: STORY-LED, high wonder. The image is everything: an emperor with absolute power lecturing HIMSELF to stay humble and good, in a private diary. Answer = the vivid fact (it was never written for publication / written in a war camp) or the move (the powerful man checking his own ego). The philosopher-emperor is the marquee figure; lead with the scene, not 'who wrote the Meditations.'

topics.name: Seneca: The Tutor and His Calm Death
topics.scope: The Stoic who tutored the boy-emperor Nero, grew immensely rich, and was finally ordered by that same pupil to take his own life — which he did calmly, dictating to scribes to the end; the Letters on how to live; the gap between his wealth and his teaching.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism; Tacitus, Annals XV; Seneca, Letters to Lucilius
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE; darker, higher tier. The death scene is the payoff: Nero's own tutor, ordered to die by his pupil, facing it without panic. Answer = the vivid composure or his move (philosophy is rehearsal for adversity). Don't sanctify — his great wealth vs his teaching on simplicity is a real tension worth a fair rung, not a strawman. No verdict on whether he was a hypocrite; present the facts.

topics.name: Apatheia: Not Emotionless, but Unenslaved
topics.scope: Correcting the modern misread of 'stoic' = cold and feelingless; apatheia means freedom from being RULED by destructive passions (rage, terror, craving), not the absence of all feeling; the Stoic still loves, still acts, but is not jerked around by impulse.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism (section on passions / eupatheiai); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic that fixes a famous misunderstanding. The hook: 'stoic' in everyday speech means a robot with no feelings — that's wrong. Answer = the real distinction: not feeling nothing, but not being a slave to passion (you can grieve without being destroyed). Choices are real positions on what self-mastery means. This correction is itself the lesson; keep the Greek term in context only.

topics.name: Amor Fati: Loving Your Fate
topics.scope: Not just enduring what happens but WILLING it — loving your fate as if you'd chosen every part of it; Epictetus' image of the actor who plays well whatever role the playwright assigns (beggar or king); wishing things to be as they are.
topics.source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8 & 17; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations
topics.framing_note: A clean MOVE with a vivid handle. The actor image is the hook: you don't choose your part, only how well you play it. Answer = the move (don't demand events bend to your wish; align your wish to events) or Epictetus' line 'do not seek for things to happen as you wish, but wish for them as they happen.' Distinguish from passive resignation — it's an ACTIVE embrace. Latin term to context.

topics.name: Memento Mori & Premeditatio Malorum
topics.scope: Remembering death to live well (the slave whispering 'remember you will die' behind the triumphing general; 'you could leave life right now'); and rehearsing misfortune in advance — picturing loss before it comes — so disaster never ambushes you and gratitude sharpens.
topics.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations; Seneca, Letters 91 & 99; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
topics.framing_note: Two paired MOVES, vivid scenes available. Memento mori hook: the slave behind the Roman general murmuring 'remember you are mortal' at the height of glory. Premeditatio hook: imagining you've already lost what you love, so its return feels like a gift. Answer = the practice and its POINT (death-awareness fuels living; rehearsed loss disarms fear), not the Latin label. The 'kiss your child goodnight as if for the last time' image is real Stoic counsel.

topics.name: The View From Above
topics.scope: Marcus Aurelius' mental zoom-out: picture your troubles from high above — your city a dot, your worry one of countless lives across all of time — and the thing that felt enormous shrinks to its true size; cosmic perspective as a tool against pettiness and pride.
topics.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII & IX; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic, more reflective, higher tier. The hook is the zoom-out itself: rise above the map until your huge problem is a speck. Answer = the move and what it does (rescales worry and ego against the vastness of time and the world), not a definition. Keep it concrete — a specific grievance shrinking — rather than abstract cosmology. Pairs with memento mori as perspective practices.

topics.name: The Obstacle Is the Way
topics.scope: Marcus Aurelius' idea that 'the impediment to action advances action; what stands in the way becomes the way' — a blocked path is itself the material for virtue; adversity is the training ground, not merely something to survive.
topics.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic with an everyday handle. The hook: what blocks you (an unfair setback, a difficult person) is exactly what lets you practice patience, courage, ingenuity. Answer = the reframe (the obstacle becomes the path / the raw material for character), not the slogan as a label. Choices are real responses to hardship (curse it, flee it, or use it). Keep it from sliding into toxic positivity — it's about agency, not denial.

topics.name: Cato the Younger: Dying Free
topics.scope: The incorruptible Roman senator and Stoic who opposed Caesar's rise; after defeat, he chose to die by his own hand rather than live under one-man rule or accept Caesar's pardon — refusing to owe his life to a tyrant; the Stoic model of integrity over survival.
topics.source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism
topics.framing_note: STORY-LED, higher tier, real moral weight. The hook: he would not let Caesar 'forgive' him, because accepting the pardon would grant Caesar the right to grant it. Answer = the reason for the refusal (some things matter more than staying alive; his liberty was his to keep) or the vivid act. Handle the death soberly — it's the ancient exemplar of integrity, presented straight, not glamorized.

topics.name: Living According to Nature & the Cosmopolis
topics.scope: The Stoic slogan 'live according to nature' = live by REASON, the part that makes us human; and the cosmopolis — since all people share reason, every person is a fellow citizen of one world-city, so the wise are 'citizens of the world,' not just of their tribe.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism; Marcus Aurelius, Meditations
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic, more conceptual, higher tier. 'Live according to nature' is easily misread as 'go wild / be primal' — the real meaning is the opposite: live by reason. Answer = that correction, plus the cosmopolis move (shared reason makes a stranger a fellow citizen). Present the world-citizen idea on its own terms as the Stoics meant it; gloss the terms in plain language, don't lecture in jargon.

topics.name: Virtue Is the Only Good
topics.scope: The hard core of Stoic ethics: only virtue (wisdom, justice, courage, self-control) is truly GOOD; health, wealth, and reputation are 'preferred indifferents' — nice to have, fine to pursue, but not what makes a life good or bad; the sage is happy even on the rack.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism (the indifferents); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism; Cicero, De Finibus III
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic, the strand's most demanding claim, top tier. The hook: a Stoic would rather be a good person in chains than a wicked one in a palace. Answer = the distinction (virtue is the only real good; everything else is 'preferred but indifferent'), presented as a genuine, defensible position to reason about — choices are rival views of what makes a life go well. Don't caricature it as not caring about anything; it's a ranking, not indifference to all.

topics.name: Diogenes of Sinope
topics.scope: The marquee Cynic: living in a giant clay wine-jar; carrying a lit lamp in daylight 'looking for an honest man'; telling Alexander the Great 'stand out of my sunlight'; eating and sleeping in public to show how little a good life needs.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Diogenes the Cynic; Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI; IEP: Cynics
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA goldmine, pure wonder. Lead with the vivid scene; the answer is the POINT of the stunt, not its name. The jar, the lamp, and the Alexander line teach 'virtue needs almost nothing' and 'a free man fears no king.' Keep the sunlight retort as the payoff. Names allowed; no jargon.

topics.name: Diogenes' Defacing of Convention
topics.scope: The deliberate-provocation side of Cynicism: plucking a chicken to mock Plato's 'man is a featherless biped'; 'defacing the currency' (he literally did, then made it his life's mission to deface false social custom); doing private acts in the marketplace to expose convention as arbitrary.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Diogenes the Cynic; Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI
topics.framing_note: MOVE strand with shock-value hooks. The plucked chicken is a vivid refutation by counterexample (Plato's tidy definition fails). 'Deface the currency' doubles as the Cynic mission — reject counterfeit values. Handle the shameless public acts at grade-10 level: the PHILOSOPHICAL point (convention is not nature) is the answer, kept respectful of the idea under the antics.

topics.name: Antisthenes & the Birth of Cynicism
topics.scope: The founder: a student of Socrates who took the master's toughness to the extreme; virtue is enough for happiness and can be taught by deeds; 'I would rather go mad than feel pleasure'; the simple cloak and staff that became the Cynic uniform.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Antisthenes; IEP: Cynics; Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI
topics.framing_note: Traces Cynicism back to Socrates — the lineage IS the move (self-sufficiency taken to its limit). The answer is the core claim: virtue alone suffices, external goods are dispensable. Present 'virtue is enough' as a real, demanding position to reason about, not a slogan. The cloak/staff/wallet detail is a concrete vivid handle.

topics.name: Crates & Hipparchia
topics.scope: Crates of Thebes gave away a fortune to live as a beggar-philosopher and was beloved as a peacemaker who walked into homes to settle quarrels; Hipparchia, a noblewoman, refused every wealthy suitor to marry him and live the Cynic life publicly as an equal — one of the first Western women to live openly as a philosopher.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Cynics; IEP: Hipparchia; Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA with a strong human payoff. Crates renouncing wealth and being welcomed as 'the door-opener' is vivid; Hipparchia choosing the beggar over rich suitors and debating men at a symposium is the marquee gem. The answer is the memorable act/choice. Present Hipparchia on her own terms — a real philosopher's life, not a curiosity; no anachronistic framing.

topics.name: The Cynic Idea: Live According to Nature
topics.scope: What unites the stunts: shamelessness (anaideia) as honesty about what's natural; self-sufficiency (autarkeia); 'I am a citizen of the world' (Diogenes coining 'cosmopolitan'); freedom through wanting almost nothing; the training (askesis) that hardens you against fortune.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Cynics; IEP: Cynics
topics.framing_note: The MOVE behind the antics — make this the synthesis rung. Lead with a concrete scene (Diogenes content with a cup, then throwing it away after seeing a boy drink from his hands). The answer is the reasoning: fewer wants = more freedom; 'citizen of the world' is the cosmopolitan move. Gloss Greek terms plainly. Connects forward to Stoicism (Zeno learned from Crates) in context.

topics.name: Epicurus & the Garden
topics.scope: Epicurus founded a school in a garden outside Athens where women and slaves studied as equals; he taught that pleasure is the highest good — but redefined: the steady pleasure of a calm mind and body, not indulgence; friendship as one of life's greatest goods; 'live unnoticed.'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; IEP: Epicurus; Diogenes Laertius, Lives X
topics.framing_note: STORY + MOVE keystone. CORRECT the popular misreading head-on: 'epicurean' = foodie is wrong; Epicurus prized simple bread, water, friends, and freedom from fear. The Garden admitting women and slaves is a vivid, memorable fact. The answer is the redefined pleasure (tranquility), not the modern caricature. Lead with the welcoming Garden scene at T1.

topics.name: Ataraxia & the Limits of Desire
topics.scope: Tranquility (ataraxia) as the goal; the Epicurean sorting of desires — natural and necessary (food, shelter, friends), natural but unnecessary (luxury), and empty/vain (fame, endless wealth); why chasing the empty desires makes you miserable; pleasure has a ceiling — once pain is removed, more cannot improve it.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus; Principal Doctrines
topics.framing_note: MOVE strand — clean reasoning to follow. The desire-sorting is a genuinely useful life tool: which wants are worth chasing? The answer is the category/reasoning (an empty desire has no natural limit, so it never satisfies), not a label. Lead with a concrete scene (a king who has everything and is still anxious vs a friend sharing bread). Keep terms glossed; the move carries the tier.

topics.name: Death Is Nothing to Us
topics.scope: Epicurus' famous argument against the fear of death: 'where death is, I am not; where I am, death is not' — so death is never actually experienced by anyone, and a thing you can never experience cannot harm you; the symmetry argument (you don't fear the eternity BEFORE your birth, so why fear the eternity after?).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus; Lucretius, De Rerum Natura III
topics.framing_note: A clean MOVE topic — follow the argument step by step. The answer is the logical move (death is never present TO a subject, so it can't be a harm to that subject), and at higher tiers the standard objection (deprivation: it robs you of future goods). CONTESTED enough at T5 to present the objection as a real reply, no verdict; but the core argument's STRUCTURE is the teachable thing. Lucretius' symmetry is the vivid handle.

topics.name: The Tetrapharmakos: The Four-Part Cure
topics.scope: The pocket-sized Epicurean remedy for anxiety, preserved on a Herculaneum scroll: don't fear the gods (they don't meddle with us), don't fear death (it's nothing to us), the good is easy to get (simple needs), the terrible is easy to endure (real pain is brief or bearable).
topics.source: Philodemus (Herculaneum Papyrus 1005); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; IEP: Epicurus
topics.framing_note: A compact 'four-medicine' summary — a few gem questions. The answer is the SUBSTANCE of each cure (e.g. 'the good is easy to get' because natural needs are few), not the Greek name. The image of a four-drug salve repurposed as soul-medicine is the memorable hook. Each line previews a deeper Epicurean move, so cross-reference the death-cure to the 'death is nothing' ladder in context.

topics.name: Lucretius & the Swerve
topics.scope: The Roman poet Lucretius put Epicurus' physics into the epic 'On the Nature of Things': everything is atoms and void; the soul is atoms too, so it dies with the body (nothing to fear after death); the 'swerve' (clinamen) — atoms veer unpredictably, leaving room for free will in a world of falling particles.
topics.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius; IEP: Lucretius
topics.framing_note: MOVE with a wonder hook — atomism long before microscopes. The answer is the reasoning: if the soul is material it can't survive the body, so fear of an afterlife is groundless; the swerve is a clever move to save free will from strict determinism (pairs with the free-will strand — cross-ref in context). Note the manuscript's dramatic 1417 rediscovery as a vivid aside, not as trivia to recall.

topics.name: Confucius / Kongzi & the Analects
topics.scope: The wandering teacher who never won the office he sought; taught the Way for a fallen age; the Analects were his sayings written down by students after his death.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: SPINE keystone, equal plane with the Greeks. STORY/DRAMA lead: the teacher exiled and ignored by the rulers he advised, yet his pupils preserved every word. Payoff = the vivid fact (he never wrote a book; the Analects are remembered sayings; he aimed to restore a broken order), never 'when was he born' rote.

topics.name: Ren (Humaneness)
topics.scope: Ren as the supreme virtue — humaneness, the feeling-with and acting-for other people that makes someone fully human.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius
topics.framing_note: MOVE taught through concrete relationship scenes, not foreign vocabulary. Ren = treating people as people; the cultivated person carries it everywhere. Answer = what humaneness DOES in a scene (lifting up others, not asking 'what is ren'). Present seriously on its own terms, the equal of any Greek virtue.

topics.name: Li (Ritual Propriety)
topics.scope: Li as doing things the right way — the bows, manners, ceremonies and customs that shape a rough person into a good one.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius
topics.framing_note: MOVE, scene-led: li is the form that makes feeling real (a clumsy thank-you vs a sincere one done well). Confucius' claim is that practicing the right forms cultivates virtue from the outside in. Answer = the point of the ritual, never the term. No 'empty etiquette' strawman — li shapes character.

topics.name: The Confucian Golden Rule (Negative Form)
topics.scope: Shu / reciprocity: 'Do not impose on others what you do not desire for yourself' — the rule stated as a restraint, not a command.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: MOVE with a sharp hook: it is the Golden Rule in NEGATIVE form (don't do harm, vs the Western 'do unto others'). The contrast is the lesson — restraint over imposition. Vivid scene of someone about to wrong another; answer = the reciprocity move. Note the parallel to Jesus' version in context, no verdict on which is better.

topics.name: Filial Piety (Xiao)
topics.scope: Xiao: honoring parents, elders and ancestors as the ROOT from which all other virtue grows; loyalty learned first at home.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT (partiality is just): family bonds are the seedbed of virtue, the GIVER's duty rooted in relationship — fits the bank's partiality stance naturally, no warp. Scene-led (a child caring for an aging parent). Answer = the claim that virtue starts at home, not the Chinese term. Present at full strength, no caricature.

topics.name: The Junzi (The Cultivated Person)
topics.scope: The junzi / 'gentleman' vs the petty person (xiaoren) — nobility of CHARACTER earned by self-cultivation, open to anyone, not nobility of birth.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius
topics.framing_note: MOVE via contrast scenes: the junzi seeks what is right, the petty person seeks gain; the junzi blames himself, the petty person blames others. The radical move = Confucius redefined nobility from BLOODLINE to CULTIVATED CHARACTER, open to all. Answer = the distinguishing trait in a scene, never the term as a label.

topics.name: The Rectification of Names
topics.scope: Zhengming: 'Let the ruler be a ruler, the father a father, the son a son' — disorder comes when words and reality drift apart; fix the names, fix the world.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; IEP: Confucius
topics.framing_note: MOVE, higher-tier: when a 'father' won't father or a 'ruler' won't rule, the title is a lie and society cracks; setting words right sets duties right. Vivid fork (a king who keeps the name but abandons the role). Answer = the reasoning (names carry obligations), not the label. A clean precision-of-language move kids can reuse.

topics.name: The Five Relationships & Social Harmony
topics.scope: The five bonds (ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger sibling, friend-friend) — each with reciprocal duties; harmony when each side keeps its part.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius; Core Knowledge; AP World History
topics.framing_note: MOVE, relationship-scene led. The key insight = the duties run BOTH ways (the ruler owes care, not just the subject obedience), so it isn't mere submission. Answer = the reciprocal obligation in a concrete bond. Present on its own terms; touch the order-and-hierarchy theme straight, no modern sneer and no endorsement-as-verdict.

topics.name: Mencius: Human Nature Is Good
topics.scope: Mencius' proof that we are born good: ANYONE seeing a child about to fall into a well feels a flash of alarm — the 'sprout' of compassion we all share; virtue is growing the sprouts.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mencius; IEP: Mencius
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED fork (pairs with Xunzi) — present as a REAL position at full strength, NO verdict. The child-at-the-well is a marquee vivid MOVE: the instant pang proves the goodness is already IN us. Answer = the logic of the sprout argument or the well image, not 'Mencius said so.' His optimism about human nature is the half of the debate that must stand on its own.

topics.name: Xunzi: Human Nature Is Crooked
topics.scope: Xunzi's rival claim: people are born selfish and crooked, like warped wood that must be steamed and bent straight; goodness is a hard-won ACHIEVEMENT of teaching, ritual and effort.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Xunzi; IEP: Xunzi
topics.framing_note: The other half of the CONTESTED fork — steel-manned, NO verdict, never the 'pessimist villain.' The crooked-wood / warped-board image is the vivid MOVE: left alone we go bad, so culture and effort MAKE us good. Answer = the reasoning (goodness is made, not born) or the bent-wood image. Set squarely against Mencius as a live, unsettled question.

topics.name: The Mandate of Heaven
topics.scope: Tianming: a ruler holds power only while he serves the people justly; misrule, famine and revolt are signs Heaven has WITHDRAWN the mandate — the right to overthrow a tyrant.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mencius; Core Knowledge; AP World History
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE, high wonder. The striking move = legitimacy is CONDITIONAL on serving the people, so a tyrant forfeits his throne (Mencius defends overthrow). Vivid scene of a dynasty falling as the sign of lost mandate. Answer = the conditional-legitimacy principle or the vivid omen, not 'what is the Mandate.' A real proto-accountability idea, presented straight.

topics.name: Laozi & the Dao De Jing
topics.scope: the archive-keeper who rode west and was asked to write down his wisdom before leaving through the gate; the Dao De Jing as the founding text; 'the Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao'; the sage who leads least; soft overcomes hard; uncertain whether one man or a legend
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Laozi; IEP: Laozi (Lao-tzu); Core Knowledge: World Religions
topics.framing_note: STORY-led keystone, on its own terms beside the Greeks (no 'mystical East'). Lead T1-T2 with the vivid scene: the old archivist riding west, stopped at the pass, asked to leave a book. Payoff = the named text or the paradox ('the Way you can name isn't the real one'). T4 = soft-conquers-hard. No jargon in the stem.

topics.name: Wu Wei (Effortless Action)
topics.scope: non-forcing / acting WITH the grain of things, not against; water that wears down rock yet yields to a hand; the ruler who governs by NOT meddling; doing by not-doing; NOT laziness but the absence of strain and forcing
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Daoism; IEP: Daoist Philosophy; SEP: Laozi (wu wei)
topics.framing_note: Marquee MOVE topic via the vivid water image (soft, yielding, yet it carves canyons). The move: stop forcing; succeed by going with the grain. Correct the misread that wu wei = doing nothing / being lazy — it's effortless RIGHT action. Scene-led (a gardener, a river, a meddling vs hands-off ruler); answer = the principle, not the term.

topics.name: The Dao (the Way)
topics.scope: the nameless source and pattern that runs through everything and can't be pinned down in words; naming it loses it; the uncarved block (pu) — natural simplicity before we shape and label it; living in accord with the Way
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Daoism; IEP: Daoist Philosophy
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic on the limits of language. The handle: some things shrink when you slap a label on them (try defining 'a game' or 'love'). The uncarved block = natural wholeness before we carve it into named pieces. No metaphysical verdict; present as the Daoist position among rivals. Gloss every term in plain English.

topics.name: Zhuangzi's Butterfly Dream
topics.scope: Zhuang Zhou dreams he is a butterfly, flitting happily, knowing nothing of being a man; he wakes — and now cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamt a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he is a man; the transformation of things; how do you know which state is the 'real' one?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zhuangzi; IEP: Zhuangzi (Chuang-Tzu)
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED skepticism MOVE, scene-led, NO verdict (pairs with Descartes' dream argument + Brain-in-a-Vat — note the lineage in context). The vivid scene IS the question: which side of the dream is real, and how could you ever check from inside? Choices are real positions on knowing-you're-awake. Keep the wonder; don't resolve it.

topics.name: Cook Ding & the Ox
topics.scope: the butcher whose blade has stayed sharp 19 years because he never hacks bone — he slips through the natural gaps in the joints, the knife gliding where there is space; skill so deep it becomes effortless; mastery as flowing WITH the grain rather than muscling through
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zhuangzi; IEP: Zhuangzi (Chuang-Tzu)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE — the blade that never dulls because the cook finds the gaps. It shows wu wei in action: the master succeeds by following the natural structure, not by forcing. Lead with the image (sharp after 19 years); answer = WHY (he slips through the spaces, never hits bone). A concrete bridge from wu wei to real expertise.

topics.name: The Useless Tree
topics.scope: the giant gnarled tree the carpenter passes by — too twisted for timber, too knotty for tools, so no one ever cut it down; its very 'uselessness' let it grow huge and ancient; questioning whether being prized and useful is always the good fate
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zhuangzi; IEP: Zhuangzi (Chuang-Tzu)
topics.framing_note: Mini-gem MOVE that flips a common assumption: the useless tree SURVIVES precisely because no one wanted it. Scene-led (the carpenter walking past the worthless giant). The move: 'useful' by the world's measure can be a trap; what looks worthless may be free. Light, witty Zhuangzi voice; no verdict, just the inversion. Pairs with the Daoist suspicion of striving.

topics.name: The Happiness of Fish
topics.scope: Zhuangzi on the bridge: 'see how happy the fish are!'; his friend Huizi: 'you are not a fish — how do you know they're happy?'; Zhuangzi: 'you are not me — how do you know that I don't know?'; the playful debate over whether we can ever know another mind's experience
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zhuangzi; IEP: Zhuangzi (Chuang-Tzu)
topics.framing_note: Mini-gem MOVE on the problem of other minds, told as the witty bridge exchange (Zhuangzi vs the logician Huizi). The scene carries it: can you ever truly know what another creature feels? Choices are real positions (Huizi's strict skepticism vs Zhuangzi's reply). No verdict; link to Nagel's bat in context. Keep it playful.

topics.name: Mohism & Mozi (Impartial Care)
topics.scope: Mozi against Confucius: love should be IMPARTIAL — care for the stranger's family as for your own, weigh every person equally; judge customs by what actually benefits people, not by tradition; condemnation of offensive war and of wasteful, ruinously expensive funerals and music
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mohism; IEP: Mohism
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT preview: the impartial-care-vs-graded-care fork PREVIEWS the modern partiality debate (Singer's impartialism vs Williams; partiality-is-just is the bank's line) — but frame on its OWN Warring-States terms here, no modern verdict. Present BOTH at full strength: Mozi (every life counts the same) vs Confucius (love rightly runs deepest for your own family). The move, scene-led, not the label.

topics.name: Legalism & Han Feizi
topics.scope: Han Feizi's cold realism: people act from self-interest, not virtue, so a state must run on clear LAW, strict rewards and punishments, and the ruler's hidden power — never on the hope that leaders will be good; the doctrine that armed the Qin unification (and its own author's death in a Qin prison)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Legalism in Chinese Philosophy; IEP: Han Fei
topics.framing_note: The cynical-about-human-nature FOIL to Confucius and Mozi, presented STRAIGHT and steel-manned (not a cartoon tyrant). The move: if you can't trust people to be good, design rules and incentives that work even with selfish people (echo Hobbes/public-choice in context, no verdict). Han Feizi dying in a Qin cell is the dramatic hook. Plain language.

topics.name: The Buddha & the Four Sights
topics.scope: Prince Siddhartha Gautama leaves the palace after seeing old age, sickness, death, and a wandering ascetic; the Great Renunciation; enlightenment under the Bodhi tree; the Middle Way between palace luxury and self-starvation
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Buddha; Core Knowledge; AP World Unit 1
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead, serious on its own terms (NO 'mystical East' tone). Sheltered prince meets the four sights one by one and walks away from a kingdom; answer = the vivid sight or the Middle Way move (neither indulgence nor starvation), never 'what year' or 'which city' rote. The vivid T1-T2 base of the strand.

topics.name: The Four Noble Truths & the Eightfold Path
topics.scope: Life contains suffering (dukkha); suffering arises from craving/clinging; craving can cease; the Eightfold Path is the way out (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Buddha; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddhism
topics.framing_note: The Buddha's core diagnosis as a clean MOVE: the cause of suffering is craving, not the world itself. Frame like a physician's diagnosis-prescription (problem, cause, cure, treatment). Answer = the specific truth or the craving-causes-suffering insight, not a memorized list count. Gloss dukkha in plain language ('unsatisfactoriness').

topics.name: Anatta & the Chariot (No-Self)
topics.scope: The monk Nagasena tells King Milinda that 'Nagasena' is only a name; a chariot is nothing over and above its wheels, axle, frame and pole; so the self is just the bundle of its parts, with no fixed soul underneath
topics.source: Milindapanha (King Milinda's Questions), the chariot simile; SEP: The Buddha (anatta / non-self)
topics.framing_note: Marquee CONTESTED identity MOVE that pairs with Ship of Theseus and Parfit. The chariot argument is clean — follow the logic: take away the parts and no extra 'chariot' remains. Put the claim in Nagasena's mouth; choices are competing views of the self (soul, body, memory, bundle), no verdict. Answer = the reasoning move, not the term.

topics.name: Impermanence, Karma, Samsara & Nirvana
topics.scope: Everything is impermanent (anicca); dependent origination — things arise from conditions; karma and the wheel of rebirth (samsara); moksha/nirvana as release — the candle flame going out, not a place
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddhism; Core Knowledge: World Religions
topics.framing_note: Serious, on its own terms — karma as cause-and-effect of action, NOT a Western 'cosmic scoreboard' cartoon. Nirvana is the EXTINGUISHING of craving (the flame blown out), not a heaven. Answer = the specific concept's vivid handle (the going-out flame, the wheel of rebirth, conditions giving rise to things), not a vocabulary match. Gloss all Sanskrit/Pali terms.

topics.name: Nagarjuna & Emptiness
topics.scope: Nagarjuna's Middle Way (Madhyamaka): all things are 'empty' (sunyata) of fixed independent essence because everything exists only in dependence on other things; neither truly existent nor truly non-existent
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nagarjuna; IEP: Nagarjuna
topics.framing_note: The strand's hardest, most technical MOVE — keep tier high and lean. Emptiness = NOT nothingness; it means nothing has a self-contained essence; a thing is only what it is in relation to everything else. Give a concrete handle (a 'whole' chariot vs its parts; a 'long' stick only long next to a short one). Choices are rival metaphysical positions, no verdict.

topics.name: The Upanishads: Atman is Brahman
topics.scope: The Upanishads' great teaching: your deepest self (Atman) is identical to the ground of all being (Brahman); 'tat tvam asi' — 'thou art that'; the One behind the many appearances
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Brahman; IEP: Indian Philosophy (Vedanta); Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: Covered SERIOUSLY as a real metaphysics, equal plane with the Greeks (it even shaped Schopenhauer). The marquee MOVE is the identity claim 'thou art that' — your innermost self is the same reality underlying everything. Present as a position among rivals (vs the bundle-self, vs many separate souls), no verdict. Answer = the unity claim itself ('thou art that'), gloss Atman/Brahman plainly.

topics.name: Shankara & the Rope Mistaken for a Snake
topics.scope: Shankara's Advaita (non-dualism): in dim light you see a snake where there is only a rope; likewise the everyday world of many separate things is superimposed on the one Brahman through ignorance; knowledge dissolves the illusion
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sankara; IEP: Advaita Vedanta
topics.framing_note: Pure vivid MOVE: the rope-snake error is a perfect concrete hook — you weren't seeing a real snake, just misreading the rope, and knowledge (light) ends the fear instantly. The move = appearance vs reality (pairs with Plato's Cave). Present non-dualism as a serious position, no verdict; answer = the rope-snake recognition (it was never there), not the term 'adhyasa'.

topics.name: Jainism, Ahimsa & the Blind Men and the Elephant
topics.scope: Jain radical non-violence (ahimsa) toward all living things; many-sidedness (anekantavada): the blind men each touch one part of an elephant — rope, fan, pillar, wall — and each is partly right; truth has many sides
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jainism; Core Knowledge: World Religions
topics.framing_note: Vivid T1-T2 base. The blind men & the elephant is a marquee perspectivism MOVE — each man honestly reports what he touched and each is partial; the answer is that everyone has a piece, no one the whole. Ahimsa via concrete scenes (the monk sweeping the path so as not to crush an insect). Answer = the partial-truth recognition / the non-harm principle, never a date or a sect-name. No exoticizing.

topics.name: The Bhagavad Gita: Arjuna's Dilemma
topics.scope: On the battlefield Arjuna freezes — to fight his duty means killing his own cousins, teachers and kin; Krishna counsels acting from duty (dharma) without attachment to the fruits of action — duty versus compassion
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Indian Ethics; Core Knowledge; The Bhagavad Gita
topics.framing_note: STORY-led, a genuine duty-vs-compassion FORK — present as contested, no verdict; choices are real positions (do your duty / refuse to kill kin / act without attachment to outcome). The vivid scene is the warrior laying down his bow at the moment of battle. Answer = the move (act from duty, detached from the fruits) or Arjuna's vivid crisis, not 'who is Krishna' trivia.

topics.name: Mohandas Gandhi & Satyagraha
topics.scope: Gandhi turns ancient ahimsa into a political method — satyagraha, 'truth-force' / nonviolent resistance; refusing to cooperate with injustice without striking back; the Salt March; suffering injustice rather than inflicting it
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mohandas Gandhi; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: Mini gems anchoring the strand to a name kids already half-know, and showing ancient ahimsa cashed out in action. The MOVE = nonviolent resistance: you neither obey the unjust law nor hit back — you accept the penalty openly. Answer = the vivid act (the Salt March; refusing to fight back) or the truth-force idea, not biography-dates. Method neutral, no hagiography.

topics.name: The Six Orthodox Schools (Darshanas)
topics.scope: A map of classical Indian philosophy as a real, rigorous tradition of debating schools — including Nyaya (logic and the rules of valid reasoning) and Samkhya (a dualism of consciousness and matter) — not a single 'Eastern mysticism'
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Indian Philosophy; SEP: Epistemology in Classical Indian Philosophy
topics.framing_note: Mini, corrective gems: India had FORMAL LOGIC and structured schools that argued for centuries (Nyaya literally means 'logic'/'method') — counters the 'no real reasoning, just mysticism' stereotype. Keep it as 1-3 recognition rungs (e.g. which school = the logicians). Answer = the school's actual move (rules of valid inference; consciousness distinct from matter), not rote Sanskrit-list recall. Serious, on its own terms.

topics.name: The House of Wisdom & the Translation Movement
topics.scope: Baghdad's Bayt al-Hikma; Muslim scholars translating + extending Greek philosophy (Aristotle, Galen, Euclid) while Europe lost it; the knowledge later flowing back to the Latin West
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Islamic Philosophy; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Arabic and Islamic Philosophy of Language and Logic
topics.framing_note: Straight intellectual history, NO 'clash of civilizations' framing. The MOVE: ideas are preserved and sharpened by whoever argues with them, not owned by a tribe. Vivid T1 payoff = Aristotle survived in Arabic and came BACK to Europe through translation. Answer = the named act of preserving/translating reason, never 'what year' or 'which caliph' rote.

topics.name: Avicenna's Floating Man
topics.scope: Ibn Sina's thought experiment: a man created fully formed, floating in the void, blindfolded, touching nothing, sensing nothing — yet still certain that he himself exists; the self known without the body
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Sina's Metaphysics; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Avicenna (Ibn Sina)
topics.framing_note: Marquee self/consciousness MOVE — make the floating-in-the-void SCENE the question, the payoff = he still knows HE exists with no senses.
