Follow the logic (does this show the self isn't just the body?). Note in CONTEXT it anticipates Descartes' 'I think therefore I am' by 600 years. Choices = real positions on mind/body, no verdict; gloss any term.

topics.name: Avicenna on Necessary vs Contingent Being
topics.scope: Ibn Sina's essence/existence distinction; everything we meet COULD have not existed (contingent) and needs a cause; only a Necessary Being exists by its own nature and stops the chain of borrowed existence
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Sina's Metaphysics; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Avicenna
topics.framing_note: A clean reasoning MOVE that previews Aquinas' cosmological argument (note the lineage in context). Concrete handle: a unicorn's whole 'whatness' is clear even though none exist — so existence is something ADDED. Follow the argument from borrowed-to-self-standing existence; choices = competing positions, no verdict on God. Keep 'essence/existence' glossed in plain words.

topics.name: Al-Ghazali's Crisis of Doubt
topics.scope: The greatest scholar of his age abandoning his Baghdad chair, struck mute by doubt; the Deliverance from Error; concluding that demonstrative reason has limits and direct mystical knowledge of God is its own path
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: al-Ghazali; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: al-Ghazali
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead — the famous man at the height of fame walking away because he can no longer trust his own certainty (a real skeptical episode, like Descartes' doubt). The MOVE: how far can proof reach? Present 'reason has limits, the mystic knows directly' as a serious position, not a retreat. Theology-overlap stays even-handed; no smug-believer/atheist voice. Answer = the vivid act or the move, not a date.

topics.name: Al-Ghazali on Causation: the Fire and the Cotton
topics.scope: Occasionalism — al-Ghazali's claim that fire does not really burn cotton; God burns it directly, and the constant pairing only LOOKS like causation; a challenge to the necessity of cause and effect
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: al-Ghazali; Wikipedia: Occasionalism
topics.framing_note: A vivid causal-philosophy MOVE — the SCENE (touch flame to cotton; what REALLY does the burning?) carries the rung. Striking parallel to Hume: we never SEE the necessity, only the constant pairing (cross-reference in context). Follow the argument; choices = real rival views of cause (genuine power vs mere habit vs divine act), no verdict. Answer = the reasoning, never the word 'occasionalism'.

topics.name: Averroes & the Defense of Reason
topics.scope: Ibn Rushd answering al-Ghazali with The Incoherence of the Incoherence; the great commentator on Aristotle; faith and philosophy as two honest paths to one truth; deny causation and science/law collapse
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE: the rebuttal whose very title throws the insult back ('the incoherence of The Incoherence'). The MOVE: two roads, one truth — reasoning and revelation needn't war. His Aristotle commentaries lit up Latin Europe (note in context). Present the reason-defending position at full strength against al-Ghazali; it's a real fork, no verdict. Answer = the move or the named work-as-reply, not trivia.

topics.name: The Mu'tazila vs the Ash'ari
topics.scope: The great Islamic theological fork: can reason ALONE tell good from evil and is God BOUND by justice (Mu'tazila), or is good simply whatever God commands and justice is His will (Ash'ari)?
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mu'tazila; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Arabic and Islamic Philosophical Theology (Kalam)
topics.framing_note: The Euthyphro dilemma in Islamic dress — a CONTESTED reason-vs-revelation fork (cross-reference Euthyphro in context). Put each side in a character's mouth: one says burning the innocent would be wrong even if commanded; the other says good just IS what God wills. Both serious positions at full strength, NO verdict. Choices = the competing reasonings, plain language, never the school NAMES as the answer.

topics.name: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah & the Cycle of Empires
topics.scope: The Muqaddimah; asabiyyah / group solidarity as the fuel of power; hardy desert tribes conquering soft cities, then their grandchildren going soft — why no dynasty outlasts about three generations; the first social science
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Khaldun; Wikipedia: Asabiyyah; Wikipedia: Muqaddimah
topics.framing_note: A striking proto-social-science MOVE — he looks for the LAWS behind history's rise-and-rot, not just the story. Vivid handle: tough outsiders bound by loyalty take over, comfort dissolves the bond, the third generation loses it. Lead with the cycle as a pattern to recognize. Answer = the named force (group solidarity / the three-generation cycle), not 'what century'. Straight history, no exoticizing.

topics.name: Maimonides & the Guide for the Perplexed
topics.scope: The rabbi-physician reconciling the Torah with Aristotle for those torn between faith and reason; negative theology — we can only say what God is NOT (not a body, not weak, not many), never capture what He IS in words
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Maimonides; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Moses Maimonides
topics.framing_note: Jewish tradition covered SERIOUSLY on its own terms, equal plane. The marquee MOVE = negative theology: language about God only works by DENIAL, so 'God is good' means 'God lacks no good' — a real, careful position (parallels Aquinas and Avicenna, note in context). The reconciling-faith-and-reason project mirrors Averroes for a different scripture. Choices = competing positions, no verdict; answer = the move, never 'who wrote the Guide'.

topics.name: Augustine of Hippo: the restless youth & the garden conversion
topics.scope: The wild young Augustine ('make me chaste, but not yet'); the stolen pears taken just for the thrill of doing wrong; the breakdown in the Milan garden and the child's voice 'take up and read' (tolle lege) that turned his life; the long road from pleasure-seeker to bishop.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Augustine; Augustine, Confessions Books II & VIII; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead. Answer = the vivid memorable thing: the 'not yet' prayer, the pears stolen for the thrill alone, the garden voice 'take up and read.' The pear theft is a real moral puzzle (why love wrong for its own sake?) not just a tale. No smug-believer or smug-atheist voice. Avoid date/place trivia.

topics.name: The Confessions as the first autobiography
topics.scope: Why the Confessions is counted the first true autobiography in the West: a book addressed to God that confesses a whole inner life of doubt, lust, and turning; the new move of examining one's OWN soul on the page rather than recounting deeds.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Augustine; IEP: Augustine; Augustine, Confessions
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. The memorable point is the INVENTION: a book that turns the examining gaze inward (the unexamined-life move from Socrates, now in first person). Answer = 'the first inward self-examination written as a life,' not 'in what year' or 'how many books.' Keep it about the new kind of writing, not biography trivia.

topics.name: Augustine on the puzzle of time
topics.scope: Confessions XI: if the past is already gone and the future not yet here, where does time actually EXIST? 'What then is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it, I do not.' Augustine's move: time is measured in the MIND — memory, attention, expectation — not out in the world.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Augustine (on time); Augustine, Confessions Book XI; IEP: Augustine
topics.framing_note: Marquee MOVE. Set the SCENE as the puzzle (past gone, future not yet, present a knife-edge); choices are rival positions on where time lives. Augustine's mind-answer is one position among rivals (vs time as a real outer river), CONTESTED — no verdict. Lead with the 'if no one asks me, I know' line; it's the hook. Plain language.

topics.name: Evil as privation (the absence of good)
topics.scope: Augustine's answer to how a wholly good creator can allow evil: evil is not a THING with its own existence but a LACK, a corruption of good — like blindness is missing sight or a hole is missing wood. Whatever exists, insofar as it exists, is good; strip all good and the thing ceases to be.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Augustine; IEP: Augustine; Augustine, Confessions & Enchiridion (privatio boni)
topics.framing_note: Clean MOVE feeding the philosophy-of-religion strand. Concrete handles carry it (blindness = no sight; rust = corroded iron; a hole = missing wood). Answer = the privation move itself ('evil is a lack/corruption of good, not its own substance'), not the term 'privatio boni' (context). Present the position as contested; the metaphysics is the lesson, no piety.

topics.name: Free will & the origin of evil
topics.scope: If God made everything and God is good, where did evil come from? Augustine's reply (On Free Choice of the Will): evil enters through the MISUSE of free will, not from God; a will that freely turns from greater goods to lesser ones is the source. The free-will defense: genuine freedom is worth the risk of its abuse.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Augustine; IEP: Augustine; Augustine, De libero arbitrio (On Free Choice of the Will)
topics.framing_note: MOVE feeding the problem-of-evil ladder. Answer = the free-will defense ('evil comes from creatures misusing free choice, so the blame is theirs not the maker's'). Present it with its real pressure point (could a good maker not have made free beings who never fall?) — CONTESTED, no verdict. Pairs with philosophy-of-religion; note the link in context.

topics.name: The City of God vs the City of Man
topics.scope: Written as Rome was sacked and pagans blamed the Christians: Augustine's two-cities picture — an earthly city built on self-love and an eternal city built on love of the good — running tangled together through all of history, sorted only at the end. A philosophy of history born from catastrophe.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Augustine; IEP: Augustine; Augustine, The City of God (De Civitate Dei)
topics.framing_note: STORY hook (Rome falling, the blame, the answer) + MOVE (two competing loves shaping two cities, mingled until the end). Answer = the two-cities contrast (self-love vs love of the good), not 'what year Rome fell.' Frame as Augustine's reading of history, a position not a verdict. No triumphalism.

topics.name: Boethius & the Consolation of Philosophy
topics.scope: The Roman statesman Boethius, jailed and awaiting execution, writes a dialogue in which Lady Philosophy visits his cell to console him; her great image is Fortune's WHEEL, forever turning, raising men up only to cast them down — so never trust the goods Fortune lends. The bridge from the ancient world to the medieval.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius; IEP: Boethius; Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA — pure wonder. Lead with the death-cell scene and the named image: Lady Philosophy and the Wheel of Fortune turning. Answer = the vivid figure (the Wheel; never trust Fortune's borrowed gifts) or the move that true happiness can't rest on what luck can snatch back. Scene-led, symmetric voice, no date trivia.

topics.name: Boethius on foreknowledge & free will
topics.scope: Boethius's hard puzzle: if God already KNOWS today what you'll choose tomorrow, is your choice still free? His move — God does not see in TIME at all but holds past, present, and future in one eternal NOW; he knows your free act the way you watch someone act in the present, without forcing it.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius; IEP: Boethius; Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy Book V
topics.framing_note: Hardest MOVE in the strand (T4-T5). Set the dilemma clean (known-in-advance vs freely-chosen); choices are real rival resolutions. Boethius's eternal-present answer is one position among rivals, CONTESTED — no verdict. Pairs with Augustine on time AND the free-will strand; cross-link in context. Plain language: 'God sees all time at once,' no scholastic jargon.

topics.name: Thomas Aquinas, the Dumb Ox
topics.scope: The silent giant classmates mocked as the 'dumb ox'; his teacher Albert's reply that this ox's bellow would fill the world; the colossal Summa Theologica; the late mystical vision after which he called all his writing 'mere straw' and wrote no more.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas; IEP: Thomas Aquinas
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead and the strand's vivid T1 base. Answer = the memorable specific: the 'dumb ox' nickname, the bellow-fills-the-world line, the vision that made him call his life's work straw. No 'how many articles in the Summa' rote. Theology-overlap: present on its own terms within the game's framework, no smug-believer voice.

topics.name: Aquinas's Five Ways
topics.scope: Five arguments for God: the unmoved mover (motion needs a first mover), the first cause (causes can't go back forever), the contingent and the necessary (not everything can be a maybe-thing), degrees of perfection, and the governance of things toward ends.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas (Five Ways); Wikipedia: Five Ways (Aquinas)
topics.framing_note: MOVE topics, not name-recall. Follow each argument's logic, then present its classic objection (the universe might just BE the brute fact; an infinite chain might not need a first link). This is supremely contested — NO verdict on whether God exists; choices are competing reasoning moves. The cosmological move recurs in the philosophy-of-religion strand.

topics.name: Anselm's Ontological Argument
topics.scope: God = that than which nothing greater can be conceived; a being that exists in reality is greater than one existing only in the mind; so the greatest conceivable being must exist; 'faith seeking understanding.' Gaunilo's reply: the same move 'proves' a perfect lost island, which is absurd.
topics.source: IEP: Anselm: Ontological Argument; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ontological Arguments
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — the strangest argument in philosophy (proving existence from a definition). Make the SCENE the puzzle, then set Gaunilo's perfect-island reply as the live counter: the defender must show why God isn't an island. CONTESTED — no verdict; choices are real positions. Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' objection lives in the religion strand; cross-reference in context.

topics.name: Natural Law
topics.scope: A real moral law built into human nature and knowable by reason, not just decreed — the first principle 'do good and avoid evil'; humans are wired to pursue real goods (life, knowledge, community); an unjust law is a kind of failed law.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Natural Law Tradition in Ethics; Aquinas, Summa Theologica I-II
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic with concrete handles (reason can read right from wrong in our nature, not just obey commands). Frame as a real position kids can reason about, paired against its rival (morality is whatever is commanded, or whatever a society agrees). CONTESTED meta-ethics — present natural law at its strongest without declaring it the verdict; the move is 'is morality discovered or decreed?'

topics.name: Faith and Reason: Aristotle Baptized
topics.scope: Aquinas's grand synthesis — recovering Aristotle through the Muslim and Jewish commentators and fusing him with Christian thought; reason and faith as two non-warring roads to truth; 'grace perfects nature, it does not destroy it.'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas; IEP: Aquinas: Metaphysics
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — the recognition is the SYNTHESIS move (two sources of truth that don't have to fight), against the rival that says faith and reason are enemies. Note the lineage in context: he builds on Averroes and Maimonides (the Eastern/Jewish strand). No 'who tutored whom' trivia; the payoff is the harmonizing idea. Framework-respectful, symmetric voice.

topics.name: The Problem of Universals
topics.scope: Does 'redness' or 'humanity' really exist out there, or are there only particular red things and individual humans, with the general word just a label we attach? The realism / nominalism / moderate-realism fork.
topics.source: Wikipedia: Problem of universals; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Medieval Problem of Universals
topics.framing_note: Abstract MOVE topic — keep ONE concrete handle ('is RED a real thing, or just a word for many red things?'). CONTESTED — no verdict; choices are the genuine positions (universals are real / only in the mind / real but only in the things). This is the dispute the next two topics' thinkers fought over; set it up here as the live question, persons answer it later.

topics.name: Ockham's Razor
topics.scope: William of Ockham's rule — don't multiply entities beyond necessity; prefer the explanation that assumes the fewest things; his nominalism (only individuals exist, universals are just names). The razor as a thinking tool the kid reuses everywhere.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham; Wikipedia: Occamism
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic with a low, vivid T1 base — the razor is a tool kids carry into every other strand, so TEACH IT USED RIGHTLY (the simplest ADEQUATE explanation, not just the simplest; not a bludgeon against any view you dislike). Concrete scenes (two explanations for a noise — which assumes less?). Distractors = real misuses of the razor. Ties to the reasoning-virtues strand.

topics.name: Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor
topics.scope: The Franciscan 'subtle doctor' who answered Ockham's nominalism — universals ARE real in things; his signature move of haecceity / 'thisness,' the unique principle that makes each individual the very one it is and no other.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Duns Scotus; Wikipedia: Scotistic realism
topics.framing_note: Standalone gems at the strand's hard end. The marquee move = 'thisness' (what makes THIS person uniquely this individual, beyond all their shared qualities). The realist counterweight to Ockham — present as the live other side of the universals fork, no verdict. Keep the one handle concrete; gloss 'haecceity' plainly as 'thisness.' Minor figure, 2-3 rungs.

topics.name: Abelard and Heloise
topics.scope: The brilliant, arrogant logician who sharpened the scholastic method (Sic et Non — set the authorities AGAINST each other and reason it out); the tragic, forbidden love with his student Heloise; the catastrophe that ended it; their famous surviving letters.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Peter Abelard; IEP: Peter Abelard
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA hook for the strand — lead with the human story (the dazzling teacher, the doomed love, the letters), answer = the vivid specific. The philosophical payoff is his METHOD move (Sic et Non — line up clashing authorities and reason through, the engine of scholasticism). Tell the tragedy with weight, not titillation; the move, not the gossip, is the lesson.

topics.name: The Problem of Evil
topics.scope: Epicurus' old trilemma: if God is all-good AND all-powerful, why does suffering exist? The logical vs the evidential form; gratuitous suffering as the sharpest version.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Problem of Evil; IEP: The Evidential Problem of Evil
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL no-verdict: supremely contested, NEVER adjudicate whether God exists. MOVE topic — follow Epicurus' fork (able but not willing? willing but not able?). The marquee accessible scene: a child's pointless suffering. Choices are real replies (free-will defense, soul-making, denial of premises), not the believer-wins or atheist-wins label.

topics.name: Theodicy: The Free-Will & Soul-Making Defenses
topics.scope: The standard replies to evil: free will requires the possibility of choosing wrong (Plantinga's defense); Hick's soul-making (a hard world grows souls); the logical-possibility move vs the it's-actually-likely move.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Problem of Evil (Plantinga's Free Will Defense); IEP: John Hick, soul-making theodicy
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, no-verdict. These are the strongest REPLIES to evil — present each at full strength, then its objection (free will doesn't cover earthquakes; soul-making vs the suffering of animals/infants). The answer is which reasoning move a position makes, not whether the reply 'works.' Pairs with The Problem of Evil as its rejoinder.

topics.name: The Euthyphro Dilemma Applied
topics.scope: Is an act good because God commands it, or does God command it because it's good? Divine command theory vs an independent standard; the 'then God's will is arbitrary' horn vs the 'then goodness is above God' horn.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Religion and Morality; Plato's Euthyphro
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE no-verdict fork that recurs from Socrates through Islamic Mu'tazila-vs-Ash'ari. MOVE topic: set up the live two-horned dilemma, choices are the two real positions plus the 'split the horns' move. Symmetric voice — no smug-believer, no smug-atheist. The answer matches the position stated, never 'religion is wrong.' Cross-reference Socrates strand in context.

topics.name: The Cosmological Argument
topics.scope: Everything that exists has a cause; there cannot be an infinite regress of causes; so there must be a first / uncaused cause. The contingency version; the kalam version (the universe began, so it had a cause); the 'who caused God?' rejoinder.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Cosmological Argument; IEP: The Cosmological Argument
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, no-verdict. Follow the argument step by step, then the classic objection (why must the regress stop? why is the first cause exempt from needing a cause?). Choices are reasoning moves a smart person weighs, not 'God exists / doesn't.' Lower-tier base: the 'something can't come from nothing' intuition. Cross-references Aquinas' Five Ways.

topics.name: The Design Argument (Paley's Watch)
topics.scope: Paley: find a watch on the heath, its intricate fitted parts imply a watchmaker — so the eye, the world, implies a designer. The fine-tuning update; the move from order to designer.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Teleological Arguments for God's Existence; William Paley, Natural Theology (1802)
topics.framing_note: MOST accessible existence-of-God MOVE — Paley's watch is a vivid T1-T2 scene (a watch can't assemble by chance). Follow the analogy: complex order suggests a designer. No-verdict; choices are real positions. Set it up so Hume's reply (next topic) lands. The answer is the inference's structure, not whether God made the eye.

topics.name: Hume's Reply to Design
topics.scope: Hume's Dialogues: the universe is not much LIKE a watch (it's more like a vegetable or animal); a flawed world might suggest a flawed or junior designer; many hands, or none; the Epicurean hypothesis (random atoms, given infinite time, settle into order).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hume on Religion; David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779)
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — a transferable skeptical lesson about weak analogies. Philo's needling of Cleanthes: how good must the analogy be to carry the conclusion? No-verdict; this is the counter-move to Paley, not a proof of atheism (Hume left it ambiguous). The answer is the specific weakness Hume exposes in the analogy, not 'design fails.'

topics.name: The Ontological Argument & Its Critics
topics.scope: Anselm: God = that than which nothing greater can be conceived; a God existing in reality is greater than one existing only in the mind — so God must exist. Gaunilo's perfect island parody; Kant: existence is not a predicate (it adds nothing to the concept).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ontological Arguments; IEP: Anselm's Ontological Argument
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, the trickiest one — keep concrete. Follow Anselm's a-priori leap, then both classic objections (Gaunilo: this would prove a perfect island; Kant: existing isn't a property like being red). No-verdict; choices are the argument and its rebuttals. The answer is the move each critic makes, not a verdict on God. Cross-reference Anselm in Aquinas strand.

topics.name: Pascal's Wager
topics.scope: Reason can't settle whether God exists, so treat it as a bet: believe and you risk little but gain infinitely; disbelieve and you risk infinite loss. The decision-matrix move; objections: the many-gods problem, and can you choose to believe on command?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pascal's Wager; IEP: Pascal's Wager about God
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE accessible MOVE — the first real decision-theory argument (it's about betting under uncertainty, NOT about evidence). No-verdict. Follow the payoff matrix, then the killer objections: WHICH god do you bet on? Can belief even be willed? The answer is the structure of the wager or the specific objection, not 'you should believe.' A clean reasoning-under-uncertainty lesson.

topics.name: Hume on Miracles
topics.scope: Hume's 'Of Miracles': a miracle is a violation of a law of nature, supported by all past experience; a report of one is supported only by fallible witnesses — so it is ALWAYS more likely the witness erred or lied than that the law broke. The balancing-of-evidence move.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Miracles; David Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X (1748)
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — a superbly transferable lesson about weighing testimony against prior probability (the kid will reuse it on tabloid claims). No-verdict on whether miracles happen; the lesson is HOW to weigh the evidence. Present the standard reply too (Hume rigs it; cumulative testimony can be strong). The answer is the balancing principle, not 'miracles are fake.'

topics.name: The Hiddenness of God
topics.scope: Schellenberg's puzzle: if a loving God wanted a relationship with us, why are there sincere people who, through no fault of their own, can't find reason to believe? Non-resistant nonbelief as evidence against such a God; the replies (free response, soul-making, divine reasons we can't see).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Hiddenness of God (J.L. Schellenberg); IEP: The Hiddenness Argument
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, harder/T4-T5, no-verdict. A modern cousin of the problem of evil: the argument turns on the GAP between a loving God and honest nonbelief. Present Schellenberg's reasoning AND the serious replies at full strength. Symmetric voice. The answer is the specific inferential step or reply, not whether God is hiding. Keep it accessible despite the high tier.

topics.name: William James & the Will to Believe
topics.scope: James: for a 'live, forced, momentous' choice that evidence can't settle, we have the right to believe on our passional nature; religious experience as data (Varieties of Religious Experience); the pragmatist test — does the belief work in a life?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William James; William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896) and The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902)
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — James answers the evidentialist (Clifford: 'it is wrong always to believe on insufficient evidence'). Set up the live fork: when evidence is silent and you must choose, who's right — Clifford or James? No-verdict; both as real positions. The answer is the move (forced/momentous option, or the demand for evidence), not a piety verdict. Pairs with the next topic.

topics.name: Faith vs Evidence: Kierkegaard's Leap
topics.scope: Kierkegaard: real faith is a passionate commitment BEYOND what reason can demonstrate — the leap, not a conclusion; objective uncertainty held with subjective certainty. Versus evidentialism (Clifford / Locke): proportion belief to the evidence, full stop. Fideism vs evidentialism as the fork.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Søren Kierkegaard; SEP: Faith; W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877)
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, the strand's capstone fork. Kierkegaard's leap vs Clifford's evidentialism — present BOTH at full strength, no-verdict, symmetric voice (the user is not Christian; the bank teaches neither faith nor doubt as correct). The answer is which reasoning move a position makes about belief and evidence. Cross-reference Kierkegaard in the Existentialism strand; keep this one focused on the epistemology of faith.

topics.name: Bacon's Four Idols of the Mind
topics.scope: The four ways thought goes wrong (Novum Organum): Idols of the Tribe (human nature distorts), the Cave (your own quirks/upbringing), the Marketplace (words mislead us), the Theatre (inherited dogma we never tested).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Francis Bacon; IEP: Francis Bacon (Novum Organum, Book I)
topics.framing_note: MOVE-led critical-thinking toolkit that pairs with the fallacy ladder. Each Idol is a way the mind fools itself; the answer is the SPECIFIC trap (words bewitching reason at the Marketplace; untested systems as stage-plays at the Theatre), never the Latin label. Vivid handle per Idol. Celebrate as a real diagnostic kids reuse.

topics.name: 'Knowledge is Power' & the Experimental Method
topics.scope: Bacon's break with Aristotle's armchair: test nature, don't just reason about it; build knowledge from many particular observations (induction); the famous claim that understanding nature gives us command over it.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Francis Bacon; Core Knowledge / AP European History: the Scientific Revolution
topics.framing_note: The engine of modernity, celebrated as a real achievement. MOVE: the shift from deducing how things SHOULD behave to GOING AND CHECKING. Answer = the method's core (gather evidence, test, generalize cautiously) vs the old appeal to authority. 'Knowledge is power' means understanding yields mastery — present straight, not cynically.

topics.name: Galileo: Authority vs. Observation
topics.scope: The telescope's moons of Jupiter and Venus's phases backing Copernicus; the 1633 trial and forced recantation; the legend that he muttered 'and yet it moves'; the real clash of received authority against what the eye can verify.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Galileo Galilei; IEP: Galileo; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead, told STRAIGHT — no cartoon church-vs-science. The real story is messier (politics, ego, a friendly pope turned foe). Answer = the vivid move (what the telescope SHOWED, the recantation under threat, 'and yet it moves' as legend labeled as legend). The deep move: a claim's truth doesn't bow to authority — observation can overturn the experts.

topics.name: The Copernican Revolution & Cosmic Humility
topics.scope: The Earth dethroned from the center of the cosmos; the unsettling demotion of humanity from the middle of everything; how a simpler model (sun-centered) displaced centuries of Earth-centered certainty.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nicolaus Copernicus; Core Knowledge: the Scientific Revolution
topics.framing_note: MOVE + wonder. The payoff is the IDEA's sting: we are not the center of the universe — a humbling reframe, not just an astronomy fact. Answer = the conceptual shift (Earth is one moving planet, not the fixed hub), and why people resisted it. Keep it about the reasoning leap, not 'who discovered heliocentrism' attribution trivia.

topics.name: Newton's Clockwork Universe
topics.scope: One set of laws governing apple and planet alike; 'I frame no hypotheses' (describe HOW gravity acts, don't speculate WHY); the deist watchmaker-God the clockwork suggested; the determinism question a law-governed cosmos raises.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Isaac Newton; IEP: Isaac Newton
topics.framing_note: MOVE-led. Two payoffs: (1) 'I frame no hypotheses' — describe the regularity, refuse to invent unseen causes (a method move, anti-speculation). (2) A universe running like clockwork raises the determinism problem later strands cash out (if every event follows fixed law, what of free choice?). Watchmaker-God as the deist idea it suggested, not a verdict. Gloss plainly.

topics.name: Pascal's Thinking Reed
topics.scope: 'Man is but a reed, the weakest in nature, but he is a thinking reed' — a single thought makes us nobler than the cosmos that crushes us; 'the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me' (the new vast universe's terror).
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Blaise Pascal; Pascal, Pensees
topics.framing_note: Pure wonder MOVE-gem. The payoff is the precise reversal: the universe can crush a man without knowing it, but the man KNOWS he is crushed — and that knowing is his dignity. Answer = that thought-makes-us-greater move, plus 'the eternal silence of infinite spaces' as the dread the huge new Copernican cosmos provoked. Pascal-as-scientist-philosopher, named in stem.

topics.name: Bacon's Death by Snow
topics.scope: The reported end of the man who preached experiment: Bacon stuffed a chicken with snow on a freezing road to test whether cold preserves flesh, caught a chill, and died of it — killed, fittingly, by his own method.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Francis Bacon; standard biographical accounts (John Aubrey, Brief Lives)
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA wonder anchor and a vivid T1 base for the strand. The payoff is the irony: the prophet of 'test it, don't just think it' died running an experiment (the snow-packed chicken). Answer = that specific vivid act, not a date. Label as the traditional account (per Aubrey). Lands the strand's whole point — go and CHECK — in one memorable scene.

topics.name: Descartes' methodic doubt & the evil demon
topics.scope: Descartes resolves to doubt EVERYTHING that can be doubted, to find one thing that can't: maybe his senses lie, maybe even math is rigged by an all-powerful EVIL DEMON bent on deceiving him about all of it; he tears the whole house of belief down to see what, if anything, still stands.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Epistemology; IEP: Rene Descartes; Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE lead, vivid hook. Make the evil demon the SCENE; the answer is the METHOD's point: doubt everything you possibly can to find what survives, not 'who imagined a demon.' This sets up the cogito payoff. The deceiver who could fake even 2+2=4 is the memorable image. Plain language, scene carries the tier.

topics.name: I think, therefore I am (the cogito)
topics.scope: The one thing the evil demon can't fake: even to be DECEIVED, there must be a 'me' being deceived. 'I think, therefore I am' (cogito ergo sum) — the very act of doubting proves a doubter exists. The first certain brick after the demolition, the bedrock Descartes builds modern philosophy back up from.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Epistemology; IEP: Rene Descartes; Descartes, Meditations II & Discourse on Method IV
topics.framing_note: Marquee MOVE. The harder you try to doubt your own existence, the more you prove the doubter. Answer = that self-refuting structure ('doubting requires a doubter, so I exist'), not the Latin tag (context). At T5 raise the real objection: it proves thinking happens, but a permanent 'I'? Note the lineage to Avicenna's Floating Man in context.

topics.name: The dream argument
topics.scope: Descartes' opening crack in certainty: right now, how do you KNOW you aren't dreaming? Vivid dreams feel exactly as real from the inside; there's no stamped mark that says 'this is waking life.' If you can't tell, then everything your senses report could be a dream — so the senses can't be the bedrock of knowledge.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Epistemology; IEP: Rene Descartes; Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I
topics.framing_note: MOVE with an instantly graspable hook — every kid has had a vivid dream. Answer = the reasoning (no reliable test tells waking from dreaming, so sense-experience alone can't guarantee truth), not the name. Lead T1 with the scene: pinch yourself, but you can dream a pinch too. Pairs with the Brain-in-a-Vat / Matrix; cross-link in context.

topics.name: Mind-body dualism & the pineal gland
topics.scope: Descartes splits reality in two: the MIND, a thinking thing with no size or place, and the BODY, an extended thing in space — two utterly different substances. But then the hard puzzle: if they're so different, how does deciding to raise your arm actually MOVE it? His answer — they meet at a tiny gland in the brain, the pineal gland.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Theory of Mind; IEP: Rene Descartes; Descartes, Meditations VI & The Passions of the Soul
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED mind-body position — present dualism as a REAL view at its strongest, no verdict (pairs with philosophy-of-mind; cross-link in context). The marquee payoff is the interaction problem: how can a placeless mind push a physical body? The pineal-gland 'meeting point' is the vivid, almost comic handle. Choices = rival pictures of mind and body. Gloss 'substance' plainly.

topics.name: The wax argument
topics.scope: Descartes watches a piece of beeswax: by the fire its smell, shape, color, hardness, and sound ALL change — yet he still judges it's the same wax. So what he grasps isn't through the senses (every sensed quality changed) but through the MIND alone. A small everyday scene used to prove reason, not the senses, is what truly knows.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Epistemology; IEP: Rene Descartes; Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy II
topics.framing_note: Clean MOVE with a concrete handle (the melting candle). Answer = the reasoning: every sensed property changed but 'the wax' persisted, so the intellect — not sight or touch — identifies it; the rationalist core that real knowing is by reason. Not 'what is wax made of.' Lead with the fireside scene. Sets up the empiricist clash (Locke/Hume) in context.

topics.name: Spinoza: God or Nature (excommunicated & grinding lenses)
topics.scope: At 23 Spinoza was cursed and cast out of his own Amsterdam community for his ideas; he refused a chair at Heidelberg and ground optical lenses for a quiet living. His shocking claim: God and Nature are the SAME thing (Deus sive Natura) — there is only ONE infinite substance, and everything else is a mode of it. No separate creator outside the world.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; IEP: Benedict de Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics Part I
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE keystone, high wonder. Lead with the drama (the herem at 23; the lens-grinder who turned down fame). The marquee MOVE: God IS the universe, one substance, not a maker from outside — a real, contested metaphysics presented straight, NO verdict, no smug-believer or smug-atheist voice. Answer = the God-or-Nature move, not biography. Gloss 'substance' plainly.

topics.name: Spinoza's ethics laid out like geometry
topics.scope: Spinoza wrote his great book of ETHICS the way Euclid wrote geometry: definitions, axioms, then theorems proved step by step, each stamped 'Q.E.D.' He believed morality could be deduced as rigorously as a math proof — that human emotions and the good life follow by logic from first principles, not from preaching.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Baruch Spinoza; IEP: Benedict de Spinoza; Spinoza, Ethics (Ethica Ordine Geometrico Demonstrata)
topics.framing_note: A few gems on a striking method-move: doing ETHICS as geometry. The point is the audacity — proving how to live the way you prove a triangle's angles, deduced from definitions and axioms. Answer = that geometric-deduction method, not page count. The 'Q.E.D. ending a moral proof' image is the hook; pure rationalist faith that reason alone reaches truth.

topics.name: Leibniz's monads
topics.scope: Leibniz says the ultimate building blocks of reality aren't tiny bits of matter but infinitely many MINDS — simple, indivisible 'monads,' each mirroring the whole universe from its own point of view. Famously they are 'windowless': nothing ever goes in or out, no monad truly touches another, yet all of them stay perfectly in step.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz; IEP: Gottfried Leibniz; Leibniz, Monadology
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — the strangeness is the hook (reality made of countless windowless mind-points, each mirroring everything). Answer = the picture and its payoff (no monad acts on another, yet all agree — which forces the harmony question). Gloss 'monad' plainly as 'a simple mind-point.' A real, contested metaphysics at its strongest, no verdict. Pairs with the next rung (harmony).

topics.name: Pre-established harmony & sufficient reason
topics.scope: If no monad touches another, why does mind seem to move body and body to affect mind? Leibniz: like two perfect clocks wound at the start to chime together forever, God set every monad in advance so they only SEEM to interact. Behind it the Principle of Sufficient Reason — nothing is so without a reason WHY it is so.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz; IEP: Gottfried Leibniz; Leibniz, Monadology & Discourse on Metaphysics
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic — the two-synchronized-clocks image is the vivid handle for pre-established harmony (Leibniz's rival answer to Descartes' mind-body problem; cross-link in context). The Principle of Sufficient Reason is a transferable tool: always ask 'why THIS rather than otherwise?' Answer = the reasoning, not the labels. Present harmony as one contested solution among rivals, no verdict.

topics.name: The best of all possible worlds
topics.scope: Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil: a perfect God, with infinitely many possible worlds to choose from, must by the Principle of Sufficient Reason have picked the BEST one — so despite its suffering, this is the best of all possible worlds. The claim Voltaire would later savage through the relentless misfortunes of Candide.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz; IEP: Leibniz: Metaphysics; Leibniz, Theodicy
topics.framing_note: A few gems on a famous MOVE feeding the philosophy-of-religion strand. Answer = the argument's structure (a perfect chooser with a sufficient reason must pick the best option available), not the catchphrase. Honor the mockery: Voltaire's Candide replies that real suffering makes it hard to swallow — a genuine objection, no verdict on God. Cross-link to the problem of evil.

topics.name: The Empiricist Wager: All Knowledge from Experience
topics.scope: the core empiricist move vs the rationalists: nothing is in the mind that was not first in the senses; ideas trace back to impressions; the contrast with Descartes' innate reason
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Empiricism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Rationalism vs. Empiricism
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic and the strand's gateway. Lead with the plain fork: do we KNOW by thinking it out (reason) or by checking the world (experience)? Choices are the two competing methods in plain words. Answer = the empiricist test (trace the idea back to something you actually saw, heard, touched). Gloss 'empiricism' as a method, never as a term to define. No verdict on which camp wins; this just names the move the whole strand uses.

topics.name: Locke's Blank Slate (Tabula Rasa)
topics.scope: the mind at birth as white paper with no innate ideas; all furniture of the mind written by experience; sensation + reflection as the two fountains of knowledge; the attack on 'innate principles'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Locke; Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), Book II
topics.framing_note: Vivid T1 base: a newborn mind as blank paper, every idea later written by what the child sees and does. The MOVE is Locke denying we are born already knowing things. Touches the nature/nurture and male/female-difference debates lightly (the slate is not infinitely blank) — note in context, do NOT warp the topic into a verdict. Answer = the image or the move, never 'define tabula rasa'.

topics.name: Primary vs Secondary Qualities
topics.scope: Locke's split: size, shape, motion really in the object (primary) vs colour, taste, sound, warmth only POWERS to make sensations in us (secondary); the lukewarm-water demo (same bowl feels hot to one hand, cold to the other)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Primary and Secondary Qualities in Early Modern Philosophy; IEP: John Locke
topics.framing_note: MOVE with a killer demo: hold one hand in ice, one in hot water, then both in lukewarm — the SAME water feels hot and cold, so warmth is in us, not the water. Lead with the scene; answer = where the quality really lives (in the thing vs in the perceiver). Sets up Berkeley's attack next. Keep 'primary/secondary' glossed; the demo carries the tier, not the vocabulary.

topics.name: Locke on Personal Identity: The Prince and the Cobbler
topics.scope: identity = continuity of MEMORY/consciousness, not same body or soul; the prince's mind waking in the cobbler's body (where does the PERSON go?); the sleeping/drunk man and responsibility; the gap-in-memory problem
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Locke on Personal Identity; Locke, Essay II.xxvii
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED identity fork — apply no-verdict. The prince's memories wake up inside the cobbler's body: which one is now the prince? Put the claim in Locke's mouth (the PERSON follows the memory); choices = memory view, body view, soul view, no-self view as real competing positions. Cross-reference Ship of Theseus and Indian anatta in context. Vivid SCENE leads; the answer matches the stated reasoning, not a label.

topics.name: Berkeley's Idealism: To Be Is To Be Perceived
topics.scope: esse est percipi; there is no mindless matter, only minds and ideas; the tree in the quad no one sees; God's perceiving keeps the world in being; why this is NOT 'denying the world is real'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley; IEP: George Berkeley
topics.framing_note: Sounds insane on first read = perfect hook: does the tree in the empty courtyard still exist when nobody looks? Lead with that scene; distractors are coherent rival epistemologies (matter exists unseen / it persists by God's gaze / it is just ideas) at full strength — Berkeley is steel-manned, never mocked. No verdict on whether matter exists. Gloss 'idealism'; never ask 'what does esse est percipi mean'.

topics.name: Hume's Fork: Relations of Ideas vs Matters of Fact
topics.scope: two and only two kinds of knowable claim — relations of ideas (true by definition, deny them and you contradict yourself: 2+2=4) vs matters of fact (known only by experience, deniable without contradiction: the sun will rise); the 'commit it to the flames' test
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: David Hume; Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748)
topics.framing_note: Clean MOVE and the master-tool for the rest of Hume. Teach the sorting test: can you deny it without contradicting yourself? '2+2=5' breaks; 'the sun won't rise' merely surprises. Choices = which bin a sample claim falls in / what the bins track. Answer = the working distinction, not the phrase 'Hume's fork'. Sets up induction and is-ought as the payoffs. Gloss the jargon in plain words.

topics.name: Hume's Problem of Induction
topics.scope: no logic guarantees the future resembles the past; every inductive proof secretly assumes the very thing it tries to prove (circularity); we rely on it anyway by habit/custom, not reason; Russell's chicken fed daily until the neck-wringing
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Problem of Induction; Hume, Treatise of Human Nature (1739), Book I
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE transferable move — the strand's best logic training. The bread nourished you a thousand times; what proof is it will TOMORROW? 'It always has' assumes the future copies the past — the thing in question. Lead with Russell's chicken (vivid) at lower rungs. Answer = the circularity / the habit, never 'Hume'. No verdict that knowledge is impossible — the point is the gap, and that we leap it by custom.

topics.name: Hume on Causation: Constant Conjunction
topics.scope: we never SEE one ball MAKE the other move — only B following A, again and again; the 'necessary connection' is a habit of mind we project, not a force we observe; the rooster's crow and the sunrise as the cautionary case
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: David Hume — Causation; Hume, Enquiry, Section VII
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, pairs with post-hoc and correlation-vs-causation fallacies (cross-ref). Lead with the billiard balls: you see the click and the roll, never the 'making'. The rooster crows, the sun rises — constant conjunction is NOT causation. Choices = what we actually observe vs what we assume. Answer = 'we see the pattern, never the power; the connection is added by the mind'. No verdict that causation is fake — it's about what's OBSERVED.

topics.name: Hume's Is-Ought Gap
topics.scope: you cannot derive what OUGHT to be from what merely IS; the silent leap from 'is' and 'is not' to 'ought' and 'ought not'; facts alone never deliver a duty; the missing premise a value argument needs
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hume's Moral Philosophy; Hume, Treatise III.i.1
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE move — feeds the whole ethics strand (cross-ref). A speaker stacks facts ('this is natural', 'most people do it', 'it has always been so') then jumps to 'so you OUGHT to'. The answer names the SUBSTANTIVE gap: a fact alone never settles a value — a value premise was smuggled in. NOT 'name the fallacy'. Connects to appeal-to-nature and appeal-to-tradition. No verdict on any particular value claim.

topics.name: Hume's Bundle Theory of the Self
topics.scope: look inward for the 'I' and you only ever catch a particular perception — heat, light, a thought — never a self HAVING them; the self as a bundle/stream of perceptions with no owner behind them
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hume — Personal Identity; Hume, Treatise I.iv.6
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED identity move — no verdict. Put it in Hume's mouth: go hunting inside for the SELF and you only ever find a feeling or a thought, never the finder. Choices = bundle/no-owner view vs an enduring-self view vs Locke's memory-thread, at full strength. Strikingly echoes the Buddhist no-self (anatta) and the chariot argument — note the parallel in context. Answer matches the stated reasoning, not 'bundle theory' as a label.

topics.name: Reason Is the Slave of the Passions
topics.scope: Hume's claim that reason alone never moves us to act — it only finds means; the WANTING comes from feeling/passion; 'reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions'; the provocation that reason serves desire, not the reverse
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hume's Moral Philosophy; Hume, Treatise II.iii.3
topics.framing_note: Standalone gem, 2-3 rungs, high provocation. Hume flips the usual picture: reason is a brilliant MAP but never the engine — desire decides where you GO. Present as a real position to reason about (choices = reason rules / passion rules / they share the wheel), no verdict; it's the foil for Kant's duty-over-inclination later (cross-ref). Answer = the move (reason finds the how, feeling sets the what), never the bare quotation.

topics.name: Hume's Missing Shade of Blue
topics.scope: Hume's own counterexample to his rule that every idea copies a prior impression: shown a spectrum of blues with one gap, a person could imagine the missing shade never seen — a crack in strict empiricism Hume admitted and shrugged off
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: David Hume; Hume, Enquiry, Section II
topics.framing_note: Standalone gem, 2-3 rungs, T4-T5 — rewards the kid who followed the strand. The delight: Hume builds the rule 'no idea without a prior impression', then names his OWN exception (the unseen blue you could still picture) and waves it through. Answer = what the case threatens (an idea with no matching impression). Pairs with the empiricist-wager opener as the honest crack in it. No jargon; the colour-gap scene carries it.

topics.name: The Categorical Imperative (Universalizability)
topics.scope: Act only on a rule you could will EVERYONE to follow; the lying-promise that destroys promising; perfect vs imperfect duties; the contradiction-in-conception test.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy; IEP: Kant; Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)
topics.framing_note: The deontology keystone MOVE. Lead with a concrete scene: could EVERYONE break a promise to escape a debt? If universal lying kills trust, the rule self-destructs. Choices are real moral positions in plain language; answer = the universalizability test, never the term 'categorical imperative' as recall.

topics.name: Ends, Never Merely Means (The Humanity Formula)
topics.scope: The second formulation: treat people always as ENDS in themselves, never MERELY as tools; using vs respecting a person; the dignity of rational beings.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy; Groundwork II
topics.framing_note: Marquee accessible MOVE. Vivid scene: is the merchant who tricks a child USING her as a mere tool? The line is between using-only and using-while-still-respecting. Choices are competing readings of a concrete case; answer = the ends-not-merely-means distinction, glossed plainly, not the jargon.

topics.name: Duty vs Inclination (The Good Will)
topics.scope: A good will is the only thing good without qualification; moral worth lies in acting FROM duty, not from feeling or self-interest; the shopkeeper who is honest only because it pays.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy; Groundwork I
topics.framing_note: A real, contested MOVE (critics say Kant undervalues kind feeling). Scene: does the merchant who deals fairly ONLY because it profits him act morally? Present Kant's answer AND the objection that warmth should count, no verdict. Answer = duty-vs-inclination distinction, not the phrase 'good will'.

topics.name: The Murderer at the Door
topics.scope: Kant's notorious hard case: must you not lie even to a killer asking where your friend is hiding? Absolute rules vs consequences; the deontology-vs-results fork.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy; Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797)
topics.framing_note: The famous hard case AGAINST Kant. Vivid forcing scene: the killer at your door, your friend hidden inside. Present it as a GENUINE problem that strains absolute rules; choices are real positions (never lie / lie to save a life / stay silent), NO verdict. Sets up the deontology-vs-consequences fork.

topics.name: The Copernican Turn in Knowledge
topics.scope: The mind SHAPES experience rather than passively copying it; space, time, and cause are lenses we bring to the world, not features we simply find in it; why objects must conform to our cognition.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Critique of Metaphysics; Critique of Pure Reason (1781/1787), Preface B
topics.framing_note: A real epistemology MOVE, contested (vs Hume's pure empiricism and naive realism). Plain handle: we view everything through built-in glasses we can never remove, so the world's order partly comes from US. Scene-led, no verdict; answer = the mind-shapes-experience move, not the label 'transcendental idealism'.

topics.name: Phenomena vs Noumena (The Thing-in-Itself)
topics.scope: The world-as-it-appears (phenomena) vs the thing-in-itself (noumenon) we can never reach; we know appearances structured by our own forms, never reality bare.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Critique of Metaphysics; Critique of Pure Reason
topics.framing_note: Harder, abstract MOVE — keep it high-tier and concrete. Plain handle: you only ever see the painting THROUGH tinted glass; the canvas-as-it-truly-is stays hidden. Present as a real position with rivals (is the unreachable thing-in-itself coherent?), no verdict. Answer = the appearance/thing-in-itself split, glossed.

topics.name: The Antinomies of Reason
topics.scope: Reason contradicts ITSELF on the biggest questions — the universe has/has-no beginning, freedom exists/all is caused — equally strong proofs on both sides; the limits of reason beyond experience.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Critique of Metaphysics; Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic
topics.framing_note: A few high-tier prestige gems. The striking MOVE: equally rigorous arguments prove BOTH 'the world had a first moment' and 'it didn't' — a signal that reason has overreached past experience. Scene the clash, no verdict on the metaphysics; answer = recognizing reason's self-contradiction at its own limits.

topics.name: The Crooked Timber of Humanity
topics.scope: Kant the man and his vivid lines: 'the starry heavens above and the moral law within'; 'out of the crooked timber of humanity no straight thing was ever made'; the clockwork-regular bachelor of Konigsberg; 'What is Enlightenment? Dare to know.'
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant; Kant, 'What Is Enlightenment?' (1784); Critique of Practical Reason (conclusion)
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA gems and wonder. The man so punctual neighbors set clocks by his walk; 'Dare to know' as Enlightenment's motto; awe at two things — the stars above and the moral law within. Answer = the vivid named line or its meaning, never dry biography trivia (no 'what year', no 'which city' rote).

topics.name: Hegel's Dialectic
topics.scope: Ideas develop by collision: a position (thesis) provokes its opposite (antithesis), resolved in a higher synthesis that keeps what was true in both; contradiction as the engine of progress, not a flaw to avoid.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hegel's Dialectics; IEP: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic. Teach the dialectic as a PATTERN of how ideas grow, with one concrete worked example (a claim breeds its objection, the better view absorbs both), NEVER as the words 'thesis/antithesis' to memorize. Payoff = recognizing the move (contradiction drives the next step). Gloss every term; no verdict on whether history really works this way.

topics.name: The Master-Slave Dialectic
topics.scope: Two self-consciousnesses fight for recognition; the loser submits as bondsman. But the master, recognized only by a slave he doesn't respect, gets hollow recognition, while the slave, shaping the world through work, grows toward real independence. Who is truly free?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hegel (Phenomenology of Spirit, Lordship and Bondage); IEP: Hegel
topics.framing_note: The strand's most ACCESSIBLE move and a vivid SCENE. Lead with the reversal: the master depends on the slave's recognition and the slave's labor builds real competence, so who actually depends on whom? Answer = that reversal, not the label. Previews Marx (note in context). CONTESTED reading kept open; choices are real positions on freedom and recognition.

topics.name: Hegel's Philosophy of History
topics.scope: History as the unfolding of Spirit toward freedom; the 'cunning of reason' (great ambitions unintentionally advance a larger pattern); 'the owl of Minerva flies only at dusk' (wisdom understands an age only after it has ended).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hegel; IEP: Hegel (Lectures on the Philosophy of History)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. The owl of Minerva is the wonder hook (you can only understand the day once dusk falls). The cunning of reason is a clean move (private passions serve an end no one aimed at, akin to the invisible hand, note in context). No verdict on whether history has a direction. Keep 'Spirit' in plain language (a culture's shared mind/freedom growing over time).

topics.name: Schopenhauer's Will
topics.scope: Beneath the world we perceive lies a single blind striving, the Will; we are its puppets. Life swings between the pain of unmet desire and the boredom of satisfied desire, never resting; pessimism as the honest verdict on craving.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Arthur Schopenhauer; IEP: Schopenhauer (The World as Will and Representation)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE, high wonder. The pain-versus-boredom pendulum is the vivid, kid-graspable handle (get what you want and you're bored; don't and you ache). The Will is a real metaphysical position, no verdict. Gloss 'representation/Will' plainly (the world as it looks vs the blind drive underneath). Pairs with Indian no-self and Nietzsche's will to power; flag the lineage in context.

topics.name: Schopenhauer on Compassion
topics.scope: Morality is grounded in compassion (Mitleid, 'suffering-with') rather than duty or self-interest; the moral person feels another's pain as nearly their own because, at depth, the same Will animates all; aesthetic contemplation as brief escape from striving.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Arthur Schopenhauer (ethics); IEP: Schopenhauer
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic. The compassion-based ethic is a real rival to Kant's duty (note the contrast in context) presented at full strength, no verdict. Note honestly that he drew on the Upanishads ('the consolation of my life') as a serious Western-Eastern bridge, NOT exoticizing. Distractors = competing grounds of morality (duty, self-interest, virtue) in plain language.

topics.name: Feuerbach's Projection
topics.scope: God is humanity's own best qualities (love, wisdom, power) projected outward and worshipped as a separate being; 'theology is really anthropology'; to know God is to know an idealized portrait of man.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ludwig Feuerbach; IEP: Ludwig Andreas von Feuerbach
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, clean and self-contained. The projection move is the payoff (the divine = humanity's ideal qualities turned into a separate being). The user is not Christian and the bank declares no verdict on God's existence: present this as one serious POSITION among rivals, no smug-atheist voice. Feeds the philosophy-of-religion and Marx ('opium') strands; note the lineage in context.

topics.name: From Hegel to Marx and Nietzsche
topics.scope: The fork after Hegel: the Young Hegelians flip his system, keeping the dialectic but making material/economic conditions (not Spirit) the driver, feeding Marx; while Schopenhauer's blind Will and 'God is dead' atmosphere feed Nietzsche.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hegel (legacy/reception); IEP: Karl Marx; IEP: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: BRIDGE topic, 2-3 gems only. Shows how one teacher's system split into two opposed legacies (Marx inverts the dialectic onto economics; Nietzsche inherits the post-Hegelian crisis of value). A recognition move (spotting the inheritance), not name-recall. No verdict on either heir; keep it as intellectual lineage, lightly setting up the Marx and Nietzsche strands.

topics.name: The State of Nature
topics.scope: The founding thought-experiment: what are humans like with NO government, no laws, no police? Hobbes' war of all-against-all vs Locke's law-of-nature vs Rousseau's peaceful solitary savage as three rival pictures of the same blank slate.
topics.source: Britannica: State of nature (political theory); IEP: Social Contract Theory; SEP: Contractarianism
topics.framing_note: The vivid T1-T2 GATEWAY to the whole strand: 'imagine no rules at all — what happens?' The CONTESTED move is that the SAME blank slate yields three pictures (terror, rough order, lost paradise) — no verdict; choices are the competing pictures. Answer = the rival diagnosis of human nature, never the term 'state of nature' as a label.

topics.name: Hobbes & the Leviathan
topics.scope: Life without a sovereign is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; the war of every man against every man; we hand near-total power to one sovereign (the Leviathan) and trade liberty for security; the covenant; why even a bad ruler beats civil war.
topics.source: SEP: Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy; IEP: Thomas Hobbes; Hobbes, Leviathan (1651)
topics.framing_note: STEEL-MAN him: Hobbes is the bank's strongest case FOR strong authority, not a tyranny-cartoon. Lead with the famous 'nasty, brutish, and short' line and the absolute-sovereign trade. His ANSWER to 'why obey?' is fear-of-chaos. CONTESTED vs Locke — no verdict. Payoff = the vivid trade (security for liberty), not 'who wrote Leviathan'.

topics.name: Locke's Natural Rights & Consent
topics.scope: We hold natural rights to life, liberty, and property BEFORE any government; government exists only by the CONSENT of the governed to protect those rights; legitimate power is limited and held in trust; the labor theory of property (mixing your work with the world makes it yours).
topics.source: SEP: Locke's Political Philosophy; IEP: John Locke; Locke, Second Treatise of Government (1689)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL backbone — negative rights the bank celebrates: rights PRECEDE government; no one owes you another's labor. Locke's ANSWER to 'why obey?' is consent-to-protect-rights. Pair as the live fork against Hobbes (absolute) and Rousseau (collective). Payoff = the move (rights come first, government is a trustee), no policy verdict.

topics.name: Locke's Right of Revolution
topics.scope: When a government breaks the trust and turns on the rights it was made to protect, the people may rightfully dissolve it; rebellion is laid at the feet of the tyrant who started the war, not the people; this is the engine behind the American Declaration.
topics.source: SEP: Locke's Political Philosophy (Dissolution of Government); Locke, Second Treatise ch. 19
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT: distinct ladder from Locke's rights (per brief — same thinker, two topics). The MOVE: legitimacy is conditional, so revolution against a trust-breaker is justified, not mere rebellion. Set up the lineage to 1776 in context. Answer = the conditional-legitimacy reasoning, not 'Locke influenced Jefferson' trivia.

topics.name: Rousseau & the General Will
topics.scope: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'; the general will (the common good of the whole, not just the sum of private wants); we surrender to the community and gain civic freedom; the danger that one can be 'forced to be free'; majority can mistake its own will.
topics.source: SEP: Jean Jacques Rousseau; IEP: Jean-Jacques Rousseau; Rousseau, The Social Contract (1762)
topics.framing_note: STEEL-MAN, do NOT flame: Rousseau's ANSWER to 'why obey?' is that obeying the general will IS obeying yourself. Lead with 'born free, everywhere in chains'. Present 'forced to be free' as the genuine TENSION it is — no verdict, but let the kid see why critics fear it. Contested vs Locke's individual rights. Answer = the move, never the slogan as label.

topics.name: Rousseau's Noble Savage & Amour-Propre
topics.scope: Humans were freer and gentler before society; civilization corrupts; amour-propre (vanity that craves to outrank others by comparison) is the poison property and society introduced; 'the first man who fenced a plot and said this is mine' began inequality.
topics.source: SEP: Jean Jacques Rousseau; Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755)
topics.framing_note: WONDER-LED companion ladder. Vivid scene: the first fence and 'this is mine' as the birth of inequality. Amour-propre = wanting to be ranked above others, not just to live. Present as a REAL position (civilization-as-corruption) to reason about — Locke would say property secures liberty; no verdict. Answer = the comparison-vanity insight, not the phrase 'noble savage'.

topics.name: Montesquieu & the Separation of Powers
topics.scope: Divide government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches so that power checks power; 'power should be a check to power'; liberty dies when the same hands make, enforce, AND judge the laws; the influence on the U.S. Constitution's design.
topics.source: SEP: Montesquieu; IEP: Baron de Montesquieu; Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT (structural safeguard of liberty the bank prizes). The MOVE: don't trust good rulers — design so no one hand makes, enforces, AND judges. Vivid handle: a single hand holding all three is tyranny waiting. Concrete, kid-graspable. Answer = the check-power-with-power reasoning, never 'name the three branches' rote.

topics.name: The American Founding as Applied Contract
topics.scope: The Declaration's claim of unalienable natural rights and government 'deriving just powers from the consent of the governed'; Locke's social contract put into a real founding; the Federalist on faction and the need to check power because men are not angels.
topics.source: AP U.S. Government; Declaration of Independence (1776); The Federalist No. 10 & No. 51 (Madison)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT: the social contract made real. Connect Locke's consent + natural rights to the Declaration's actual words. Federalist 51 ('if men were angels, no government would be necessary') is the marquee MOVE — checks exist because power corrupts. No partisan verdict; teach the REASONING (consent, faction, checks). Answer = the move, not a date or signer count.

topics.name: Burke & the Generational Contract
topics.scope: Society is a partnership 'between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born'; reform should be gradual and grow from inherited institutions, not be torn down for an abstract blueprint; his early warning that the French Revolution would end in terror and a strongman.
topics.source: SEP: Edmund Burke; IEP: Edmund Burke; Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL: the traditionalist spine. Burke's contract spans the dead and the unborn, not just today's voters — the marquee MOVE against revolutionary rationalism. Lead with the 'living, dead, and to be born' partnership. Steel-man Rousseau as the foil he answers. His Terror prediction is vivid wonder. Answer = the generational-partnership/gradual-reform reasoning, no policy verdict.

topics.name: Why Obey? Consent, Tacit Consent & the Problem of Obligation
topics.scope: If you never signed any contract, why are you bound to obey? Locke's TACIT consent (use the roads, accept the protection — you've consented); Hume's hard objection (the contract is a fiction — the peasant can't really 'leave'); fair-play and gratitude as rival grounds of obligation.
topics.source: SEP: Political Obligation; IEP: Social Contract Theory; Hume, 'Of the Original Contract' (1748)
topics.framing_note: The CAPSTONE move that turns the strand reflexive: present Hume's sharp objection at full strength (no one signed; 'consent' by not emigrating is hollow for a poor man). CONTESTED — choices are real rival grounds (tacit consent, fair play, gratitude), no verdict. Steel-man both the contract defenders and Hume. Answer = the competing ground of obligation, not a label.

topics.name: The Leviathan Frontispiece
topics.scope: The famous 1651 engraving: a giant crowned sovereign whose body is made of hundreds of tiny individual people, towering over the land with sword and crozier — a single picture of Hobbes' whole argument that the many become one body under one ruler.
topics.source: SEP: Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy; Hobbes, Leviathan (1651) title-page engraving
topics.framing_note: WONDER mini-gem: pure NAMED-IMAGE payoff — the king built out of tiny people is the social contract in one picture (the many become one body). Use the striking visual as the hook; answer = what the image MEANS (individuals merged into one sovereign body), never 'who drew it' or the year as the point.

topics.name: Mill's Harm Principle
topics.scope: On Liberty's core rule: the only reason to use power over someone against their will is to prevent harm to OTHERS; your own good (body or mind) is never sufficient warrant; self-regarding acts are your own business
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill (On Liberty); IEP: Mill
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT: the engine of negative liberty. MOVE topic, vivid T1 base (may the town stop a man drinking himself sick if he harms no one else?). The hard rungs probe the edge: where does self-regarding end and harm-to-others begin? Choices are real positions on where liberty stops. No verdict on the hard cases; the principle itself is the recognizable move.

topics.name: The Marketplace of Ideas
topics.scope: Mill's defense of free speech: silencing an opinion robs the human race; even a FALSE opinion sharpens the truth by forcing us to defend it; an unchallenged truth decays into 'dead dogma' held without understanding
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill (On Liberty ch. 2); Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT. MOVE topic. The counter-intuitive payoff is the hook: even a WRONG opinion is useful (it keeps the truth alive instead of a slogan no one can defend). Choices = real reasons for/against suppression. The recognized move is 'truth needs a live challenger'; no verdict on any specific banned view.

topics.name: The Tyranny of the Majority
topics.scope: Mill (drawing on Tocqueville): democracy can oppress without a tyrant; the majority's opinion and custom coerce the individual through social pressure, not just law; the danger of conformity over the dissenter
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill; Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. I
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT (coercion beneath consent). MOVE topic: tyranny doesn't need a king; the crowd and 'what everyone thinks' can crush a person just as hard. Vivid scene: the lone dissenter shunned by the whole village. Choices = real positions on whether majority opinion can be a kind of tyranny. Pairs with Tocqueville's soft despotism. No verdict.

topics.name: Higher and Lower Pleasures
topics.scope: Mill's refinement of utilitarianism: pleasures differ in KIND, not just amount; the competent judge who has known both prefers the higher; 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill (Utilitarianism); IEP: Mill
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic with a marquee line ('better Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied'). The payoff is that line and the 'competent judge' test (only one who has tasted both pleasures can rank them). Choices = real positions on whether all pleasures are equal. Sets up the experience-machine and hedonism debates elsewhere; no verdict on the ranking, the move is what's recognized.

topics.name: Berlin's Two Concepts of Liberty
topics.scope: Isaiah Berlin's 1958 distinction: NEGATIVE liberty (freedom FROM interference, how many doors are open to you) vs POSITIVE liberty (freedom TO master yourself, be your own 'real' self) and how positive liberty can be twisted to justify coercion 'for your own good'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Isaiah Berlin; SEP: Positive and Negative Liberty
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL (the master key to the strand). MOVE topic: negative = leave me alone; positive = make me my better self. Berlin's warning is the deep payoff: positive liberty can flip into 'we know your TRUE will, so forcing you is really freeing you.' Choices = real positions, never a declared verdict. Steel-man positive liberty before showing the danger. Higher tier, plain handles (doors open vs being your own master).

topics.name: Negative vs Positive Rights
topics.scope: The diagnostic distinction: a NEGATIVE right asks others only to leave you alone (speech, life, property); a POSITIVE 'right' is a claim on someone else's labor or goods (a right to be GIVEN housing, healthcare); who must do what to satisfy each
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Rights; moral_vision §3.9; Bastiat, The Law
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL (moral_vision §3.9: rights are negative; no entitlement to another's labor; charity is a high virtue, not the receiver's right). Teach as a MOVE the player RECOGNIZES (a right that costs others nothing vs one that obligates a specific person to provide) — NEVER a declared policy verdict. T1-T2 handle: 'leave me alone' vs 'give me this.' Choices = real positions. Steel-man the positive-rights side; the recognition skill is the lesson.

topics.name: Tocqueville's Soft Despotism
topics.scope: Democracy in America: how a mild, busy, parental state ('an immense tutelary power') can smother liberty not by terror but by managing every detail until citizens are content, passive children; equality eroding freedom
topics.source: Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT. MOVE topic, vivid and modern-feeling: tyranny that doesn't break you, it tucks you in — a kindly state that handles everything until you forget how to choose. The payoff is that image ('benevolent schoolmasters' / a network of small rules), not the term. Choices = real positions on whether comfort-by-the-state can cost freedom. Pairs with Mill's tyranny of the majority. No verdict.

topics.name: Wollstonecraft and Equity Feminism
topics.scope: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: women have the same reason as men and so deserve the same EDUCATION; denied learning, not denied nature, is why they seem lesser; the root of equity feminism (equal treatment, not interchangeability)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mary Wollstonecraft; IEP: Wollstonecraft
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL (equity-feminism per moral_vision: fair treatment + real differences, vs gender-feminism's interchangeability). STORY+MOVE: Wollstonecraft's actual argument is about REASON and EDUCATION — give girls real schooling, not ornamental training. The payoff is her concrete claim (equal minds deserve equal teaching), not a label. No caricature in either direction; present her real case at full strength. Vivid T2 base (why teach a girl only to be decorative?).

topics.name: FDR's Second Bill of Rights
