topics.scope: FDR's 1944 case for positive economic rights — a right to a job, food, housing, medical care, education — as the strongest steel-manned argument that political liberty is empty without economic security ('necessitous men are not free men')
topics.source: FDR 1944 State of the Union (Second Bill of Rights); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Rights
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT as the steel-manned FOIL to negative rights (moral_vision: FDR's positive-rights case presented at its STRONGEST, the bank's line falls with Hayek/Nozick/Bastiat — but NO sneering, no strawman). MOVE topic: present FDR's real argument forcefully (a starving man's 'freedom' is hollow), then the counter (whose labor must provide it?) as competing positions. No declared verdict; the player weighs a genuine fork. Pairs directly with Negative vs Positive Rights.

topics.name: Power Tends to Corrupt (Acton)
topics.scope: Lord Acton's maxim 'power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely; great men are almost always bad men' — the case for limiting and dividing power because no one is safe to trust with all of it
topics.source: Lord Acton, 1887 letter to Bishop Creighton; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT (why power must be limited and divided — the spine of the liberty strand). Mini gem, vivid T1 base: the famous line itself and its punch ('great men are almost always bad men'). The payoff is the maxim and its reasoning (trust no one with ALL the power), not a date. Pairs with Montesquieu's separation of powers in the social-contract strand. Concrete, quotable, kid-graspable.

strands.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas

topics.name: Adam Smith & the Invisible Hand
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: the butcher, brewer & baker feed you from self-interest not benevolence; self-interest unintentionally serving others; division of labor in the pin factory; the impartial spectator inside us from The Theory of Moral Sentiments
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Adam Smith's Moral and Political Philosophy; IEP: Adam Smith; Wealth of Nations (1776) & Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL, method-neutral. The MOVE is unintended order — order arising from people pursuing their own ends, with no designer. Lead T1 with the butcher/brewer/baker: answer = 'we get dinner from their self-interest, not their kindness,' never 'name the book.' Pair this Smith with the sympathy/impartial-spectator Smith so it's one mind, not a caricature. No policy verdict.

topics.name: Hayek & the Knowledge Problem
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: the information to run an economy exists only as scattered fragments in millions of minds; no central planner can gather it; prices condense that knowledge into a single signal; spontaneous order vs designed order; the fatal conceit
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Hayek; Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (American Economic Review, 1945)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL keystone. The recognition is the KNOWLEDGE PROBLEM: the facts needed to plan are dispersed, never held by one mind, so a price is how strangers signal what's scarce. Handle: tin gets scarce, the rising price makes thousands economize with no one ordering it. Choices = rival moves (a planner computes it / a price gathers it). No verdict.

topics.name: Bastiat's Broken Window (The Seen & the Unseen)
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: the shopkeeper's son smashes a window; the crowd says the glazier's work is good for trade; Bastiat's reply — count the suit or shoes the shopkeeper now CAN'T buy; the seen vs the unseen; destruction is never net gain
topics.source: IEP: Frederic Bastiat; Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL, the strand's most kid-graspable MOVE: the SEEN vs the UNSEEN. Lead T1 with the smashed window and the crowd cheering the glazier — answer = 'the shoes the shopkeeper now can't buy,' the cost you DON'T see, never the fallacy's name (to context). Higher tiers apply it to other 'destruction helps trade' claims. Teach the tool; no policy verdict.

topics.name: Bastiat's Candlemakers' Petition
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: Bastiat's satire: candlemakers petition the government to block out the sun (their ruinous free competitor) so lamp- and candle-trades can boom; the absurdity exposes the protectionist logic by pushing it to its limit
topics.source: IEP: Frederic Bastiat; Bastiat, 'The Candlemakers' Petition' / Economic Sophisms (1845)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT, method-neutral. A reductio-as-satire MOVE: the petition pushes 'shut out the cheaper competitor to save our jobs' to its extreme — boarding up windows against the SUN — so the kid feels the argument's structure, not a slogan. Answer = what the joke exposes (that logic on any rival turns absurd), not the label. No verdict.

topics.name: Public Choice (Buchanan & Tullock)
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: politicians and bureaucrats follow incentives too — they aren't selfless angels; concentrated benefits & dispersed costs (a tariff enriches a few firms a lot while costing millions of shoppers pennies each); rent-seeking; rational ignorance
topics.source: IEP: Public Choice Theory; James Buchanan & Gordon Tullock, The Calculus of Consent (1962); Buchanan Nobel Prize (1986)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL, method-neutral. The MOVE is INCENTIVE RECOGNITION applied to government: drop the assumption officials act only for the public good and ask what THEY gain. Handle: concentrated benefits, dispersed costs — a few who gain a lot lobby hard; millions who each lose a little don't notice, so the lobby wins. Choices = rival incentive moves. No verdict.

topics.name: Sowell: Trade-Offs & 'Compared to What?'
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: 'there are no solutions, only trade-offs'; the demand to ask 'compared to WHAT?' and 'and then what happens?'; the constrained vision (humans are limited, weigh trade-offs) vs the unconstrained vision (problems can be solved if we just try)
topics.source: IEP/standard curriculum on Thomas Sowell; Sowell, A Conflict of Visions (1987) & Applied Economics
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL, method-neutral. Two transferable MOVES: 'compared to WHAT?' (judge a plan against the next-best real option, not perfection) and 'only trade-offs, never solutions.' T2 handle: any 'this fixes it' claim — answer = ask what we give up and what happens next, not the slogan. Constrained-vs-unconstrained vision is the T5 rung. No verdict on any policy.

topics.name: Friedman: Results, Not Intentions
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: judge a policy by what it actually DOES, not by what it was meant to do; good intentions are not results; a price ceiling meant to help can create shortages; the discipline of asking about real-world effects
topics.source: Standard curriculum / IEP economics; Milton Friedman, Free to Choose (1980) & Capitalism and Freedom (1962)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT, scrupulously method-neutral. The MOVE is RESULTS-NOT-INTENTIONS: separate what a plan is SUPPOSED to do from what it actually produces, since they can diverge. Handle, no side taken: a rule meant to make something cheaper can backfire, so ask for the measured effect, not the motive. Choices = rival moves (judge by aim / outcome / proposer). No verdict.

topics.name: I, Pencil (Spontaneous Coordination)
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: Leonard Read's essay narrated by a pencil: NO single person on earth knows how to make it — the wood, graphite, brass, rubber, lacquer pull in thousands of strangers who never met and don't share a goal; order without a master plan
topics.source: Standard curriculum / FEE; Leonard E. Read, 'I, Pencil' (1958), later popularized by Milton Friedman
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT, method-neutral; pairs with Smith and Hayek. The MOVE is SPONTANEOUS COORDINATION: a pencil needs more knowledge than any one mind holds, yet uncoordinated strangers make it — loggers, miners, lacquer-makers who never met. Answer = 'no one knows how to make it, yet it appears,' not the author. Friedman popularized Read's essay; don't misattribute.

topics.name: Spontaneous Order vs Designed Order
topics.strand: The Knowledge Problem & Economics of Ideas
topics.scope: the general MOVE behind the strand: some valuable order is MADE on purpose (a watch, an army), some GROWS without a designer (language, footpaths worn across a lawn, money, common law); telling the two apart
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Hayek (spontaneous order); Hayek, Law, Legislation and Liberty; Adam Ferguson on 'the result of human action but not of human design'
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT, method-neutral — the strand's unifying recognition. The MOVE: tell order someone DESIGNED from order that EMERGED from many actions with no plan. Non-economic T2 handles so it's not just markets: a desire-path worn across a lawn, the growth of language, the rise of money. Choices = rival moves (designed / grew / pure chance). No verdict.

topics.name: Karl Marx & the Communist Manifesto
topics.scope: Who Marx was: the exiled, impoverished philosopher-journalist scribbling in the British Museum reading room while his children went hungry; with his lifelong backer Friedrich Engels (a factory owner's son) he wrote the 1848 Manifesto closing 'Workers of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your chains.'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: STORY-LED T1 base, the named subject carries the stem. The vivid hook: a penniless exile predicting the fall of the whole industrial order from a library desk, bankrolled by a capitalist friend. Payoff = the famous closing call or that detail, not 'what year was the Manifesto.' Present him as a real, serious thinker; the historical record gets its own rung. No cartoon villain, no hagiography.

topics.name: Alienation: The Worker Estranged from His Labor
topics.scope: Marx's genuine insight: the factory worker is cut off from the thing he makes (it belongs to the owner and he can't afford it), from the act of working (a numbing fragment on a line, not creative), from his own human nature, and from other people; his labor feels like it belongs to someone else.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx (alienation); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
topics.framing_note: Marx AT HIS STRONGEST — alienation is a real, felt observation, presented as a serious position to reason about, not flame-bait. MOVE topic: a concrete scene (a man who builds beautiful things he will never own, doing one tiny step forever). Answer = the substantive idea (work that should express you instead feels stolen and meaningless), not the label 'alienation.' Choices are real rival readings of factory work. No verdict, no strawman.

topics.name: Historical Materialism & Class Struggle
topics.scope: Marx's engine of history: it's not ideas but ECONOMICS (who owns the means of production) that drives everything; 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles'; the owners (bourgeoisie) versus the workers (proletariat); the base (economy) shapes the superstructure (law, religion, culture).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx (historical materialism); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Marx & Engels, The Communist Manifesto
topics.framing_note: Steel-man the claim: a genuine lens (follow the money to explain a law or a war). MOVE topic — a scene where material interest, not stated ideals, explains a group's behavior. Answer = the substantive move (economics drives the conflict; the haves and have-nots), not the term. Bourgeoisie/proletariat glossed plainly as owners/workers. Present as a real theory to weigh; the T5 fork is whether it explains too much. No verdict.

topics.name: Commodity Fetishism & 'Religion Is the Opium of the People'
topics.scope: Two of Marx's sharpest images: commodity fetishism (we treat the price of a thing as if value lived inside the object, forgetting the human labor and relationships that made it) and 'religion is the opium of the people' (faith as a painkiller that dulls the suffering of the poor instead of curing its cause).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Marx, Capital Vol. I (the fetishism of commodities)
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, higher tier. The opium line is famously misquoted as sneering contempt; the fuller meaning is gentler (a comfort for real pain) — teach the actual nuance. Answer = the substantive idea behind each image (a price hides the human work; faith soothes rather than fixes misery), not the slogan. User is not Christian and the bank takes no verdict on religion — present Marx's claim as his position, symmetric voice, no editorial.

topics.name: The Labor Theory of Value and the Marginalist Reply
topics.scope: Marx held that the value of a good comes from the labor poured into it (so profit is unpaid labor skimmed from the worker); the marginalist revolution (Menger, Jevons, and Böhm-Bawerk's direct critique) answered that value is SUBJECTIVE and set at the margin — the diamond-water puzzle, where life-giving water is cheap and useless diamonds dear.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx (value); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Carl Menger / Austrian economics; Böhm-Bawerk, Karl Marx and the Close of His System
topics.framing_note: Present BOTH at full strength, no false equivalence. State Marx's labor theory honestly as the serious claim it was, then the marginalist refutation as a clean MOVE: the diamond-water paradox shows value can't be just labor (water takes little labor yet sustains life). Answer = the reasoning (value is what the next unit is worth to someone, not hours sunk in), not the names. Method neutral — teach the argument, declare no policy verdict. Glossed terms.

topics.name: The Communist Record: What Actually Happened
topics.scope: The historical ledger stated plainly: regimes built on Marx's promise — the Soviet Union, Maoist China, the Khmer Rouge, and others — produced famine, gulags, and mass killing; The Black Book of Communism documents a death toll on the order of 65 to 100 million across the 20th century.
topics.source: Courtois et al., The Black Book of Communism (Harvard Univ. Press, 1999); AP World History; standard 20th-century historiography
topics.framing_note: moral_vision HONESTY rule: state the record as SOBER FACT, no gloating, no cartoon. This is the factual counterweight to the alienation insight, kept at the same calm register — the bank neither flames Marx nor hides the toll. Answer = the documented fact (the scale of death, the named source), not a sermon. Higher tier and handled with weight, not glee. Pairs with the alienation and ideas rungs as the full, fair picture.

topics.name: Rawls & the Veil of Ignorance
topics.scope: John Rawls' thought experiment: design the rules of society from behind a 'veil of ignorance,' not knowing whether you'll be born rich or poor, gifted or struggling, into any race or family — what rules would you pick if you might be ANYONE? Justice as fairness; the difference principle (inequalities are just only if they help the worst-off most).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Original Position; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Rawls; Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971)
topics.framing_note: The marquee accessible MOVE of modern justice — present at FULL strength, no verdict (it's one of the contested pair). Vivid SCENE: you write society's rules before you know who you'll be. Answer = the move (choose as if you might end up the worst-off, so design for them), or recognizing the veil's purpose. Choices are real positions on fairness. Steel-man it fully even though the bank's own line leans Nozick — this strand declares no winner.

topics.name: Nozick, the Wilt Chamberlain Argument & the Entitlement Theory
topics.scope: Robert Nozick's reply to Rawls: justice is about HOW you got your holdings (justly acquired, justly transferred), not about matching any pattern; the Wilt Chamberlain case — if everyone freely pays a star a quarter to watch him play, the resulting inequality is just, and 'liberty upsets patterns'; taxing earnings to redistribute is likened to forced labor; the minimal night-watchman state.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Robert Nozick's Political Philosophy; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Distributive Justice; Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT (negative rights; no entitlement to another's labor) — but present as a MOVE the player RECOGNIZES, never a declared verdict. The Wilt Chamberlain case is the vivid accessible scene: many free choices add up to inequality — is that unjust? Answer = the reasoning (justice tracks how holdings arose, and keeping liberty means accepting unequal results), not the label. Steel-man Rawls as the live opponent; the fork stays open in its own rung.

topics.name: Rawls vs. Nozick: Fairness or Liberty?
topics.scope: The defining modern-justice fork drawn head to head: Rawls says a just society is arranged to lift its worst-off members, even if that means redistribution; Nozick says a just society protects each person's free choices and rightful holdings, even if that means deep inequality — fairness of outcomes versus liberty of process.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Distributive Justice; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Original Position; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Robert Nozick's Political Philosophy
topics.framing_note: The marquee CONTESTED pairing — apply no-verdict RIGOROUSLY; a thoughtful person on either side must not be marked wrong. Put each side's claim in a character's mouth with a forcing case (the veil vs. Wilt Chamberlain), choices = the two real positions stated at full strength. False equivalence is the failure mode: be substantive on BOTH (Rawls' fairness reasoning AND Nozick's liberty reasoning), not a lukewarm 'both have a point.' The bank's lean stays out of the key.

topics.name: 'From Each According to His Ability, to Each According to His Need'
topics.scope: Marx's famous slogan for the imagined final stage of communism, where labor is given freely by ability and goods are taken freely by need; the enduring objection — what happens to the incentive to produce when reward is detached from effort and contribution?
topics.source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Program (1875); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx
topics.framing_note: MOVE gem, higher tier, kept to a couple of rungs. State the ideal honestly and at its most appealing (contribute what you can, receive what you need), THEN the real, serious objection (incentives) as a competing reasoning move — not a sneer. Answer = the substantive tension (decoupling reward from effort, and what that does to the will to produce), not the slogan as a label. Steel-man the aspiration; let the incentive critique stand on its merits. No verdict declared.

topics.name: Who Nietzsche Was
topics.scope: The lonely, sickly thinker with the enormous mustache: a pastor's son who became a professor at 24, quit over his health, then wandered cheap alpine boarding houses writing in furious bursts between blinding migraines; he collapsed weeping in a Turin street in 1889 (reportedly hugging a beaten horse) and spent his last years mad and silent.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA lead, the named subject carries the stem; vivid T1 base (the mustache, the sickly hermit, the youngest-ever professor). Payoff = a memorable specific fact (writing through agonizing migraines; the Turin breakdown over a flogged horse), never 'what year was he born.' He is the tragic, solitary figure, not a villain — set the human scene the later ideas hang on.

topics.name: God Is Dead
topics.scope: A madman runs into the market with a lantern in daylight crying 'God is dead, and we have killed him' — meaning Europe no longer truly believes the religion it inherited, so the foundation under all its values has quietly fallen away; the dread question is what holds value up now that the old ground is gone.
topics.source: Nietzsche, The Gay Science 125; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE MOVE. CRITICAL: present as a PROBLEM/crisis Nietzsche poses, NOT atheist cheerleading and NOT a boast — the madman is alarmed, even grief-struck. Payoff = the real claim (the shared belief that grounded values has collapsed; where does meaning come from now?), with the lantern-in-daylight scene as the hook. Choices = real responses to the crisis. User is not Christian; no smug believer or atheist voice. No verdict on God.

topics.name: Eternal Recurrence
topics.scope: A demon creeps into your loneliest hour and says: you will live this exact life, every joy and every pain, over and over, infinitely, with nothing new ever added — would you gnash your teeth and curse, or fall down grateful? Nietzsche's test: live so that you would say a wholehearted YES to repeating it forever.
topics.source: Nietzsche, The Gay Science 341; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: A superb personal MOVE with a vivid SCENE (the demon's whisper). Payoff = the test itself — not a cosmology claim but a way to weigh your life: would you will it again, identically, forever? Choices = real life-stances (only the good parts; cursing the deal; affirming the whole). Tie to amor fati (loving your fate). Keep it concrete and personal, not metaphysical proof; no jargon in the stem.

topics.name: The Will to Power
topics.scope: Nietzsche's guess at the basic drive underneath everything alive: not mainly the urge to survive or to feel pleasure, but the urge to grow, to overcome resistance, to master and CREATE — the artist making a work, the athlete pushing a limit, the thinker conquering a problem, all expressing one striving to expand.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic, higher tier. CRITICAL CORRECTION baked in: this is NOT 'crush the weak' or political conquest — his sister and the Nazis reduced it to brute domination; for Nietzsche it is creative self-overcoming (the artist, the scholar, the self disciplining itself). Payoff = the real reading (a drive to grow and create, not just to survive), with everyday handles. Present as one thinker's provocative hypothesis to reason about, no verdict.

topics.name: The Ubermensch (the Overman)
topics.scope: Once the old God-given values have collapsed, who creates new ones? Nietzsche imagines the 'overman' — a person strong and honest enough to forge his OWN values out of himself rather than inherit them from a crowd or a creed; an ideal to grow toward, an answer to 'God is dead,' not a finished super-being.
topics.source: Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic, higher tier, directly answering the 'God is dead' crisis. CRITICAL: this is NOT a master race or a biological superman (the Nazi distortion) — it is a person who creates his own values after the old ones fail. Payoff = that real meaning (self-created values vs inherited ones). Choices = real positions on where values should come from. Keep the German term in context; the idea, not the word, carries the rung.

topics.name: Master Morality, Slave Morality & Ressentiment
topics.scope: Nietzsche's provocative history of how 'good' and 'evil' got their meanings: the strong and confident first called THEMSELVES 'good' (noble, capable) and others merely 'bad'; the weak and resentful then flipped it — branding the strong 'evil' and their own meekness 'good' — a revolt born of envy he calls ressentiment; morality, he argues, has a hidden HISTORY.
topics.source: Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: A MOVE topic to FOLLOW, no verdict — present as Nietzsche's provocative analysis, not endorsed fact. Two payoffs: (1) ressentiment — values arising from suppressed envy; (2) the genealogy move — that our moral words have a history and weren't simply handed down from above. Steel-man it as a serious challenge, but do NOT let it read as 'might makes right' approval. Choices = real readings of where moral labels come from. Terms to context.

topics.name: The Last Man
topics.scope: Nietzsche's nightmare opposite of the overman: the 'last man' — a comfortable, risk-averse, incurious nobody who has invented his little pleasure for the day and his little pleasure for the night, blinks contentedly, takes no chances, asks no hard questions, and is proud to have nothing left to strive for.
topics.source: Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra (Zarathustra's Prologue); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: A MOVE gem with a vivid handle and a lower-tier hook (the smug, blinking, comfort-seeking nobody). Payoff = what Nietzsche FEARS we'll become — a creature so cozy it has stopped reaching, risking, or wondering. Choices = real life-stances (safe contentment vs striving). The 'last man blinks' image is the memorable anchor. A warning, not a slur at ordinary people; keep it about the danger of giving up aspiration.

topics.name: The Nazi Forgery: Setting the Record Straight
topics.scope: Nietzsche DESPISED German nationalism and antisemitism, mocking both in print and breaking with his sister Elisabeth over the Jew-hatred of the colony she founded; after his collapse she seized his papers, stitched unpublished scraps into the book 'The Will to Power' he never sanctioned, forged letters, courted Hitler and Mussolini, and handed the Nazis a Nietzsche he would have loathed.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche; Britannica: Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT correction of a famous smear — honest intellectual history, told straight. Payoff = the real facts (he attacked antisemitism and nationalism; his antisemite sister edited/forged the link and 'The Will to Power' was assembled without his consent). His own line: he called her an antisemitic 'llama' he'd parted from. NO sensationalizing the Nazis; the move is separating what a thinker SAID from what others made of him after he could no longer object.

topics.name: Existence Precedes Essence
topics.scope: A letter-opener is built FOR a purpose that comes before it exists; a person is not — you are flung into the world first, with no instruction manual or fixed nature, and then make yourself by what you choose and do. The existentialist's core move: for a human, existence comes first and the 'what you are' is built afterward, by you.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sartre's Existentialism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism; Sartre, Existentialism is a Humanism
topics.framing_note: THE strand's keystone MOVE and gateway. The letter-opener/paper-knife contrast is the T1 hook: a tool has a purpose before it exists; you don't. Payoff = the real claim (no pre-set human nature; you define yourself by choosing), choices are rival views of where a person's identity comes from. CONTESTED — no verdict on human nature; present as the existentialist's position to reason about. Gloss 'essence' plainly.

topics.name: Kierkegaard's Leap of Faith & the Three Stages
topics.scope: The melancholy Dane who broke off his own engagement to write; his picture of life as three ways to live — the aesthetic (chase pleasure and novelty, then despair of emptiness), the ethical (live by duty and rules), and the religious (a 'leap of faith' to commitment that reason alone can't prove); each higher stage entered by a choice, not an argument.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Kierkegaard, Either/Or
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. T2 hook: the man who jilted his fiancee Regine to devote himself to writing about choice. Payoff = the three-stage ladder and the leap (commitment beyond what reason can guarantee), not 'name the stages' rote. The leap is a real position vs evidentialism (believe only on proof) — no verdict; user is not Christian, present the religious stage straight, no smug believer or atheist voice. Gloss terms.

topics.name: Abraham & the Knight of Faith
topics.scope: Kierkegaard's hardest case: God orders Abraham to kill his own beloved son Isaac, and Abraham raises the knife — is he a would-be murderer or the highest model of faith? Kierkegaard calls it a 'suspension of the ethical': the knight of faith obeys a command above all rules and human reasons, looking utterly ordinary from outside while a storm rages within.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Kierkegaard, Fear and Trembling
topics.framing_note: STORY/DRAMA, higher tier, real weight. The raised knife is the unforgettable SCENE. CONTESTED fork — Kierkegaard asks whether faith can override ethics; present as a genuine, troubling problem with no verdict (the ethical reading 'this is attempted murder' must be a live, defensible choice). The knight of faith looks completely normal — that twist is the payoff. Theology-overlap: tell the Genesis story straight, no doctrinal sneer either way.

topics.name: Anxiety: The Dizziness of Freedom
topics.scope: Kierkegaard's idea that dread is not fear of any one thing but the vertigo of FREEDOM itself — standing at a cliff edge, what grips you is not just the fall but the sickening awareness that you COULD jump, that nothing decides for you; anxiety is 'the dizziness of freedom,' the feeling of facing your own open possibilities.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety
topics.framing_note: A MOVE gem with a vivid handle (the cliff edge: the lurch is realizing you could jump). Payoff = the distinction — anxiety differs from fear: fear has an object, anxiety is the dizziness of facing your own freedom and possibility. Choices = real readings of where dread comes from. Connects forward to Sartre's 'condemned to be free.' Keep it concrete and personal; gloss 'dread/angst' in plain words, no jargon in the stem.

topics.name: Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor
topics.scope: In Dostoevsky's parable, Christ returns and the old Inquisitor jails him, charging that freedom is too heavy for ordinary people: 'You gave them freedom when they needed bread.' Better, he says, to take their terrible liberty away and give them security, miracle, and someone to obey — so they can be happy as contented children rather than free and afraid.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism; Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (Book V)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE, the freedom-vs-security fork. SCENE: the silent Christ, the Inquisitor's accusation that people will trade their freedom for bread and a master. CONTESTED — present the Inquisitor's case at full, unsettling strength (it's persuasive on purpose) AND the answer to it; no verdict. Ties straight to the political strands (Hobbes' security trade, soft despotism) and to Nietzsche's last man. Tell the parable straight; the dilemma carries it.

topics.name: Dostoevsky's Underground Man
topics.scope: Dostoevsky's spiteful narrator who insists a person will act against his own clear self-interest — choose pain, ruin, '2+2=5' — just to prove he is FREE and not a piano key worked by laws; and the haunting worry that 'if God does not exist, everything is permitted' — that with no higher ground, nothing is forbidden.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism; Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground & The Brothers Karamazov
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, higher tier. Two payoffs: (1) the Underground Man's revolt — people will sabotage their own interest to prove they aren't predictable machines (a jab at 'rational self-interest' models); (2) 'everything is permitted' as the moral vertigo when the old ground is gone (pairs with Nietzsche's God-is-dead). CONTESTED — present as a problem posed, no verdict, choices are real responses. Keep the spiteful voice without endorsing nihilism.

topics.name: Sartre: Condemned to Be Free
topics.scope: Sartre's radical claim that there is no excuse: with no God-given purpose and no fixed nature, you are totally responsible for what you make of yourself — even refusing to choose IS a choice. He calls this being 'condemned to be free': freedom is not a gift to enjoy but a weight you can never put down, and blaming your nature or circumstances is a dodge.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sartre's Existentialism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre; Sartre, Being and Nothingness & Existentialism is a Humanism
topics.framing_note: DEEP keystone, the strand's center of gravity. Payoff = the move (radical freedom + total responsibility; 'condemned' because you can't escape choosing). T2 handle: 'I had no choice' is the lie this idea attacks. Choices = real positions on how free and responsible a person is — CONTESTED (a determinist must not be auto-wrong), no verdict. Builds on existence-precedes-essence and Kierkegaard's dread; leads into bad faith.

topics.name: Bad Faith & 'Hell Is Other People'
topics.scope: Sartre's 'bad faith' = lying to yourself that you have no choice — like his café waiter playing TOO perfectly at being a waiter, hiding behind the role so he needn't own his freedom. And 'hell is other people': the gaze of others can pin you into a fixed version of yourself you didn't pick, freezing the free, ever-becoming person into a thing seen from outside.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sartre's Existentialism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre; Sartre, Being and Nothingness & No Exit
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, two vivid scenes. Bad faith: the over-acting waiter pretending his role leaves him no freedom (self-deception about choice). 'Hell is other people': correct the misread — NOT 'people are awful' but the Look fixing you into something you didn't choose, from his play No Exit. Payoff = each real meaning, not the slogan as a label. Choices = real readings of self-deception and the gaze. Higher tier; gloss the French terms in context.

topics.name: Camus & the Myth of Sisyphus
topics.scope: Camus' Absurd: we hunger for meaning and the universe answers with silence, and that clash is 'the absurd.' His image is Sisyphus, doomed by the gods to roll a boulder uphill forever only to watch it roll back — yet Camus says do not despair and do not pretend: face it with revolt, and 'one must imagine Sisyphus happy' in the struggle itself.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Albert Camus; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Albert Camus; Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus
topics.framing_note: DEEP keystone, very high wonder. The boulder rolling back forever is the T2 SCENE. Payoff = the absurd (our craving for meaning vs a silent universe) and Camus' answer (revolt, not despair or false hope; 'imagine Sisyphus happy'). His opening 'the one serious question is whether to go on living' is profound — handle with weight, never glib; choices are real responses to a meaningless task. Ties the bank's meaning-of-life thread together. No verdict on meaning.

topics.name: Camus Rejected the Existentialist Label
topics.scope: Though forever grouped with Sartre, Camus insisted he was NOT an existentialist and disliked the label; the two were friends who later split bitterly (over politics and Camus' rejection of revolutionary violence). His answer to the absurd was not Sartre's system but revolt, lucidity, and solidarity — facing a meaningless world honestly and still choosing to live and to care.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Albert Camus; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Albert Camus
topics.framing_note: A precision mini-gem, higher tier. Payoff = the real fact (Camus refused the existentialist label and broke publicly with Sartre) plus the substance of the difference (revolt and lucidity vs Sartre's framework; the famous falling-out). Corrects the lazy 'they're all the same' grouping. Tell it straight as intellectual history — the split was real and over serious stakes (violence, communism); no taking sides on the quarrel.

topics.name: Simone de Beauvoir: Becoming a Woman
topics.scope: Beauvoir applied existential freedom to women's lives: 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' — meaning the social ROLE of 'woman' is built by upbringing and expectation, not simply handed by birth; she analyzed how women had been cast as 'the Other,' defined always against man as the default, and called for them to claim themselves as free, self-defining people.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Simone de Beauvoir; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Simone de Beauvoir; Beauvoir, The Second Sex
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic. Per equity-feminism (moral_vision): present the REAL argument at its strongest — the 'becomes a woman' line is about social ROLE and expectation, not denying that men and women differ. Payoff = the move ('the Other'; the role is constructed, freedom to define oneself), no caricature in either direction (not flamed as gender ideology, not endorsed as the last word). Note she was Sartre's lifelong partner only insofar as it shaped the work. Gloss 'the Other.'

topics.name: Heidegger: Being-Toward-Death & 'the They'
topics.scope: Heidegger's claim that you live authentically only by facing that YOUR death is yours alone and unavoidable ('being-toward-death') — most people flee it. And 'the They' (das Man): the faceless anonymous crowd — 'they say,' 'one does it this way' — that quietly lives your life FOR you, making your choices by default until you wake up and own them yourself.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Martin Heidegger; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Martin Heidegger; Heidegger, Being and Time
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, the strand's most abstract — keep it top-tier and concrete. Two payoffs: (1) being-toward-death (owning your own mortality wakes you to live authentically); (2) 'the They' — the anonymous 'everyone' that decides for you until you reclaim the choice (a sharp, kid-relatable handle: who is 'they' in 'they say'?). Choices = real positions on conformity and authenticity. Strictly the IDEAS, not the notoriously dense jargon; gloss every term plainly.

topics.name: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems
topics.scope: 1931, age 25: any system big enough for arithmetic holds TRUE statements it can never PROVE; the result that shattered Russell & Whitehead's ten-year Principia
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems; SEP: Kurt Gödel
topics.framing_note: Marquee STORY/DRAMA rung (the SEP/moral_vision exemplar). Lead with the drama: a quiet 25-year-old in 1931 proves that math can never prove all its own truths, ending the dream Russell chased for ten years. Names ARE allowed; payoff = the 1931 result told through CONSEQUENCE (the dream died), never the word 'incompleteness' decoded.

topics.name: Russell's Paradox
topics.scope: the barber who shaves everyone who doesn't shave himself — so who shaves the barber? the self-reference trap that broke Frege's life's work as it went to print
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Russell's Paradox
topics.framing_note: Kid-graspable MOVE goldmine — the barber paradox is pure wonder and a real logical trap. Lead with the barber SCENE: try both answers and both contradict. T4-T5: Russell's letter reaching Frege as Volume II printed, gutting his system. Answer = the contradiction itself (he can't shave himself AND can't not), never the term 'paradox'. Choices are real attempts to escape it.

topics.name: Russell's Theory of Descriptions
topics.scope: 'the present king of France is bald' — not false, but a hidden claim that exactly one such king EXISTS; how to talk sense about things that aren't there
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descriptions; SEP: Bertrand Russell
topics.framing_note: A clean MOVE: a sentence about a king who doesn't exist isn't nonsense — it secretly claims 'there is one and only one king of France, and he's bald,' which is simply FALSE. Lead with the puzzle scene (is the bald-king claim true, false, or meaningless?). Strawson's reply (it's neither — the question doesn't arise) is the live counter. No jargon — the trick is the payoff.

topics.name: Frege: Sense vs Reference
topics.scope: the morning star and the evening star are both Venus — same THING, different way of being given; why 'a = b' can teach you something 'a = a' can't
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Gottlob Frege; SEP: Frege's Theorem and Foundations for Arithmetic
topics.framing_note: A genuinely surprising MOVE. Ancient astronomers tracked a bright morning star and a bright evening star as two things — then learned both are Venus. The discovery was real news, yet 'Venus is Venus' is empty. So a name carries more than what it POINTS at — a way of presenting it. Lead with the star scene; answer = the two-handles insight, not the word 'sense'.

topics.name: Principia Mathematica
topics.scope: Russell & Whitehead's ten-year attempt to derive ALL of math from pure logic; the proof that 1+1=2 arrives hundreds of pages in
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Principia Mathematica; SEP: Bertrand Russell
topics.framing_note: Mini gem (2-3 rungs) that SETS UP Gödel. The wonder fact: two men spent a decade building math up from logic so carefully that '1+1=2' isn't proved until deep in the work. Lead with that absurd-sounding image. The point: the dream was to make mathematics airtight from the ground up — which makes Gödel's later wrecking-ball land. Answer = the audacious goal, not a date.

topics.name: The Liar Paradox & Self-Reference
topics.scope: 'This sentence is false' — if it's true it's false, if it's false it's true; the ancient self-swallowing loop behind Russell's and Gödel's bombshells
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Liar Paradox; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Liar Paradox
topics.framing_note: Mini gem and a kid-magnet — a sentence that calls itself false can be neither true nor false without flipping. Lead with the sentence itself and have the player chase the loop. The cool consequence: this same self-reference trick is the engine Gödel turned on arithmetic. Answer = the loop spelled out (each answer forces its opposite), never the label 'liar paradox'.

topics.name: Early Wittgenstein: the Tractatus
topics.scope: language PICTURES the world; 'whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent'; then, believing he'd solved philosophy, he quit it to teach village schoolchildren
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ludwig Wittgenstein; IEP: Ludwig Wittgenstein
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE. A soldier writes a tiny book claiming he has finished philosophy — meaningful sentences are pictures of facts, and about ethics, God, the meaning of life you must stay silent — then walks away to teach children. Lead with the audacity and the silence line. Half of the drama is that he later DECIDES HE WAS WRONG (sets up the next topic). No jargon; the payoff is the move and the walking-away.

topics.name: Later Wittgenstein: Meaning Is Use
topics.scope: he REVERSED himself — a word's meaning is how it's USED, not a thing it labels; the beetle in the box; language-games; no single trait all 'games' share (family resemblance)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ludwig Wittgenstein; SEP: Private Language
topics.framing_note: Deep keystone — a great intellectual drama: the man who 'finished' philosophy returns and demolishes his OWN book. The beetle-in-the-box (everyone has a private box; whatever's inside drops out of how we use the word) is the marquee MOVE — vivid, kid-graspable. Family resemblance: try to name the one thing ALL games share — you can't. Answer = the move (use, not a hidden object), no jargon.

topics.name: Logical Positivism & the Vienna Circle
topics.scope: a circle of Vienna thinkers ruled a statement meaningful ONLY if you could test it — wiping out metaphysics, ethics, theology as 'nonsense'; then the rule failed its own test
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Vienna Circle; SEP: A.J. Ayer / Verificationism
topics.framing_note: MOVE with a delicious self-destruct payoff. The Circle's verification rule: if you can't test it, it's literally meaningless — so most of old philosophy gets binned. Lead with the bold cull. The kicker the player should land: apply the rule TO ITSELF — 'only testable statements are meaningful' is itself untestable, so by its own law it's nonsense. Answer = that self-refutation, not the term 'positivism'.

topics.name: Popper: Falsifiability
topics.scope: a theory is scientific only if it could be PROVEN WRONG; one black swan beats a thousand white ones; why 'it explains everything' is a weakness, not a strength
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Popper; IEP: Karl Popper
topics.framing_note: Kid-graspable marquee MOVE and a transferable thinking tool. Lead with the swan scene: no pile of white swans PROVES 'all swans are white,' but one black swan kills it — so science advances by trying to break ideas, not confirm them. The sharp twist Popper saw: a theory that 'explains everything' (and so risks nothing) isn't strong, it's unscientific. Answer = the could-it-be-wrong test, never the word 'falsifiability'.

topics.name: Quine: the Web of Belief
topics.scope: no clean line between truths-by-meaning and truths-by-fact; our beliefs face the world as one connected web, and ANY belief can be kept if you revise enough elsewhere
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Quine, Analytic/Synthetic; SEP: W.V. Quine
topics.framing_note: Higher-tier MOVE. Quine attacks the comfortable split between 'true by definition' and 'true by observation' — and pictures all our beliefs as one web hit by experience at the edges, not one statement at a time. Concrete handle: a surprising experiment never forces ONE conclusion — you choose where in the web to make the repair. Answer = the web/holism move, no jargon ('analytic/synthetic' lives in context).

topics.name: Kuhn: Paradigm Shifts
topics.scope: science isn't smooth — long stretches of 'normal science' inside a shared framework, then anomalies pile up and a REVOLUTION swaps the whole worldview (Ptolemy to Copernicus, Newton to Einstein)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Kuhn; The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (Kuhn, 1962)
topics.framing_note: Accessible MOVE — Kuhn says progress isn't a tidy staircase. Lead with a vivid flip (Earth-centered to Sun-centered): for ages everyone works inside one picture, oddities get explained away, until the cracks force a wholesale switch and the old questions stop mattering. Higher tiers: rival paradigms can talk PAST each other (incommensurability). Answer = the normal-then-revolution pattern, not the word 'paradigm'.

topics.name: Foucault's Panopticon
topics.scope: Bentham's ring-shaped prison with one unseen central tower; never knowing if you're watched, you discipline yourself; modern power normalizes rather than forbids; surveillance, schools, grades, credit scores
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Michel Foucault; Foucault, Discipline and Punish (1975)
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE accessible MOVE: the prisoner can't see the guard, so he polices HIMSELF. Lead with the vivid tower-and-cells SCENE; payoff is the recognition that modern power works by watching-and-normalizing, not by chains. Ties straight to the surveillance/grades the kid lives in. Tier-5 idea, zero tier-5 jargon. Critique target steel-manned, no verdict, method neutral.

topics.name: Arendt and the Banality of Evil
topics.scope: Eichmann at his 1961 Jerusalem trial — not a frothing monster but a 'terrifyingly normal' bureaucrat who never stopped to think; evil as thoughtlessness; thinking as the defense against it
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hannah Arendt; Arendt, Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963)
topics.framing_note: Profound and ACCESSIBLE STORY/MOVE: the man who organized deportations was a dull paper-pusher, not a fiend. Lead with the courtroom scene; the move is that the worst evil can come from sheer thoughtlessness, not monstrous hatred. Present the claim straight (it was controversial); the payoff is the unsettling specific, never the label.

topics.name: Husserl and Phenomenology
topics.scope: Describe experience exactly as it appears; bracketing / epoche (set aside whether things are 'really' out there and study how they SHOW UP); intentionality — consciousness is always OF something
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Edmund Husserl; SEP: Phenomenology
topics.framing_note: MOVE-led, more abstract. Bracketing is the marquee move: stop asking 'is it really there?' and describe how it APPEARS to you — a real shift in attitude, not mysticism. Intentionality via a concrete handle: you never just 'see', you see SOMETHING. Gloss 'epoche' plainly. This is the root the rest of the strand grows from; note it feeds Sartre/Heidegger in context.

topics.name: The Frankfurt School & the Culture Industry
topics.scope: Adorno & Horkheimer — mass-produced film/radio/pop manufactures passive consumers and false needs; the dialectic of enlightenment (reason meant to free us turned into a tool of domination)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Frankfurt School / Critical Theory; Adorno & Horkheimer, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947)
topics.framing_note: CRITIQUE TARGET, steel-manned: present the strongest version — entertainment that flatters and sedates instead of challenging really can dull a mind. The move is recognizing the claim that pop culture can be a pacifier. NO strawman, NO sneer, no verdict; the player reasons about it. Concrete handle: the same catchy song everywhere, never anything that makes you think.

topics.name: Derrida and Deconstruction
topics.scope: A text can undermine its own neat oppositions; differance — meaning is never fully present, it's deferred and defined by what a word is NOT; the suspicion of fixed 'true meaning'
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jacques Derrida
topics.framing_note: CRITIQUE TARGET, presented at REAL strength, NO strawman: the genuine insight is that words get their meaning by contrast (light only means something against dark) and a text can quietly contradict itself. The move is recognizing that claim, not parroting jargon. Keep it concrete; high tier. No mockery, no endorsement, no verdict; method neutral.

topics.name: Habermas and Communicative Action
topics.scope: The 'ideal speech situation' — let the better ARGUMENT win, free of coercion and status; reasoning as something we do together in dialogue; rescuing reason from the Frankfurt School's pessimism
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jurgen Habermas; IEP: Habermas
topics.framing_note: MOVE-led, the optimistic answer to Adorno: instead of giving up on reason, build conversations where only the 'unforced force of the better argument' decides. Concrete handle: a debate where no one can pull rank, bribe, or shout you down. The move is recognizing what an honest argument-on-the-merits requires. No verdict; present as a real position.

topics.name: Lyotard and the End of Grand Narratives
topics.scope: 'Incredulity toward metanarratives' — distrust of the big all-explaining stories (Progress, History marching to utopia) that claim to ground everything; only smaller local stories remain
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Francois Lyotard; Lyotard, The Postmodern Condition (1979)
topics.framing_note: CRITIQUE TARGET, steel-manned. The real move: be suspicious of any sweeping story that says 'history is inevitably heading toward X' and uses that to justify itself. Present the strongest version (such grand promises have been used to excuse a lot), no strawman, no verdict. Concrete: a regime promising the glorious end-state that justifies everything. Recognize the move, don't label it.

topics.name: Saussure and Structuralism
topics.scope: Language is a SYSTEM of differences, not a list of names for things; the link between a word and its meaning is arbitrary (no reason 'dog' fits the animal); meaning comes from how signs differ from each other
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ferdinand de Saussure / Structuralism; Saussure, Course in General Linguistics (1916)
topics.framing_note: MOVE-led — the structuralist foundation the whole strand reacts to. Clean accessible move: the word 'dog' isn't dog-like; a different language uses a totally different sound, so the link is arbitrary, and a sign means something only by NOT being the others. Concrete handle: why 'cat' and 'cot' mean different things by one swapped sound. Note it sets up Barthes and Derrida in context.

topics.name: Barthes and the Death of the Author
topics.scope: Once a work is out in the world, the author's intentions don't lock down its meaning; the reader makes meaning; a book is not a coded message from one mind to decode
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy / SEP survey of 20th-century French thought; Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967)
topics.framing_note: Sharp standalone MOVE that pairs with the aesthetics strand's intentional fallacy (cross-reference in context). The real move: should we read a poem by chasing what the writer 'really meant', or by what the words do for the reader? Present as a genuine fork, both sides serious, NO verdict. Concrete handle: a story that means more than its author ever planned. Recognize the move, not the slogan.

topics.name: What Is Knowledge? (Justified True Belief)
topics.scope: The classic three-part recipe for knowledge: a belief that is true AND that you have good reason to hold; why a lucky guess that turns out right isn't knowledge, and why a well-supported false belief isn't either.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Analysis of Knowledge; IEP: Epistemology; Core Knowledge intro philosophy
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, the foundation rung. Settled-structure: there IS a defensible answer here. Build it through concrete scenes (a guess that happens to be right vs a careful, reasoned belief). Answer = which case actually counts as knowing and WHY (you need truth, belief, AND a real reason), not the letters 'JTB'. Sets up Gettier next.

topics.name: The Gettier Problem
topics.scope: Justified true belief that's true only by LUCK: the stopped clock that happens to be right at the moment you glance; the man who sees a dog he mistakes for a sheep while a real sheep hides behind the hill; you believe truly, with good reason, but did you KNOW?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Analysis of Knowledge; IEP: Gettier Problems; Edmund Gettier 1963
topics.framing_note: Marquee MOVE topic, settled-structure (defensible answer per the no-verdict carve-out). The stopped clock is the killer T1-T2 scene. Answer = the recognition that the belief was made TRUE by luck, so the justification and the truth come apart — that's why it's not knowledge. Never 'name the 1963 paper'; the paper/Gettier go in context.

topics.name: The Brain in a Vat
topics.scope: How do you know you're not a brain floating in a vat, wired to a machine feeding you every sight, sound, and feeling? The modern evil demon — the Matrix made into a puzzle; can you ever rule it out from the inside?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Skepticism; Hilary Putnam, Reason Truth and History (1981); IEP: Brains in a Vat
topics.framing_note: Marquee accessible MOVE — lead with the vivid scene (the Matrix is the kid's handle). Genuinely open skeptical question: present competing positions (you can't prove it / Putnam's reply that the words wouldn't even mean what you think / it doesn't matter for living). No verdict on whether you ARE one. Descartes' demon lineage noted in context.

topics.name: The Regress Problem & the Agrippan Trilemma
topics.scope: Every reason you give needs ITS OWN reason — and so on. So your beliefs must end one of three unhappy ways: in a circle (it proves itself), in an endless chain that never bottoms out, or by just STOPPING at something you assert without proof. Three bad exits, no fourth.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Skepticism / Epistemic Justification; Sextus Empiricus on Agrippa; Münchhausen trilemma (Hans Albert)
topics.framing_note: Higher-tier MOVE. Build it as a relentless child asking 'but WHY?' until the three exits appear. Answer = recognizing which of the three horns a given chain of reasons lands on (circle / endless / arbitrary stop). Keep 'Agrippan/Münchhausen' in context; the puzzle is in the stem. The fix-attempts (foundationalism, coherentism) are the next topic.

topics.name: Foundationalism vs Coherentism
topics.scope: Two rival answers to the regress: does knowledge rest on a BEDROCK of basic beliefs that need no further support (the foundation of a building), or does it hang together as a self-supporting WEB where each belief is held up by the others (a raft, not an anchor)?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Foundationalist Theories of Epistemic Justification; Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification; IEP: Epistemology
topics.framing_note: Contested MOVE — genuinely open, no verdict. Put each view in a character's mouth with the vivid image (the building on bedrock vs the web/raft holding itself up). Choices = the two structures plus the trilemma-fork they each answer. The kid's job is to match the reasoning to the picture, not to crown a winner or recite '-ism' definitions.

topics.name: Moore's 'Here Is One Hand'
topics.scope: The commonsense pushback at the skeptic: hold up one hand, then the other — 'here is one hand, and here is another, so an outside world exists.' Moore's bet that he's MORE certain of his hands than of any clever argument that they might be illusions.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Skepticism; G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World' (1939); IEP: Epistemology
topics.framing_note: Accessible MOVE with a memorable gesture. Answer = the structure of Moore's reply — flip the skeptic's argument: since I'm SURER my hands are real than I am of the skeptical premises, the saner move is to doubt the premises. Open question, present as a real position the skeptic can push back on, no verdict; 'Moore' goes in context.

topics.name: The Problem of Other Minds
topics.scope: You feel your own pain and joy directly — but you only ever SEE other people's behavior, never their inner experience. So how do you know anyone else is truly conscious, and not a clever robot acting the part? The inference from 'acts like me' to 'feels like me'.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Other Minds; IEP: Problem of Other Minds
topics.framing_note: Vivid MOVE — the robot/zombie handle is irresistible to kids. Genuinely open: present the analogy argument (they're built like me and act like me, so they likely feel like me) AND its weakness (a sample of one — yourself). Choices = real positions, no verdict on whether others are conscious. Pairs with philosophical zombies in the mind strand; cross-ref in context.

topics.name: The Problem of Induction (Russell's Chicken)
topics.scope: The chicken is fed by the farmer every single morning, so it 'reasonably' expects breakfast — until the morning its neck is wrung. Past patterns never GUARANTEE the future; no amount of sunrises proves the sun rises tomorrow. Why our most natural inference has no logical lock.
topics.source: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Problem of Induction; David Hume lineage
topics.framing_note: Pure vivid wonder + a transferable MOVE. The doomed chicken is the unforgettable scene. Settled-structure on the LOGICAL point: answer = recognizing that piling up past cases never logically forces the next one — the future could break the pattern. Hume's deeper version and 'induction' go in context. Ties to Hume in the empiricists strand.

topics.name: The Lottery & Preface Paradoxes
topics.scope: It's rational to believe your one ticket will lose — yet that holds for EVERY ticket, and one must win. And an author rationally believes each sentence of her careful book, yet also rationally admits the book surely contains some error. When 'very probably true' and 'flat-out believe it' come apart.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epistemic Paradoxes; Henry Kyburg (lottery); D.C. Makinson 1965 (preface)
topics.framing_note: Higher-tier MOVE for the strand's ceiling. Concrete handles (your raffle ticket; the honest author's disclaimer). Answer = spotting the tension between believing something because it's overwhelmingly LIKELY and the fact that a heap of such beliefs can't all be held without contradiction. Open structural puzzle, competing responses; names to context. Keeps the technical bite without jargon.

topics.name: Descartes' Dream Argument
topics.scope: Right now — how do you know you're not dreaming? Dreams feel totally real from inside; you've been fooled before. If no certain mark separates waking from dreaming, can you trust ANY belief drawn from the senses? The doubt that launches modern philosophy.
topics.source: René Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy (1641), Meditation I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Epistemology; Zhuangzi's butterfly cross-reference
topics.framing_note: Strong T1-T2 base for the strand — every kid has had a too-real dream. MOVE topic: answer = the recognition that without a reliable test to tell dreaming from waking, sense-based certainty crumbles. Open skeptical question, no verdict on whether you're dreaming. Echoes Zhuangzi's butterfly (Daoism strand) and feeds Descartes' cogito in the rationalists strand — note in context.

topics.name: The Ship of Theseus
topics.scope: A ship has every rotted plank swapped one at a time over years; T-late adds Hobbes' twist: hoard the old planks and rebuild a SECOND ship from them. Same ship? Which is the real one?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Identity Over Time; Material Constitution; IEP: Persistence in Time
topics.framing_note: Vivid T1 base: replace one plank, still your ship? Build the staircase one plank at a time to the fission twist (restored ship vs reassembled old planks). CONTESTED persistence puzzle — no verdict: choices are real moves (continuity of form, original matter, spatiotemporal path). The SCENE is the question; never 'how many planks' rote.

topics.name: The Sorites Paradox (the heap)
topics.scope: Remove one grain from a heap — still a heap. Repeat. Since one grain never makes the difference, you reach the absurd 'no grains make a heap.' Where does the heap stop? Bald, tall, rich follow the same form.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sorites Paradox (Wright's 'tolerance'; the forced march)
topics.framing_note: Vivid handle: when does a pile of sand stop being a 'heap'? The MOVE is spotting that vague words tolerate tiny changes yet collapse over many. Choices are real responses (no sharp line exists / there's a hidden cutoff we can't see / 'heap' has degrees). Pairs with the line-drawing fallacy; the answer is the reasoning, not 'vagueness' as a word.

topics.name: Personal identity over time
topics.scope: Are you the same person as your 4-year-old self — sharing no atoms, almost no memories? The contested fork: the memory/psychological view (Locke), the same-body view, the same-soul view, and the no-self view.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Personal Identity; Locke on Personal Identity; IEP: Personal Identity
topics.framing_note: Accessible T2 lead: are you the same person as your kindergarten photo? Marquee CONTESTED fork — put each criterion in a character's mouth with a forcing case (amnesia, a swap), choices are competing schools, and a defender of any view must NOT be markable wrong. Cross-reference Indian no-self (anatta) and Heraclitus' flux in context. No -ism jargon in the stem.

topics.name: Parfit's teleporter
topics.scope: A scanner records every atom, destroys your body, and rebuilds a perfect copy on Mars — did YOU travel, or die while a duplicate wakes up? Parfit's twist: the scanner malfunctions and makes TWO copies. Which is you?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Personal Identity (Parfit; branching/fission; 'what matters' is continuity, not identity)
topics.framing_note: Sci-fi SCENE kids love (Star Trek transporter). CONTESTED — no verdict: Parfit's own claim ('survival isn't identity; what matters is continuity') is ONE character's position among rivals (you die and a copy lives / you survive as the copy / identity just fails to apply). The branching case is the forcing constraint — one body can't be two. Choices are real moves, not labels.

topics.name: The statue and the lump of clay
topics.scope: A sculptor shapes clay into a statue. The lump and the statue sit in the exact same place, made of the exact same stuff — yet squash it and the statue dies while the lump lives on. One object here, or two?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Material Constitution (the David/Lump coincidence puzzle)
topics.framing_note: Concrete scene: smash the statue and the clay survives but the statue doesn't — so they have different fates in the same spot. CONTESTED constitution puzzle, no verdict: choices are real moves (two coincident things / one thing under two descriptions / the statue is just clay-arranged-statue-wise). The forcing wedge is the differing survival conditions. Keep it about the puzzle, not 'constitution' as a term.

topics.name: Endurance vs. perdurance (how things persist)
topics.scope: Is a banana wholly present at every moment of its life (it endures, all of it here now), or is the whole banana a four-dimensional 'worm' and today's banana just one TIME-SLICE of it (it perdures)?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Temporal Parts; IEP: Persistence in Time (endurantism / perdurantism / four-dimensionalism)
topics.framing_note: Technical, so keep it T4-T5 and lean. Plain handle: is 'you' fully here right now, or is the real you the whole life-long stretch and today is one slice of it? CONTESTED — no verdict: choices are the two genuine rival pictures (wholly-present-each-moment vs. a sum of time-parts), plus how each one dissolves the Ship of Theseus. Ban 'perdurantism' from the stem; the SCENE-image carries it.

topics.name: Does only the present exist? (presentism vs. eternalism)
topics.scope: Is the past truly GONE and the future not yet real, so only NOW exists? Or are all times equally real — yesterday's breakfast and next year's birthday as real as this instant — the 'block universe' where 'now' is like 'here'?
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Eternalism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Temporal Parts (presentism / block universe)
topics.framing_note: Wonder hook: is the dinosaur era still 'out there' the way Australia is, just somewhere you can't reach? CONTESTED — no verdict: put each view in a character's mouth (only the present is real / all times are equally real / the past is fixed but the future open), choices are real positions. The 'now is like here' analogy is the vivid payoff. No physics jargon; keep it intuitive.

topics.name: Free will vs. determinism
topics.scope: If every event is fixed by prior causes — the same way a struck billiard ball MUST roll — then were your 'choices' ever really up to you? The clean three-way fork: hard determinism, libertarian free will, and the compatibilist middle.
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Free Will; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Compatibilism
topics.framing_note: T2 base via a vivid handle (the falling domino had no choice — do you?). Marquee CONTESTED debate — apply no-verdict hard: three genuine positions (choices are an illusion / there's real undetermined freedom / freedom is acting on your own desires even if caused), each in a character's mouth. A libertarian and a hard determinist must BOTH be safe from being marked wrong. Choices state the reasoning, never the -ism.

topics.name: Laplace's demon
topics.scope: Laplace imagined a mind that knows every atom's position and speed plus all the laws — it could compute the entire future and the entire past in one formula. If such prediction is possible, is there any room left for a free choice?
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Free Will; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Causal Determinism (Laplace's demon)
topics.framing_note: Vivid SCENE: a super-intellect reads the universe like a clock and foretells your next word. The MOVE is seeing what the demon assumes (total determinism) and where it could fail (quantum indeterminacy, or that prediction needn't kill freedom). CONTESTED — no verdict: choices are real replies (foreknowledge defeats freedom / chance reopens it / being predictable isn't being unfree). Pairs with free-will/determinism.

topics.name: Compatibilism (freedom in a caused world)
topics.scope: The middle move: freedom isn't escaping causes — it's acting on YOUR OWN desires without being forced. A man choosing tea over coffee acts freely even if caused; a man with a gun to his head does not. Hume's and Frankfurt's reconciling line.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Compatibilism; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Free Will (Hume; Frankfurt)
topics.framing_note: The reconciling MOVE: redefine 'free' as unforced-and-acting-on-your-own-will, so determinism and responsibility can both be true. CONTESTED — no verdict: present it as a serious position AND its strongest objection (the consequence argument: if the past + laws fix everything, you couldn't have done otherwise). A hard incompatibilist must not be marked wrong. Choices are reasoning moves; vivid handle = coerced vs. uncoerced choice.

topics.name: Frankfurt's willing addict (could you have done otherwise?)
topics.scope: Frankfurt's case: a man takes the drug he's addicted to — but he also WANTS to want it; the addiction is beside the point, he'd choose it anyway. Plus the neuroscientist who'd intervene only if you wavered (but you never do): responsible, with no other option open?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Compatibilism (Frankfurt cases; second-order desires; Principle of Alternative Possibilities)
topics.framing_note: Subtle T4-T5 capstone. Two clean MOVES: (1) the willing addict shows freedom can be about endorsing your OWN desire, not about whether you could have resisted; (2) the standby-neuroscientist case attacks 'you're only responsible if you could have done otherwise.' CONTESTED — no verdict: choices are real positions (alternatives still needed / endorsement is what matters / the setup begs the question). The drama is in the dilemma; name the principle in context only.

topics.name: The Turing Test / Imitation Game
topics.scope: Turing's question: if a machine converses by teletype so well you can't tell it from a human, is that enough to call it thinking? Replace 'can machines think?' with a behavioral test.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Turing Test; Turing 1950 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (Mind)
topics.framing_note: STORY+MOVE; the accessible T1 anchor. Turing's move: drop the unanswerable 'can it think?' and substitute a concrete test (indistinguishable conversation). Answer = the substitution itself, or its classic limit (behavior may not equal understanding). Ban 'does the computer really feel'; ask which move Turing makes.

topics.name: Mary's Room / The Knowledge Argument
topics.scope: Jackson's color scientist who knows ALL the physics of vision but has only ever seen black-and-white; when she finally sees red, does she learn a new fact? If yes, physical facts aren't all the facts.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Qualia: The Knowledge Argument (Frank Jackson 1982 'Epiphenomenal Qualia')
topics.framing_note: The marquee MOVE of the strand. Scene-led: complete physical knowledge, first sight of red. The defensible move is the knowledge-argument structure (if she gains a fact, physicalism is incomplete). Choices are real replies (new fact / only a new ability / no new fact). Note Jackson later doubted his own argument in context.

topics.name: The Chinese Room
topics.scope: Searle's man in a room shuffling Chinese symbols by a rulebook he follows blindly; outsiders think the room understands Chinese, but he understands nothing. Syntax (symbol-shuffling) is not semantics (meaning).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Chinese Room Argument (John Searle 1980 'Minds, Brains, and Programs')
topics.framing_note: Keystone MOVE: 'syntax is not semantics' — running a program never yields genuine understanding. Lead with the vivid room. Answer = that distinction, or the famous Systems Reply (maybe the whole room understands even if the man doesn't). Present reply as a real rival, no verdict on which wins. Ban 'does AI truly understand' as an open-ender.

topics.name: Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?'
topics.scope: Even with every physical fact about a bat's echolocating brain, you can't know what it's LIKE to be the bat from the inside; the subjective point of view escapes objective physical science.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Consciousness; Thomas Nagel 1974 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (Philosophical Review)
topics.framing_note: MOVE: the gap between objective description and subjective experience (the 'what-it's-like'). Vivid handle: full bat-brain science, still no clue what sonar-perceiving FEELS like. Answer = the subjectivity point, not 'bats are weird.' Pairs with Mary's Room as a cousin argument; cross-reference in context. Defensible target: which limit Nagel identifies.

topics.name: The Mind-Body Problem (the framing fork)
topics.scope: How do mind and body relate? The contested fork: dualism (mind is non-physical), materialism/identity theory (mind just IS the brain), and functionalism (mind = what a system DOES, not what it's made of).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Dualism; Mind/Brain Identity Theory; Functionalism
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED — strict no-verdict. Put each position in a character's mouth with its reasoning (Descartes' thinking-thing vs the brain-IS-mind reply vs 'mind is software not hardware'). Choices match the stated reasoning; a competent holder of any view must not be marked wrong. Pairs with Descartes' dualism in the Rationalists strand. The fork is the lesson, not a winner.

topics.name: Philosophical Zombies & the Hard Problem
topics.scope: A 'zombie' physically identical to you, behaving identically, but with NO inner experience whatsoever; if that's even conceivable, physical facts alone can't explain consciousness — Chalmers' 'hard problem'.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Zombies; David Chalmers 1995 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness'
topics.framing_note: Hardest tier-cap MOVE; keep it accessible. The zombie's move: conceivability of an experience-free physical duplicate suggests experience is something extra (the hard problem = why is there felt experience at all?). Answer = that structural point or its rebuttal (maybe zombies aren't really conceivable). CONTESTED — no verdict; present both as serious positions.

topics.name: Leibniz's Mill
topics.scope: Leibniz: imagine a thinking machine blown up to the size of a mill you can walk inside; you'd see only gears pushing gears, never a single perception. Mechanism alone seems unable to show you a thought.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Leibniz's Philosophy of Mind; Leibniz, Monadology §17
topics.framing_note: MOVE + wonder; a 1714 ancestor of the Chinese Room and 'where in the brain is the feeling?' Vivid: stroll among giant gears, find no perception among the parts. Answer = the move (you won't FIND experience by inspecting mechanism), not 'mills are big.' Defensible structure; present the materialist reply (experience isn't a part, it's the whole working) as a real rival.

topics.name: The Inverted Spectrum
topics.scope: What if your inner experience of red is what I'd call green, and vice versa — yet we both learned the word 'red' for tomatoes, so we'd never detect the swap? A challenge to whether experience is captured by behavior or function.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Inverted Qualia; Functionalism (Block & Fodor; Shoemaker)
topics.framing_note: MOVE: if a systematic color-swap leaves all behavior identical, then the felt quality (quale) floats free of function — a problem for functionalism. Vivid handle: my red could be your green and no test reveals it. Answer = that point (behavior under-determines inner experience) or the reply that an undetectable difference is no difference. No verdict.

topics.name: The Ship of the Self: The Brain Transplant
topics.scope: Locke-style: if your memories and personality could be transplanted into another body, who wakes up — you, or them? Tests whether 'you' tracks the brain/mind or the body. (Personhood follows continuity of mind, not matter.)
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Personal Identity; John Locke 'Essay' II.xxvii (the prince and the cobbler)
topics.framing_note: CONTESTED identity MOVE within mind. Forcing scene: your mind in another's body — who is who? Choices = the real schools (memory/psychological view, body view, soul view). Match the character's stated reasoning; no verdict. Cross-references the metaphysics strand's Ship of Theseus and Parfit's teleporter; keep the SCENE the question, the vocabulary in context.

topics.name: The Trolley Problem
