topics.scope: Divert the runaway trolley to kill one instead of five; the Footbridge twist (PUSH the large man to stop it); the surgeon who could harvest one healthy patient to save five — why pulling a lever feels different from pushing a person.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Doing vs. Allowing Harm; IEP: Trolley Problem (Foot 1967, Thomson 1985); Core Knowledge / AP ethics survey
topics.framing_note: Marquee CONTESTED fork — vivid scene leads, choices are real positions (most save five / killing is not letting-die / using a person as a tool is the line), NO verdict. The payoff is WHY footbridge feels different (doing vs allowing; means vs side-effect), never 'one or five' arithmetic. Names (Foot, Thomson) go to context.

topics.name: Consequentialism / Utilitarianism (the move)
topics.scope: Judge an act by its RESULTS — the greatest good for the greatest number; Bentham's felicific calculus; Mill's higher vs lower pleasures ('better Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied'); act vs rule versions; the move applied to a concrete dilemma.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Consequentialism; IEP: Utilitarianism (Bentham, J.S. Mill)
topics.framing_note: Present as a MOVE the player APPLIES (count up who's helped vs harmed), not a label to recall. T1 base: 'which choice helps the most people?' The marquee tension — would it justify sacrificing one innocent for many? — is the live fork, no verdict. Mill's 'Socrates dissatisfied' line is the vivid payoff. Bentham/Mill to context.

topics.name: Deontology / Duty (the move)
topics.scope: Some acts are just WRONG no matter the outcome; act from duty, not consequences; rights and rules that can't be traded away; a promise that binds even when breaking it would help more — the duty move set against the consequences move.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Deontological Ethics; IEP: Kant's Moral Philosophy
topics.framing_note: A MOVE the player applies, not a label. The handle: 'are there things you must not do even to make things turn out better?' Pairs against utilitarianism as the live fork (the innocent-sacrifice case splits them). Keep Kant's machinery in the dedicated Kant strand; here teach the duty-vs-results contrast through a concrete scene. No verdict on which wins.

topics.name: Virtue Ethics (the move)
topics.scope: Don't ask 'what's the rule?' or 'what are the outcomes?' — ask 'what would a GOOD person do here?'; character over calculation; the courageous/honest/generous person as the measure; how virtue ethics answers a dilemma differently from rules or results.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Virtue Ethics; IEP: Virtue Ethics (Aristotelian lineage)
topics.framing_note: The third MOVE — the player asks what a person of good character would actually DO. Vivid T1 handle: 'what would the bravest, kindest person you know do?' Set beside the duty move and the results move so the three become tools the player picks up, not -ism labels. Aristotle's full apparatus lives in his own strand; here it's the character-first lens applied to a scene.

topics.name: Nozick's Experience Machine
topics.scope: A machine that floods you with guaranteed bliss for life — any experience you want, indistinguishable from real — but you float in a tank, doing nothing real. Would you plug in forever? Most refuse — so pleasure can't be ALL that matters.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hedonism; Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974); IEP: Robert Nozick
topics.framing_note: A clean MOVE-argument against pure hedonism — the SCENE is the question, choices are real positions (plug in / refuse because we want to DO things, contact reality, BE a certain person). The payoff is the reasoning ('if pleasure were everything you'd plug in — but you wouldn't'), not the word 'hedonism'. No verdict on whether to plug in; the lesson is what the refusal reveals.

topics.name: The Utility Monster & the Repugnant Conclusion
topics.scope: Two famous problems FOR utilitarianism: Nozick's utility monster (a being that gets so much more pleasure from each resource that the math says feed it everything, starving everyone else); Parfit's repugnant conclusion (the total-happiness sum prefers billions of barely-worth-living lives to a smaller, thriving population).
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Repugnant Conclusion; Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia; Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984)
topics.framing_note: Higher-tier MOVE topics — both expose where 'maximize total welfare' breaks against intuition. Vivid handles: the insatiable monster the calculus must feed; the swarm of barely-OK lives the sum 'prefers'. Choices are real responses (bite the bullet / reject pure aggregation / cap it). No verdict — these are stress-tests of a theory, not refutations declared. Nozick/Parfit to context.

topics.name: The Doctrine of Double Effect
topics.scope: The line between INTENDING a harm and merely FORESEEING it as a side-effect: the bomber who targets civilians vs the one whose strike on a factory foreseeably kills nearby civilians; giving pain medicine that eases suffering but foreseeably hastens death — same outcome, different moral verdict?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Doctrine of Double Effect; IEP: Principle of Double Effect (Aquinas lineage)
topics.framing_note: A subtle MOVE — the player learns to spot the intend/foresee distinction that splits cases with identical outcomes. It's the engine UNDER the trolley footbridge contrast, so cross-reference. Choices are real positions (intention changes the verdict / only outcomes matter / it's a dodge). Concrete medical and rescue scenes, not the Latin name. Aquinas to context. No verdict on whether the doctrine holds.

topics.name: Singer's Drowning Child
topics.scope: Peter Singer's challenge: you'd wade in and ruin an expensive new outfit to save a drowning child in front of you — so why is letting a faraway child die of a preventable disease, when your money could save them, any different? Distance and numbers, he argues, are morally irrelevant.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Peter Singer / The Demandingness Objection; Singer, 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT: Singer's impartialism is the explicit FOIL. Present the argument at FULL strength (the parallel is genuinely uncomfortable) — then the live fork is the demandingness reply and the distance/relationship reply, set up so 'One Thought Too Many' can answer it. Choices are real positions, no verdict; the player meets the strongest case for impartial duty AND the grounds to push back.

topics.name: 'One Thought Too Many' (Williams)
topics.scope: Bernard Williams: a man can save only one of two drowning people; one is his wife; he saves her. If he first pauses to confirm it's morally PERMITTED to favor his wife, he's had 'one thought too many' — the love itself should be reason enough. Impartiality asks too much.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Impartiality / Bernard Williams; Williams, 'Persons, Character and Morality' (1981)
topics.framing_note: VISION-CENTRAL: partiality is the SUBSTANTIVE position, the direct answer to Singer's foil — that a parent for a child, a spouse for a spouse, rightly acts WITHOUT first running an impartial calculation. The vivid payoff is the 'one thought too many' line itself. Choices are real positions (partiality is justified / impartiality still binds / it depends). Steel-man the impartialist reply; no verdict, but the bank's weight is here.

topics.name: Moral Luck
topics.scope: Two equally reckless (or equally negligent — both skipped a brake check) drivers; one happens to have a child step into the road and kills them, the other's road is clear. Same choice, same character — but we blame one far more. Can luck in how things turn out change how guilty you are?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Moral Luck (Nagel & Williams, 1979); IEP: Moral Luck
topics.framing_note: A marquee CONTESTED MOVE — genuinely open, no verdict. The vivid twin-driver scene carries it. Choices are real positions (guilt tracks the act/will only, so they're equally culpable / outcomes matter, so the killer is worse / luck is everywhere and undermines blame). Nagel/Williams to context. Pairs with the free-will strand (control and responsibility) — cross-reference.

topics.name: Moral Relativism vs Realism
topics.scope: Are right and wrong DISCOVERED (real facts, true everywhere, like math) or INVENTED (made by each culture or person)? The relativist points to how customs differ across societies; the realist points to things that seem wrong everywhere (torturing a child for fun). The clash over whether morality is objective.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Moral Realism; Moral Relativism; IEP: Ethical Relativism
topics.framing_note: A CONTESTED foundational fork — no verdict. The claim goes in a character's mouth ('different cultures, different morals, so none is truly right'), choices are competing positions (cultural relativism / individual subjectivism / moral realism / the disagreement is overstated). The vivid handle: a custom one culture honors and another condemns vs an act that looks wrong everywhere. Avoid the cheap 'tolerance refutes itself' gotcha — present each side at strength.

topics.name: Care Ethics
topics.scope: Morality grounded in CARE and concrete relationships rather than abstract rules or sums — Gilligan's 'different voice' and Noddings' caring relation; the mother-child bond as the model of moral response; then the real scrutiny: dependency, scaling beyond those near to us, root causes, and parochialism.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Feminist Ethics / The Ethics of Care; Gilligan, In a Different Voice (1982); Noddings, Caring (1984)
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT: care ethics is DEFINED FAIRLY THEN SCRUTINIZED — never endorsed, never strawmanned. Define it at its real strongest (attending to actual people in relationship vs cold rule-following), then the live forks are the standard critiques: does it scale past those we already love? does it neglect justice and root causes? does it trap the carer in dependency? Choices are real positions, no verdict. Gilligan/Noddings to context.

topics.name: The Is-Ought Problem in Ethics
topics.scope: Hume's gap applied to morality: you can pile up all the FACTS about the world (what IS) and never logically squeeze out a single OUGHT. 'It's natural' or 'most people do it' describes how things ARE — it doesn't prove how they SHOULD be. The hidden leap from description to prescription.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hume's Moral Philosophy; IEP: Hume (the is/ought gap, Treatise III)
topics.framing_note: A clean transferable MOVE — the player learns to spot the silent jump from 'is' to 'ought' in a moral argument (and ties to the appeal-to-nature fallacy). 2-3 gems: name the leap in a concrete claim ('animals do X, so people should too'). Defensible answer here — this is a recognized logical point, not an open metaphysical fork — so KEY the spotting of the gap. Hume to context; no policy verdict attached.

topics.name: What Is Art? Duchamp's Fountain
topics.scope: In 1917 Marcel Duchamp bought a plain porcelain urinal, turned it on its back, signed it 'R. Mutt 1917,' titled it 'Fountain,' and submitted it to a New York art show that had promised to reject nothing — and its own committee threw it out anyway; a found factory object, picked and renamed, that forces the question of what could possibly separate art from a plumbing fixture.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Definition of Art; Britannica: Fountain (Duchamp); Tate: Readymade
topics.framing_note: STORY + MOVE keystone, the vivid T1 base. Lead with the scene (a signed urinal rejected by a no-rejection show). CONTESTED, NO verdict — payoff is the puzzle: is art the OBJECT, the artist's act of CHOOSING and naming it, or what an art-world accepts? Choices = rival answers in plain words, never '-ism' labels.

topics.name: Beauty: In the Object or the Eye of the Beholder?
topics.scope: The oldest aesthetics fork: is beauty a real feature OUT THERE in the thing, or only a feeling IN US? Hume says taste varies but some judges really are better — a trained palate that can tell fine wine from plonk, so there is a 'standard of taste'; Kant says the pleasure is subjective yet 'disinterested' (you want nothing FROM the rose, you just behold it) — and strangely we still speak as if everyone OUGHT to agree.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Hume's Aesthetics; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Aesthetics; Hume, Of the Standard of Taste
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE CONTESTED move — NO verdict; the claim sits in a character's mouth, choices are real positions (beauty in the object / only in the viewer / Hume's better-judges middle). Payoffs: Hume's expert palate (taste isn't just 'whatever you like') and Kant's puzzle (a personal pleasure that still claims to bind everyone). The wine-judge handle anchors T2.

topics.name: The Sublime
topics.scope: Beauty's overwhelming cousin: standing safe at the rail while a thunderstorm splits the sky, or craning up at an Alpine cliff that dwarfs you — a strange pleasure braided with terror and awe; Burke tied it to a thrill of fear felt from safety, and Kant said the vast or violent first crushes our imagination, then thrills us because our MINDS can still grasp the infinite the senses can't hold.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Sublime; Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful; Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment
topics.framing_note: MOVE topic, scene-led hook (the storm watched from shelter; the towering peak). Payoff = the real distinction: the sublime is awe-mixed-with-dread at the vast or mighty, NOT mere prettiness, pleasing us at a safe remove. Choices = real readings of why terror can feel exhilarating. Keep Burke/Kant in context; the SCENE and feeling carry the rungs. No verdict needed.

topics.name: The Paradox of Fiction
topics.scope: You grip the armrest as the monster stalks the heroine, your heart pounding for someone you KNOW does not exist — yet you don't leap up to warn her or call for help; so how can we genuinely feel fear, pity, or grief for characters we're certain are made up, when real emotions are supposed to need real beliefs that the thing is actually there?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Definition of Art; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Paradox of Fiction; Kendall Walton, Fearing Fictions
topics.framing_note: A kid-graspable MOVE puzzle — lead with the visceral scene (terror for a character you know is fake). Payoff = the rival escapes: maybe it isn't REAL fear but a make-believe 'quasi-emotion' (Walton); maybe we vividly imagine it true; maybe emotions don't require belief. Choices = those positions plainly. The replies are the lesson; no verdict, no jargon.

topics.name: The Paradox of Tragedy
topics.scope: We pay good money to be made miserable: a play or film that leaves us weeping and wrung-out, and we call it GREAT and come back for more — why would anyone seek out art built to cause sorrow? Aristotle's old answer was catharsis (the drama purges pity and fear, leaving us lighter); Hume thought the artistry itself converts the painful feeling into something we relish.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aesthetics of the Everyday; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aristotle's Poetics; Hume, Of Tragedy
topics.framing_note: A kid-graspable MOVE puzzle, sibling to the fiction paradox. Lead with the oddity (choosing the sad film, calling the cry 'worth it'). Payoff = rival explanations: catharsis (a purge that leaves you relieved) vs Hume's idea that beautiful telling turns pain into pleasure vs we value meaning over comfort. Choices = those positions, plainly worded. Gloss 'catharsis'. No verdict.

topics.name: The Intentional Fallacy
topics.scope: Does what a poem MEANS depend on what its author was trying to say? Wimsatt and Beardsley argued NO — once a work is out in the world it stands on its own, and 'the poet's aim' is neither available nor decisive; the words mean what they mean. So if the author insists 'I meant X' but the text plainly does Y, whose reading wins — and is hunting for hidden authorial intent a mistake?
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Philosophy of Literature; Wimsatt and Beardsley, The Intentional Fallacy; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aesthetics
topics.framing_note: Higher-tier MOVE doubling as a reasoning-fallacy hook (treating the maker's stated aim as the final word on meaning). Per the negative-flag rule the ANSWER is the SUBSTANTIVE point — a work's meaning lives in the text and may outrun the author's intention — NOT the label (to context). Present intentionalism as a real rival, no verdict.

topics.name: Tolstoy: Art as the Transmission of Feeling
topics.scope: Tolstoy's rival answer to 'what is art?': not beauty, not skill, but COMMUNICATION — a boy who really felt fear meeting a wolf, telling it so vividly that listeners feel that same fear, has made art; on this test a humble folk song that genuinely passes on a feeling can be truer art than an elaborate opera that moves no one, and 'difficult' work that transmits nothing fails.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Definition of Art; Leo Tolstoy, What Is Art?; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Aesthetics
topics.framing_note: A few gems giving 'what is art?' a contrasting answer to Duchamp. Payoff = Tolstoy's real claim (art is the infectious passing of genuine feeling from maker to audience), with the wolf-story handle. Present as one serious position — note it judges art by sincerity, demoting fine-but-cold work. Choices = rival theories of art, plainly worded. No verdict; cross-ref Duchamp.

topics.name: The Meaning of Life
topics.scope: The great open question the whole bank circles: at the height of his fame Tolstoy was stopped cold by 'why live, if death erases it all?' and nearly hid the rope; Camus answered that the universe is silent but we should imagine Sisyphus, eternally rolling his boulder, HAPPY; Nagel said we're unavoidably absurd — we can step back and see nothing 'ultimately' matters — and the fitting response is gentle irony, not despair or heroics.
topics.source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Meaning of Life; Thomas Nagel, The Absurd (1971); Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus; Tolstoy, A Confession
topics.framing_note: The capstone tying the bank together — handle with WEIGHT, never glib. Lead with a human scene (Tolstoy halted at the peak of fame; Sisyphus and his boulder). CONTESTED — NO verdict; choices = real stances (meaning is made not found / Camus' defiant embrace / Nagel's ironic shrug / it comes from beyond us). Serious and hopeful, not bleak.

topics.name: Ad Hominem (Attacking the Person)
topics.scope: Attacking the arguer's character/looks/motives instead of the argument; abusive name-calling form; why a true claim from a bad person is still true; the subtle cases where character IS relevant (a witness's honesty)
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Ad Hominem); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (ad hominem); Core Knowledge critical-thinking strand
topics.framing_note: Kid-level start: a knight calls a peasant 'too ugly to be right' about the broken bridge — yet the bridge is still out. ANSWER spells the collapse: a claim's truth doesn't depend on who says it. LABEL 'ad hominem' to context. T5 nuance: attacking a liar's honesty when weighing their TESTIMONY can be fair.

topics.name: Poisoning the Well & Circumstantial Ad Hominem
topics.scope: The circumstantial form: dismissing an argument by pointing to the arguer's bias, interest, or background ('of course he says that, he's a merchant'); poisoning the well — discrediting a speaker BEFORE they speak; why a motive to say X is not proof X is false
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Circumstantial Ad Hominem / Poisoning the Well); Walton, Ad Hominem Arguments
topics.framing_note: Distinct from abusive ad hominem: the attack is on INTEREST/bias, not insults. A guildmaster warns 'don't trust the new smith's safety claim — he just wants your coin.' ANSWER: a motive to say something doesn't make it false; the claim still needs checking on its merits. Label 'poisoning the well' to context. Bias is reason to scrutinize, not dismiss.

topics.name: Tu Quoque & Whataboutism
topics.scope: 'You do it too,' so your point is void; the hypocrisy dodge; whataboutism — deflecting a charge by pointing at the accuser's faults; why a hypocrite can still be RIGHT (a smoker telling you smoking is bad); the line between fair hypocrisy-spotting and dodging the issue
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Tu Quoque); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (tu quoque); finmasters: Tu Quoque
topics.framing_note: Vivid kid handle: a parent says 'don't lie' and the child shoots back 'but YOU lied yesterday!' ANSWER: 'don't lie' is good advice whether or not the speaker follows it — the hypocrisy doesn't refute it. Label 'tu quoque / whataboutism' to context. T5: separate a fair charge of double standards from using 'you too' to dodge answering.

topics.name: The Genetic Fallacy
topics.scope: Judging a claim true or false by its ORIGIN rather than its evidence ('that idea came from a wicked king, so it's false'; 'it started as a superstition, so it can't be true now'); why a good idea can have an ugly source and a bad idea a noble one; origin as a clue vs origin as proof
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Genetic Fallacy); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Informal Logic; 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (genetic)
topics.framing_note: Cousin of ad hominem aimed at the IDEA's birthplace, not the person. A scholar rejects a map purely because 'a thief drew it.' ANSWER: where a claim came from doesn't settle whether it's true — test the map, not the mapmaker. Label 'genetic fallacy' to context. T5: a source can hint at reliability, never replace checking the claim.

topics.name: Appeal to Authority — When It's Legitimate vs. When It Fails
topics.scope: The core lesson: deferring to a REAL expert in the RIGHT field is reasonable; the fallacy is citing a false/irrelevant authority (a famous actor on medicine), treating an expert as infallible, hiding that experts are DIVIDED, or using authority to replace evidence; expertise as a heuristic, not a proof
topics.source: Athabasca University Press, Critical Thinking, Logic & Argument, Ch. 16 'Fallacies of Expertise'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Appeal to Authority); scribbr: Appeal to Authority
topics.framing_note: CRUCIAL: teach the LEGITIMATE side, not just failure. A village trusts a famous jouster on which herb cures fever. ANSWER distinguishes a real expert in the right field from a celebrity outside theirs or a question experts dispute (authority can't settle it). Label 'appeal to authority' to context. Dismissing real experts is its own error. Method neutral, no verdict.

topics.name: Appeal to the People / Bandwagon
topics.scope: 'Everyone believes it, so it must be true'; the bandwagon ('join the crowd'); appeal to popularity and to snob-appeal; why a million people can be wrong (the whole town once 'knew' the world was flat); popularity as weak evidence vs proof
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Appeal to the People / Bandwagon); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (bandwagon); Core Knowledge critical-thinking strand
topics.framing_note: Easiest kid-level entry — start T1. A merchant: 'Everyone in the market buys this charm, so it must work.' ANSWER: how many people believe a thing doesn't make it true; a crowd can be wrong together — check if the charm works. Label 'bandwagon' to context. T4: widespread EXPERT agreement is different evidence than mere popularity.

topics.name: Appeal to Emotion & Appeal to Pity
topics.scope: Stirring fear, pity, anger, or flattery so feeling replaces reasoning; the sob story that dodges the actual question (a student begging for a grade on hardship, not work done); why a feeling can be REAL and the conclusion still not follow; emotion as motive vs emotion as evidence
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Appeal to Emotion / Appeal to Pity); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (appeal to emotion); LibreTexts: Fallacies of Relevance
topics.framing_note: Kid-near: a squire pleads 'I trained SO hard and my dog is sick, so I deserve to win the tourney.' ANSWER: the hardship is real and deserves sympathy, but doesn't bear on who fought best; pity isn't a reason the conclusion is true. Label 'appeal to pity' to context. Don't teach kids to dismiss suffering; separate compassion from proof.

topics.name: Appeal to Force / Appeal to Fear
topics.scope: Backing a claim with a threat instead of a reason ('agree, or you'll be sorry'); 'might makes right' exposed; the scare tactic where fear is manufactured to win assent; why a threat can MAKE you comply but can never make the claim TRUE
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Appeal to Force / Argumentum ad Baculum); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (appeal to fear); LibreTexts: Fallacies of Relevance
topics.framing_note: Dramatic in-setting: a baron booms 'My tax is fair — question it and you'll rot in my dungeon.' ANSWER: a threat forces obedience but settles nothing about whether the tax is FAIR; fear isn't evidence. Label 'appeal to force / fear' to context. Distinguish a real warning ('touch fire and you'll burn') from a threat used to shut down argument.

topics.name: The Red Herring
topics.scope: Diverting from the real question by dragging in an irrelevant-but-juicy side issue; the topic-change dodge that 'feels' like an answer; spotting when a reply doesn't actually address what was asked; relevance as the test — does this bear on the point?
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Red Herring / Ignoratio Elenchi); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (red herring); FIU Critical Thinking notes (Red Herrings)
topics.framing_note: The name is a hook (a fish dragged across a trail to throw off hounds). Asked why the granary is empty, the steward goes on about the hard winter. ANSWER: the winter may be real but doesn't address WHERE the grain went; the question stands. Label 'red herring' to context. Test taught: does the reply bear on the point asked?

topics.name: Appeal to Ignorance
topics.scope: 'No one has DISPROVEN it, so it's true' (and the reverse — 'unproven, so false'); treating a lack of evidence as if it were evidence; who carries the burden of proof; why 'you can't prove the ghost ISN'T in the cellar' doesn't put one there
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Appeal to Ignorance / Argumentum ad Ignorantiam); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Informal Logic; 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (burden of proof)
topics.framing_note: Rounds out the set with the burden-of-proof move. A villager insists 'no one's proven the well isn't cursed, so it must be.' ANSWER: failing to disprove a claim isn't proving it; absence of evidence doesn't establish the curse, and the asserter carries the burden. Label 'appeal to ignorance' to context. T5: a thorough failed search IS weak evidence of absence.

topics.name: The Straw Man (and Steelmanning)
topics.scope: Distorting an opponent's position into a weaker version to knock it down; T1 a knight beating up a scarecrow he calls his rival; T5 the subtle exaggerate-then-refute and the VIRTUE opposite, steelmanning / the principle of charity (answer the strongest version).
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Straw Man); Your Logical Fallacy Is: Strawman; Core Knowledge critical-thinking
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = the real position was misrepresented, so the rebuttal lands on a fake target and proves nothing; 'straw man' goes to context. Teach the VIRTUE opposite at the top tiers: steelmanning means rebuilding the other side at its STRONGEST before replying. Vivid stems: a merchant, a knight, a debating scholar. No verdict on the underlying issue.

topics.name: The False Dilemma (False Dichotomy)
topics.scope: Presenting only two options when more exist; 'either you're with us or against us'; T1 'eat your vegetables or you hate me'; T5 the hidden third way, and the rare case where only two options REALLY do exhaust the field (a true dichotomy is not a fallacy).
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (False Dilemma); fallacyfiles.org: Black-or-White; Your Logical Fallacy Is: Black-or-White
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = a real third (or more) option was hidden, so being forced to pick between two is a trick, not a logical necessity; name to context. The nuance rung: a genuine either/or (a switch is on or off) is NOT a fallacy — the error is FALSELY narrowing a spectrum to two. Vivid stems: a king's ultimatum, a tavern argument.

topics.name: Begging the Question (Circular Reasoning)
topics.scope: Assuming the very thing you set out to prove; the conclusion smuggled into a premise; T1 'I'm trustworthy because I say so'; the classic 'the holy book is true because it says it's the word of a god'; T5 the long disguised circle where the question-begging premise is reworded so it hides.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Begging the Question / petitio principii); fallacyfiles.org: Begging the Question
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = the argument secretly ASSUMES what it claims to prove, so it persuades no one who doesn't already agree; 'begging the question' / 'circular' goes to context. Distinguish from a virtuous valid argument whose premises are independently supported. Use a symmetric religious example (any tradition) per the no-verdict, fair-voice rule — the LOGIC is the lesson, not the creed.

topics.name: Equivocation
topics.scope: Sliding between two meanings of one word mid-argument; T1 'a feather is light, light things glow, so a feather glows'; 'nothing is better than eternal happiness, a ham sandwich is better than nothing, so...'; T5 the subtle real-world equivocation on a loaded political word ('freedom', 'natural', 'theory') that quietly switches sense.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Equivocation); fallacyfiles.org: Equivocation; Your Logical Fallacy Is: Ambiguity
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = one word was used in TWO different senses, so the conclusion only seems to follow; 'equivocation' to context. The marquee handle is the 'light' / 'nothing' pun chains — funny and instantly clear. Top tiers: the same trick on a serious word (a 'theory' as a hunch vs a 'theory' as a tested framework). Pure logic, no verdict on the loaded term.

topics.name: The Loaded Question
topics.scope: A question with a hidden assumption you can't answer without conceding it; T1 'have you stopped cheating on your tests?' — yes OR no admits you cheated; the complex-question trap; T5 the journalist's or prosecutor's framed question that smuggles a premise, and how to refute it (reject the presupposition, don't answer).
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Complex Question / Loaded Question); fallacyfiles.org: Loaded Question; Your Logical Fallacy Is: Loaded Question
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = the question PRESUPPOSES something unproven, so any direct yes/no concedes it — the right move is to challenge the assumption itself; 'loaded question' to context. Vivid stems: a courtroom, a suspicious innkeeper, a town gossip. Note it's a fallacy of a QUESTION, not an argument — that's the interesting twist.

topics.name: No True Scotsman
topics.scope: Redefining a category on the fly to dodge a counterexample; 'no Scotsman puts sugar on his porridge' — 'my uncle does' — 'well, no TRUE Scotsman does'; T1 the porridge original; T5 the modern political/group version ('no real patriot / scientist / fan would...') that shifts the goalposts to protect a generalization.
topics.source: Antony Flew, Thinking About Thinking; fallacyfiles.org: No True Scotsman; Your Logical Fallacy Is: No True Scotsman
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = instead of admitting the counterexample, the speaker REDEFINES the word to exclude it, making the claim unfalsifiable; 'no true Scotsman' to context. Distinguish from a LEGITIMATE definition fix (sometimes a word really was used loosely) — the tell is moving the line ONLY to save face after being caught. Use Flew's actual porridge example at T1.

topics.name: The Slippery Slope (and When It's Legitimate)
topics.scope: Claiming one small step MUST cascade to disaster with no stopping point; T1 'if I let you stay up 10 minutes late you'll never sleep again'; T5 the crucial nuance — a slope argument is STRONG when each causal link is genuinely likely and FALLACIOUS when the steps are unsupported leaps; the difference IS the lesson.
topics.source: fallacyfiles.org: Slippery Slope; Wikipedia: Slippery slope; SEP: Fallacies (causal/relevance)
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = the chain only collapses to ruin if each step actually FORCES the next; if the links are merely possible, the inevitability is bluff. Name to context. CRITICAL nuance rung: NOT every slope argument is a fallacy — strength tracks how real each causal link is (the longer/looser the chain, the weaker). Teach the diagnostic, not a blanket dismissal. No policy verdict.

topics.name: The Continuum / Line-Drawing Fallacy
topics.scope: Claiming that because no SHARP line exists, a distinction is meaningless; 'one grain isn't a heap, and adding one grain never makes a heap, so heaps don't exist'; bald-man / sorites vagueness; T5 the real-world abuse ('you can't define exactly where childhood ends, so age limits are arbitrary') and why fuzzy borders don't erase real differences (day vs night, rich vs poor).
topics.source: fallacyfiles.org: Fallacy of the Heap (Sorites); IEP: Fallacies (Line-Drawing); Wikipedia: Continuum fallacy
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = a fuzzy boundary does NOT abolish a genuine distinction — a clear bald head and a full head of hair really differ even if no single hair is the cutoff; name to context. Pairs with the Sorites paradox in the metaphysics strand — cross-reference. Higher tier, abstract: keep a concrete handle (heap of sand, day vs night). The lesson is that vagueness ≠ nonexistence.

topics.name: Hasty Generalization
topics.scope: A sweeping claim drawn from too few or unrepresentative cases; T1 'one rude knight from that kingdom, so they're ALL rude'; the small-sample leap and the biased-sample leap; T5 the difference between a hasty generalization and a SOUND one (a large, representative sample really does support a general claim — the error is the LEAP, not generalizing itself).
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Hasty Generalization / Converse Accident); fallacyfiles.org: Hasty Generalization; Your Logical Fallacy Is: Hasty Generalization
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = the sample is too small or skewed to justify the sweeping conclusion, so the generalization outruns its evidence; name to context. Nuance: generalizing is NOT the fallacy — a big representative sample warrants it; the error is jumping from a handful (or a biased handful) to 'all'. Vivid stems: a traveler judging a whole land by one inn. Ties to survivorship/cherry-picking in the causal strand.

topics.name: Composition and Division
topics.scope: Assuming the WHOLE has a property because its PARTS do (composition), or each part has it because the whole does (division); T1 'each player is a star, so the team must be the best' (composition); 'the wall is heavy, so each brick is heavy' (division); T5 the subtle economic/social version (every person acting individually rational → group rationality? not necessarily).
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Composition; Division); fallacyfiles.org: Composition / Division
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = a property of the parts doesn't automatically transfer to the whole (or vice versa) — best players can make a bad team; a heavy wall can be built of light bricks. Name 'composition'/'division' to context, and KEEP them paired (they're mirror images). Top-tier handle (no warp): what's rational for one can be irrational for all together — the move, not a policy claim.

topics.name: Accident (Misapplying a General Rule)
topics.scope: Applying a sound general rule to a case it was never meant to cover; 'cutting people with knives is assault; a surgeon cuts people; so a surgeon commits assault'; 'you should always tell the truth; so tell the murderer where your friend is hiding'; T5 the recognition that good rules have justified EXCEPTIONS and rigid rule-worship is the error.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Accident); fallacyfiles.org: Accident; Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = a general rule was forced onto an exceptional case it doesn't govern, so the absurd conclusion follows from misapplication, not from the rule; 'accident' to context. The surgeon and the murderer-at-the-door (cross-ref the Kant strand) are the vivid handles. The lesson: rules have scope and legitimate exceptions; ignoring that is the fallacy. No verdict on the ethics — the LOGIC of rule-scope is the point.

topics.name: The Suppressed Correlative (and the Definist Move)
topics.scope: Redefining a term so broadly that its OPPOSITE vanishes, draining the word of meaning; 'everything is selfish — even helping others, since it makes YOU feel good' (so 'selfish' now means nothing); T5 the definist trick of redefining a word to win an argument by stipulation ('real freedom is obeying the state').
topics.source: fallacyfiles.org: Suppressed Correlative; IEP: Fallacies (Definist Fallacy); Your Logical Fallacy Is (definition abuse)
topics.framing_note: ANSWER = stretching a word to cover EVERYTHING erases the contrast that gave it meaning — if every act is 'selfish', the word no longer divides anything, so the claim is empty, not deep; name to context. Highest-tier presumption move; rare but sharp. The handle: 'if nothing can count as unselfish, calling something selfish says nothing.' A real definition must leave room for its opposite. No verdict.

topics.name: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc (After This, So Because of This)
topics.scope: Treating mere SEQUENCE as proof of cause: the rooster crows, then the sun rises, so the rooster's crowing CAUSED the dawn; the wizard waves his staff and rain falls, so the staff brought rain; why 'B came after A' is not 'A caused B'; testing a cause by seeing if removing it changes the effect
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Post Hoc); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (false cause); Core Knowledge critical-thinking strand
topics.framing_note: Easiest causal entry — start T1 with the rooster: he crows every dawn, so a boy says the rooster MAKES the sun rise. ANSWER: one thing following another doesn't make it the cause; the sun rises with no rooster. Label 'post hoc' to context. T4 test: does removing the supposed cause remove the effect?

topics.name: Correlation vs. Causation (The Lurking Third Cause)
topics.scope: Two things rise and fall together, so one must cause the other — when really a hidden THIRD thing drives both: ice-cream sales and drownings both climb in summer (the lurking cause is the heat, not the ice cream); spotting the confounding variable; correlation as a clue worth investigating vs correlation taken as proof
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (False Cause / Cum Hoc); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (false cause); Core Knowledge critical-thinking strand
topics.framing_note: Marquee handle: a town sees ice-cream sales and drownings rise together and bans ice cream. ANSWER: a hidden third cause — hot summer days — drives BOTH; ice cream drowns no one. Label 'correlation is not causation' to context. T5: a real correlation is a genuine clue to chase, not dismiss — hunt the confounder.

topics.name: Reversing Cause and Effect
topics.scope: Getting the arrow backwards — claiming A causes B when B actually causes A (or they cause each other): 'rich people own yachts, so buy a yacht to get rich'; the village sees that sick people visit the healer often and concludes the healer's visits make people sick; how to tell which way the causation really runs
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (False Cause / Wrong Direction); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (false cause); LibreTexts: Causal Fallacies
topics.framing_note: Vivid in-setting: villagers see the healer is always around the sick and conclude HER visits cause sickness — when the sick send for her. ANSWER: the arrow is flipped; sickness brings the healer, not the other way. Label 'reversing cause and effect' to context. Test: which came first, and which could exist without the other?

topics.name: Regression to the Mean (The 'Sports Illustrated Jinx')
topics.scope: Extreme results naturally drift back toward average, so the drift gets blamed on a 'cause' that did nothing: the athlete on the magazine cover after a record streak then slumps — not a jinx, just an unrepeatable peak settling down; the scolded cadet who improves and the praised one who worsens (both were outliers); luck-driven extremes don't last
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Regression); Kahneman, Thinking Fast and Slow (regression to the mean); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (false cause)
topics.framing_note: Subtler — start T3. A champion lands on the heralds' banner after a freak winning streak, then plays worse, and everyone cries 'the banner jinxed him!' ANSWER: a once-in-a-lifetime peak naturally settles toward his normal level; no jinx caused it. Label 'regression to the mean' to context. T5 twist: this fakes evidence that punishing works and praising fails.

topics.name: The Gambler's Fallacy ('Due' for a Win)
topics.scope: Believing past independent chances change the next one: a fair coin lands heads five times, so tails is now 'due' (it isn't — the coin has no memory); the dice that 'owe' you after a cold streak; why each independent trial keeps the same odds; the flip side — the hot-hand belief that a streak must continue
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Gambler's Fallacy); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (the gambler's fallacy); Core Knowledge critical-thinking strand
topics.framing_note: Clean handle: a coin lands heads five flips running, and a gambler bets the farm on tails as 'overdue.' ANSWER: a fair coin has no memory — the next flip is still 50/50; past results owe the future nothing. Label 'gambler's fallacy' to context. T5: pair with the opposite error — the belief a hot streak MUST continue.

topics.name: The Base-Rate Fallacy (Ignoring How Rare It Is)
topics.scope: Judging a positive result without weighing how RARE the thing is: a test that's 99% accurate for a disease only 1 person in 10,000 has will flag mostly HEALTHY people, because there are so many more of them; the lurking number everyone forgets is the prevalence; why a rare condition makes most 'positives' false alarms
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Base Rate); Kahneman & Tversky (base-rate neglect); Wikipedia: Base rate fallacy (medical-test example)
topics.framing_note: Marquee real-world skill — start T3 concretely. A 99%-accurate plague test flags a knight, who panics — but the plague strikes 1 in 10,000, so nearly every flag is false. ANSWER: how RARE the disease is swamps the test's accuracy; most positives are healthy. Label 'base-rate fallacy' to context. The forgotten number is the prevalence.

topics.name: Survivorship Bias (The Bullet Holes That Came Home)
topics.scope: Studying only what made it through and missing what didn't: the WWII bombers came back peppered everywhere EXCEPT the engines — so armor the engines, because the planes hit there never returned to be counted; 'these old swords lasted centuries, they don't make them like that anymore' (the weak ones broke and vanished); look for the missing data
topics.source: AMS Feature Column: The Legend of Abraham Wald; Wikipedia: Survivorship bias (Statistical Research Group, Columbia); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is'
topics.framing_note: Marquee STORY/MOVE — the WWII planes (Abraham Wald). Officers want armor where returning bombers show the most holes; Wald says armor where they show NONE — those hits downed the planes that never came back. ANSWER: you only see the survivors; the missing cases hold the lesson. Label 'survivorship bias' to context. Names allowed; the counterintuitive payoff leads.

topics.name: Cherry-Picking & Suppressed Evidence
topics.scope: Showing only the data that fits and quietly burying the rest: the seer who trumpets her three correct predictions and never mentions the thirty that flopped; the tonic-seller's wall of glowing testimonials with the failures hidden; counting the hits and ignoring the misses; demanding the WHOLE picture, not a curated slice
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Suppressed Evidence / Cherry Picking); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (cherry picking); LibreTexts: Fallacies
topics.framing_note: Vivid in-setting: a fortune-teller flaunts the three prophecies she nailed and never mentions the thirty that failed. ANSWER: counting only the hits while hiding the misses fakes a record; you need ALL the cases. Label 'cherry-picking / suppressed evidence' to context. T5: separate honest focus on relevant data from burying what cuts against you.

topics.name: The Texas Sharpshooter (Drawing the Target After You Shoot)
topics.scope: Finding a 'pattern' by picking the data AFTER the fact: the gunman fires wildly at a barn, then paints the bullseye around the tightest cluster and calls himself a crack shot; cherry-picking a cluster out of pure noise and declaring it meaningful; why a pattern you only spot in hindsight, with the target drawn to fit, proves nothing
topics.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Texas Sharpshooter); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (the Texas sharpshooter); RationalWiki: Texas sharpshooter fallacy
topics.framing_note: Lead with the scene: a man empties his musket at a barn, then paints the target around the densest cluster and brags he never misses. ANSWER: the bullseye was drawn to fit the shots; a pattern hand-picked from noise after the fact isn't a real hit. Label 'Texas sharpshooter' to context. Real prediction comes BEFORE the data.

topics.name: Misleading Averages & Statistics That Lie
topics.scope: True numbers arranged to deceive: an 'average' wealth that's huge because one dragon-rich lord lives in a village of paupers (the mean hides the typical person — the median tells the truth); the small sample dressed as proof; the percentage with no baseline ('crime up 100%!' — from one case to two); reading what a statistic actually claims
topics.source: Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Misleading Statistics); Core Knowledge critical-thinking strand
topics.framing_note: Capstone numeracy rung — start T3. A herald boasts the village's AVERAGE fortune is vast, but one dragon-hoarding lord lifts the mean while everyone else is broke. ANSWER: one outlier drags the mean; the median (the middle person) shows the typical villager is poor. Label 'misleading average' to context. T5: a percentage with no baseline ('up 100%') means little.

topics.name: Modus Ponens (the valid baseline)
topics.scope: If P then Q; P is true; therefore Q. The inference that actually follows: once you grant the rule and that the trigger fired, the result is locked in.
topics.source: IEP: Validity and Soundness; Wikipedia: Modus ponens; philosophyalevel.com: If P then Q
topics.framing_note: The valid anchor the whole strand contrasts against — teach it FIRST so the invalid twins later land. MOVE topic: a vivid rule fires (if the drawbridge is down, the knight can cross; the bridge IS down). Answer = why the conclusion is forced, not the Latin name (name to context). Ties back to Aristotle's syllogism.

topics.name: Affirming the Consequent (the sprinkler)
topics.scope: If P then Q; Q is true; therefore P — INVALID. The result happened, but something ELSE could have caused it. The famous defeater: wet grass needn't mean rain — the sprinkler.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies; FallacyFiles: Affirming the Consequent; Wikipedia: Affirming the consequent
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE invalid twin of modus ponens. The SPRINKLER is the vivid defeater — lead with the scene (the grass is wet, so it rained? not if the sprinkler ran). Answer = there are other paths to the same result, so Q doesn't pin down P; never the label (to context). At T5, the subtle real case where it masquerades as evidence.

topics.name: Denying the Antecedent
topics.scope: If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q — INVALID. The trigger didn't fire, but Q can still be true by another route. The mirror error to affirming the consequent.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies; Wikipedia: Denying the antecedent; skillfulreasoning.com: Formal Fallacies
topics.framing_note: The other invalid twin. Vivid handle: 'If you train as a knight you carry a sword; this man never trained — so he's unarmed?' (the merchant bought one anyway). Answer = the rule only tells you what P guarantees, not the only way to reach Q. Pair explicitly with affirming-the-consequent so the symmetry of the two errors is the lesson. Name to context.

topics.name: Modus Tollens (the valid contrast)
topics.scope: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P — VALID. If the promised result is absent, the trigger can't have fired. The legitimate denial that the invalid twins imitate.
topics.source: IEP: Validity and Soundness; Wikipedia: Modus tollens; philosophyalevel.com: If P then Q
topics.framing_note: The OTHER valid form — taught as the contrast that exposes denying-the-antecedent as a fake. MOVE: 'If the dragon were here the cave would be scorched; it's cold and damp — so no dragon.' Answer = why working backward from a missing result IS valid here, unlike denying the antecedent. The valid/invalid pairing is the whole point; Latin name to context.

topics.name: Converse & Inverse Errors (flipping if-then)
topics.scope: Confusing 'if A then B' with its converse 'if B then A' or its inverse 'if not A then not B'. The original promise does NOT promise the flip — 'all thumbs are fingers' isn't 'all fingers are thumbs'.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies; Wikipedia: Converse (logic); skillfulreasoning.com: Formal Fallacies
topics.framing_note: Names the SHAPE behind both invalid twins (converse = affirming consequent; inverse = denying antecedent). Vivid handle: 'every wizard wears a robe' does not make 'everyone in a robe a wizard' (the judge wears one too). Answer = a one-way rule has been silently reversed; the promise runs only A->B. Keep it concrete; the formal labels go to context.

topics.name: The Undistributed Middle
topics.scope: All A are C; all B are C; therefore all A are B — INVALID. Sharing a common category doesn't link the two: 'dogs are animals, cats are animals, so dogs are cats?'
topics.source: IEP: Categorical Syllogism; Wikipedia: Fallacy of the undistributed middle; Aristotle, Prior Analytics
topics.framing_note: Classic syllogistic error — ties straight to Aristotle's syllogism. Vivid: 'knights ride horses; bandits ride horses; so knights are bandits?' Answer = the shared middle term (animals / horse-riders) never gets fully pinned to either side, so it can't bridge them. The collapse is the lesson; the Latin name to context. Good T4 with a sneaky real-world category overlap.

topics.name: The Masked-Man Fallacy
topics.scope: You know X; you don't know the masked man is X; therefore the masked man isn't X — INVALID. What you BELIEVE about a thing can't be substituted into facts about the thing itself.
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies (Intensional); Wikipedia: Masked-man fallacy
topics.framing_note: Subtle substitution failure — keep it T4-T5. Vivid: 'I know my own brother; I don't recognize this masked knight; so this masked knight isn't my brother' (it is). Answer = facts about what someone KNOWS or doubts don't transfer to the object, so the swap is illegitimate. The reasoning, not the name (to context). A clean late-tier rung.

topics.name: The Conjunction Fallacy (Linda the activist)
topics.scope: Judging 'A and B' as more likely than 'A' alone — logically impossible, since 'A and B' is a subset of 'A'. Linda fits the feminist-bank-teller story, but that detailed combo can't beat plain bank-teller.
topics.source: Tversky & Kahneman 1983; Wikipedia: Conjunction fallacy; ScienceDirect: Conjunction Fallacy overview
topics.framing_note: MARQUEE accessible move — the LINDA case is the vivid defeater (the vivid story tempts you, but adding a detail can only narrow the odds). MOVE topic, defensible answer (settled probability, not contested). Answer = piling on a specific trait shrinks the set, so the conjunction can never be MORE probable; never the label. Representativeness/heuristic goes to context. Lead T1-base with a dice/cards version, ascend to Linda.

topics.name: Necessary vs Sufficient Conditions
topics.scope: A sufficient condition guarantees the result; a necessary one is merely required for it. Oxygen is necessary for fire but doesn't cause it; striking the match is closer to sufficient. Mixing the two breaks if-then reasoning.
topics.source: IEP: Necessary and Sufficient Conditions; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Conditionals
topics.framing_note: The concept UNDER all the conditional fallacies — naming it makes the whole strand click (affirming-consequent = treating a necessary condition as sufficient). Vivid: 'a key is needed to open the chest' (necessary) is not 'having a key opens it' (the lock could be jammed). Answer = which role the condition actually plays; the distinction is the lesson, formal terms glossed plainly in the stem.

topics.name: False Equivalence
topics.scope: treating two cases as comparable when they differ by orders of magnitude; 'both sides' flattening; the 'middle ground' / argument-to-moderation cousin where the truth is assumed to sit between two claims
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies; Bo Bennett, Logically Fallacious: False Equivalence / Argument to Moderation
topics.framing_note: VISION-RELEVANT: this is the moral_vision's named failure mode. Stem: a herald lumps a king who taxed a coin with one who razed a province as 'both abused power.' Answer = the magnitudes aren't comparable, so flattening them hides the real difference; the term to context. No verdict on which case is worse.

topics.name: The Motte-and-Bailey
topics.scope: advancing a bold, controversial claim (the bailey), then retreating to a modest, near-undeniable one (the motte) when challenged, then quietly reoccupying the bold claim once the attacker leaves
topics.source: Nicholas Shackel, 'The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology' (2005); Scott Alexander, Slate Star Codex (2014)
topics.framing_note: Marquee subtle trap, skews T4-T5. Scene: a merchant defends a wild claim, gets cornered, swaps to a safe truism, then slides back to the wild claim. Answer = one word covered two different claims and the easy one shielded the hard one; 'motte-and-bailey' to context. Castle image only to make it concrete, not to memorize.

topics.name: The Isolated Demand for Rigor
topics.scope: applying sky-high standards of proof to a claim you dislike while waving your own side's claims through; the selective, one-directional skepticism that masquerades as carefulness
topics.source: Scott Alexander, 'The Isolated Demand for Rigor' (Slate Star Codex, 2014); IEP: Fallacies (special pleading family)
topics.framing_note: Subtle T4-T5 trap, pairs with special pleading. Scene: a councilor demands a rival's plan be proven beyond all doubt, then accepts his ally's plan on a hunch. Answer = the standard of proof was switched depending on whose claim it was, so the 'rigor' is a weapon; name to context. Method stays neutral on which plan is right.

topics.name: Relative Privation
topics.scope: 'worse things exist, so this doesn't matter' / 'children are starving, so stop complaining about X'; dismissing a real problem by pointing to a bigger one elsewhere; the appeal to worse problems
topics.source: Bo Bennett, Logically Fallacious: Relative Privation / 'Not as Bad as'; IEP: Fallacies
topics.framing_note: Accessible, kid-reachable trap. Scene: a squire says his blade is dull and a knight snaps 'soldiers are dying, who cares about your sword?' Answer = a bigger problem existing somewhere doesn't make a smaller one false or unworthy of fixing; both can be real. Term to context. Note the honest cousin lightly: triage really does prioritize.

topics.name: The Gish Gallop
topics.scope: burying an opponent under a flood of many weak or false claims faster than any one can be answered, then declaring victory because most went unrebutted; quantity-over-quality as a debate tactic
topics.source: RationalWiki: Gish Gallop (named for Duane Gish); Bo Bennett, Logically Fallacious
topics.framing_note: Subtle media-age trap, T4-T5. Scene: a debater fires twenty shaky charges in one breath, and the crowd thinks the side that 'said more' won. Answer = leaving a claim unanswered for lack of time doesn't make it true; volume isn't evidence. Name to context. The skill is seeing the firehose IS the trick.

topics.name: Confirmation Bias
topics.scope: the pull to notice, seek, and remember only what fits what you already believe, and to explain away what doesn't; cherry-picking your own evidence without meaning to; why seeking disconfirming cases is the corrective
topics.source: Wikipedia: List of Cognitive Biases (confirmation bias); HKU Philosophy [F08] Cognitive Biases
topics.framing_note: Foundational bias, deep ladder. Scene: an alchemist counts every time his potion 'worked' and forgets every time it didn't, so he's sure of it. Answer = a belief that only collects supporting cases was never tested; the cure is hunting the case that would prove you wrong. Name to context. Ties to Popper and Bacon's Idols — note in context.

topics.name: Anchoring
topics.scope: the first number or framing you meet drags your judgment toward it, even when it's arbitrary or irrelevant; how an opening price, estimate, or label sets the goalposts for everything that follows
topics.source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), anchoring-and-adjustment; Wikipedia: List of Cognitive Biases
topics.framing_note: Concrete, market-flavored bias. Scene: a trader opens at an absurd price for a relic, and every later 'bargain' is judged against that made-up number. Answer = the first figure was arbitrary, so letting it set the scale corrupts the comparison; ask what the thing is worth on its own. Name to context. Vivid handle: the haggle.

topics.name: The Appeal to Nature
topics.scope: 'it's natural, therefore good' and its mirror 'it's unnatural/artificial, therefore bad'; the unexamined leap from how-things-occur to how-things-ought-to-be; why 'natural' settles nothing about safe, right, or wholesome
topics.source: Bo Bennett, Logically Fallacious: Appeal to Nature; IEP: Fallacies; ties to Hume's is-ought gap
topics.framing_note: Accessible everyday trap. Scene: a hedge-witch swears her root cure is safe 'because it grows in the ground' — but hemlock grows there too. Answer = natural doesn't mean good or safe, and made-by-hands doesn't mean bad; 'natural' is not a verdict. Name to context. This is Hume's is-ought gap in folk costume — cross-reference. No verdict on any remedy.

topics.name: Appeal to Tradition vs. Appeal to Novelty
topics.scope: the paired errors: 'we've always done it this way, so it's right' versus 'it's the new way, so it's better'; age and newness are both irrelevant to truth; when continuity or innovation IS a real reason and when it's just a slogan
topics.source: IEP: Fallacies; Bo Bennett, Logically Fallacious: Appeal to Tradition / Appeal to Novelty
topics.framing_note: Pair-taught; mild vision relevance (Burkean caution is a real argument, not the fallacy). An elder defends a rite by age alone; a reformer praises a scheme by newness alone. Answer = neither age nor novelty makes a claim true. Nuance: 'survived centuries' or 'fixes a known flaw' CAN be evidence — the error is the slogan REPLACING the reason.

topics.name: The Fallacy Fallacy
topics.scope: 'your argument has a flaw, therefore your conclusion is false' — but a bad argument FOR a claim leaves the claim's truth wide open; the difference between refuting an argument and refuting a conclusion
topics.source: 'Your Logical Fallacy Is': The Fallacy Fallacy (argumentum ad logicam); IEP: Fallacies
topics.framing_note: Subtle self-referential capstone — the meta-move guarding the whole fallacy ladder, T4-T5. Scene: a knight wins on a sloppy reason, so his rival crows 'then the opposite is true!' Answer = a broken argument sinks only that argument, not the conclusion, which may still be true for other reasons. Name to context. Antidote to weaponizing the fallacy list.

topics.name: The Backfire Effect & Motivated Reasoning
topics.scope: reasoning backward from the conclusion you WANT to be true, marshaling arguments like a lawyer for a verdict already chosen; why being smarter can make you better at defending what you already believe, not better at being right
topics.source: Wikipedia: List of Cognitive Biases (motivated reasoning); Ziva Kunda, 'The Case for Motivated Reasoning' (1990)
topics.framing_note: Subtle T5 self-awareness bias, the humbling one. Scene: a scholar who wants a prophecy true finds 'proof' everywhere and excuses every counter-sign. Answer = conclusion fixed first, reasons hired after = defense, not inquiry; cleverness just builds a better defense. Name to context. Aims inward — suspect your OWN motives when a conclusion feels too welcome.

topics.name: Occam's Razor — Used Rightly
topics.scope: VIRTUE: prefer the simplest explanation that ADEQUATELY fits the evidence — don't multiply assumptions beyond need; and the discipline of using it as a tie-breaker, NOT a bludgeon to dodge real complexity or wave away genuine evidence
topics.source: William of Ockham (lex parsimoniae); SEP: Simplicity; IEP: Fallacies (contrast with oversimplification)
topics.framing_note: POSITIVE COUNTERWEIGHT — one of two closing virtues; strong rungs. Hoofbeats at the keep: a stray horse needs fewer assumptions than a unicorn, so it's the better first bet. Answer = on the SAME evidence, fewest leaps wins. CRITICAL nuance: 'simplest' means fewest unsupported assumptions, NOT 'the answer I like' or ignoring inconvenient facts.

topics.name: Steelmanning & the Principle of Charity
topics.scope: VIRTUE and the cap of the whole reasoning ladder: answer the STRONGEST, most reasonable version of the other side — the opposite of the straw man; read an unclear claim in its best plausible light; why beating a steelman is the only victory that proves anything
topics.source: principle of charity (Quine/Davidson); 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (steelman as anti-straw-man)
topics.framing_note: THE CAPSTONE VIRTUE — the bank's positive answer to a strand of errors; strongest closing rungs. Rather than mock a foe's weakest phrasing, a councilor restates the foe's case so well the foe says 'yes, exactly,' THEN answers it. Answer = beating the strongest version is the only win that proves anything. Direct mirror of the straw man (strand 33).
